Title: One count, three processes: Rethinking administrative stability in Korea's fuel-cell and renewable licensing pipeline
Abstract: Administrative amendment counts conflate recurrent filings, schedule revisions, and changes in project ownership or specification. Title: Registered Report - Stage II: Do good, feel luckier: How cause-related marketing in unpredictable tourism products boosts tourists’ purchase intention?
Abstract: Marketing unpredictable tourism experiences like aurora or wildlife viewing poses distinct challenges due to their inherent uncertainty, yet research on effective strategies remains limited. In Stage I of this Registered Report, we proposed that cause-related marketing (CRM) would boost purchase intention for unpredictable tourism products more effectively than traditional discounts by activating a karmic investment mechanism (i.e., self-luck expectancy), especially under consumer-focused framing. Although a moderating influence of protagonist focus was observed, its effect contradicted our hypothesis. However, an unexpected finding emerged: luck primes significantly elevate self-luck expectancy and enhance purchase intention. These results suggest that practitioners should either exercise caution in deploying standard CRM from a cost-benefit perspective or enhance its utility by fostering deeper consumer moral engagement. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: From expectations to experience: How tasting plant-based fermented foods shapes consumption intentions

Title: Discrete Gauss linking integral representations of correlation trajectories for market stress diagnosis
Abstract: Market stress is commonly characterized using contemporaneous correlation levels or other low-dimensional summaries of market dependence, potentially discarding information contained in the ordered evolution of correlation states. Title: Shared but feared: A vulnerability-sensitive account of consumer responses to post-crisis service environments
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Shared service environments are typically designed to facilitate comfort, efficiency, and positive consumer experiences. In post-crisis contexts, however, these environments may also be appraised through concerns about exposure, controllability, and personal vulnerability. Building on a context-specific refinement of the organismic component within the Stimulus–Organism–Response framework, this research examines how residual infection-related fear is associated with consumer responses to shared service environments in a post-pandemic context. A two-study design was implemented within a single French-language survey (N = 425). Study 1 tested whether residual infection-related fear was associated with avoidance of public service environments through differentiated forms of health anxiety. Structural equation modeling showed that residual infection-related fear was positively associated with both personal and interpersonal health anxiety, but only personal health anxiety was associated with avoidance, yielding a significant indirect effect through the self-focused pathway. Study 2 experimentally manipulated store density (high vs. low) and sanitary signals (present vs. absent) to examine how servicescape cues influenced perceived crowding and shopping satisfaction. Results showed that higher density reduced satisfaction, but this negative effect was attenuated when sanitary signals were present. Perceived crowding did not mediate the density–satisfaction relationship. A separate exploratory analysis indicated that the overall association between sanitary signals and satisfaction was more positive among individuals reporting higher residual infection-related fear. Title: When perception meets reality: explaining measured food waste through consumer behavior in a university dining hall
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Food waste (FW) in university dining halls generates significant environmental and economic impacts, yet most studies rely on self-reported measures and rarely combine behavioral perceptions with objective waste data. This study investigates the determinants of consumer FW by integrating individual plate-waste measurements with behavioral and dining-related factors in a university dining hall setting. Data were collected from 422 diners using a 31-item questionnaire, along with individual measurements of avoidable plate waste after meals. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) and Kruskal–Wallis tests were applied to examine behavioral relationships and differences across demographic and meal-related groups. Average plate waste reached 51.5 g per person, with higher waste levels observed during lunch and among female diners. Self-perceived waste behavior, intention to reduce FW, and sensory satisfaction were directly associated with the measured amount of discarded food. In contrast, consumer knowledge, portion size perception, and available eating time influenced only perceived waste behavior, revealing a disconnect between awareness and objectively measured PW. The findings highlight the importance of dining context and meal satisfaction in shaping consumer FW and demonstrate the value of integrating subjective perceptions with objective waste measurements. By combining behavioral evidence with direct waste quantification, this study advances methodological approaches to consumer FW research and provides insights for designing more effective waste reduction strategies in institutional food services. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Using emojis to uplift emotion: Effects on mental health chatbots’ performance
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: As AI-based chatbots increasingly expand access to mental health support, understanding how text-based systems convey emotional attentiveness without face-to-face nonverbal cues is important. Emojis may serve as lightweight paralinguistic cues, yet their effects in mental health support remain unclear. Drawing on the Stereotype Content Model and psychological ownership theory, this study examines associations between emoji use and users’ emotional well-being, satisfaction, and continuance usage intention. Two scenario-based online experiments were conducted in China using random sampling through Credamo, yielding 459 valid responses (59 in the pretest and 400 in the main study). Data were analyzed using IBM SPSS Statistics 26 and the PROCESS macro. Across the experiments, emoji use was associated with more favorable emotional well-being, satisfaction, and continuance usage intention. Mediation analyses supported an indirect pathway through perceived warmth and psychological ownership, whereas the corresponding competence-based pathway was not supported. AI literacy strengthened the perceived warmth–psychological ownership association but, contrary to predictions, weakened the perceived competence–psychological ownership association. Moderated mediation analyses provided preliminary support for AI literacy strengthening the warmth-based indirect effects of emoji use on emotional well-being and continuance usage intention. The corresponding effect on satisfaction was not supported. These findings extend research on AI-mediated mental health support by identifying a warmth–psychological ownership pathway and the differentiated role of AI literacy. Title: Professional identity as the missing link: Understanding motivational pathways among hotel employees
Abstract: Hospitality research has often viewed motivation as the primary mechanism linking managerial practices to employee behavior. However, less attention has been paid to how employees interpret such practices before motivational responses emerge. Drawing on professional identity research, this study examines Professional Identity as an interpretive mechanism linking employees’ perceptions of Rewards and Transformational Leadership to Motivation and Organizational Citizenship Behavior (OCB). Using survey data from 325 frontline hotel employees in South Korea, we test an individual-level model connecting Developmental Rewards, Material Rewards, Transformational Leadership, Professional Identity, Intrinsic Motivation, Extrinsic Motivation, and OCB. The results show significant indirect associations between Developmental Rewards and Intrinsic Motivation and between Transformational Leadership and Intrinsic Motivation through Professional Identity. Developmental Rewards and Transformational Leadership were also indirectly associated with OCB through Professional Identity and Intrinsic Motivation. In contrast, the hypothesized Material Rewards pathways through Professional Identity and Extrinsic Motivation were not supported. These findings extend hospitality motivation research by highlighting the importance of identity-affirming managerial practices in frontline service settings. © 2026

Title: Tourism's temporal pathways: A deceleration framework
Abstract: This research introduces Tourism Deceleration as a theoretically grounded framework for understanding temporal recalibration in tourism. Building on social acceleration theory and consumer deceleration framework, we conceptualize tourism deceleration as a situated temporal negotiation through which travelers recalibrate pace, attention, mobility, digital connectivity, and presence. Using hybrid deductive-inductive qualitative content analysis supported by LLM-assisted coding and human validation, we analyze 367 unique Reddit posts and 21,554 comments related to slow travel and long-term travel. The findings show that decelerated travel is often negotiated through practical, social, and personal constraints rather than simply chosen as a preferred travel style. Episodic deceleration remains the most explicit form of decelerated travel, while extended duration often intersects with embodied practices, reduced mobility pressure, and selective negotiation of digital technologies. The research note contributes by distinguishing tourism deceleration from slow tourism and explaining how travelers manage time under conditions of choice, context, and constraint. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Terrorism and altruistic giving: Evidence from child sponsorship
Abstract: We study how terrorist attacks targeting educational institutions affect private development aid through child sponsorship. Conceptually, terrorist events may increase sponsorship by signaling greater need or reduce it if affected communities are seen as less effective destinations to support. We combine global administrative data from Plan International on child sponsorship across 50 countries over the 2008-2018 period, aggregated at the Primary Sampling Unit (PSU) level, with geocoded terrorism events from the Global Terrorism Database. Our core specification focuses on attacks against educational institutions within 20 km of each PSU. We estimate the causal effect using a heterogeneity-robust difference-in-differences approach suited to staggered, non-absorbing treatments. We find that attacks on educational institutions reduce the share of sponsored children by about 3 percentage points, a 4 percent decline relative to the mean. Back-of-the-envelope calculations suggest this corresponds to funding losses of approximately US$615,000 across affected communities over the study period. Since sponsorship is geographically targeted, these losses fall on the specific communities, underscoring the need to buffer local development funding against security shocks. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Optimal reinsurance, investment and dividend strategies with square-root factor model
Source title: Journal of Mathematical Analysis and Applications
Abstract: This paper studies the optimal reinsurance, investment and dividend strategies for an insurer who aims to maximize the expected discounted utility of dividend payments together with a discounted terminal value at ruin. The insurer can invest in a risky asset with price dynamics given by a square-root process, which includes the CEV, Heston and 4/2 models as special cases. We consider two types of instantaneous dividend utilities: exponential and logarithmic functions. The problem is formulated as a stochastic control problem with double stochastic state processes and nonlinear optimization objectives. Using dynamic programming, we derive the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equations with nonlinear gradient components and provide analytical solutions for optimal strategies under both utilities. Our results show that the square-root factor process significantly influences the optimal policies, specially for the optimal investment. We also conduct numerical analyses under the 4/2 model to illustrate the impact of various parameters on optimal strategies. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: The evolving science of negotiation alternatives: New contexts, new perspectives
Abstract: We review the past decade (2016 – present) of empirical research on negotiation alternatives across multiple disciplines, including dyadic bargaining, international trade, and civil conflict interventions. Three themes emerged in our analysis: First, research has focused on how the effects of a negotiator's BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) are not person-invariant but are instead moderated by the characteristics of the party who “holds” the BATNA. Second, studies are establishing the conditions under which negotiation alternatives can backfire and hurt a negotiator's performance. Third, an emerging stream of research challenges our conventional understanding of BATNA by highlighting its perceptual nature and the possibility that it may exist on multiple levels within a given negotiation. We close by outlining future directions for each of these emerging themes. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Wu J.; Chen H.; Long R.
Title: Exploring the evolution of public cognition toward generative AI through sentiment-topic mining and community detection in social graphs
Abstract: The swift advancement of Generative AI(GAI) improves content production efficiency and generates commercial value, yet it presents complex governance issues, including misinformation and technological misuse. To investigate the cognitive evolution of the public and the characteristics of the online opinion ecosystem regarding GAI, this study collected 105,384 GAI-related posts and comments from Sina Weibo between 2023 and 2026. A semantic-topological social graph(ST-Graph) was constructed from textual semantics, engagement feedback, and user profile features, and a Contrastive Learning-based Graph Neural Network(ConGNN) was employed for node representation learning and community detection. Additionally, StructBERT-based sentiment classification was combined with DeepSeek-based key attribute and trigger-word extraction to analyze emotional orientations and cognitive focuses across communities. Experimental findings indicate that ConGNN achieved the highest Silhouette, ARI, and NMI values among the compared methods, while the yearly community partitions yielded Silhouette coefficients ranging from 0.4002 to 0.4476. These results indicate relatively clear separation in the learned representation space and consistent clustering under the evaluated settings, supporting the effectiveness of ConGNN for the constructed ST-Graph. Sentiment analysis shows that public attitudes toward GAI are generally positive, but vary across publishing entities. Public figures garner the greatest number of remarks, with positive feedback from Enterprises constituting the predominant share(49.3%). Government mainly garner neutral feedback(70.9%), however Media and Organizations/Institutions observe a greater share of negative remarks(38.9% and 41.2%). Aspect-level analysis further indicates that public cognition is shifting from early technological expectations and substitution anxiety toward institutional concerns, especially demands for anti-counterfeiting, content credibility, and digital governance mechanisms. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Nodding of virtual humans does not necessarily increase customer trust: a temporal analysis
Abstract: Virtual humans can potentially facilitate engaging customer interactions, but remain rarely used in customer service. Their embodiment enables virtual humans to use non-verbal listening cues like nodding. Nodding is theorized to increase trust in virtual humans, but literature on this effect is scarce, inconsistent, and only uses measurements after interactions. This study therefore aims to research how nodding of virtual humans influences customer trust, by (1) studying the following hypothesized mediation: nodding (social cue) triggers perceived responsiveness (social signal), which subsequently increases trust (social response); and (2) studying temporal trust dynamics within a customer interaction using exploratory analyses. An online experiment (N = 429) was performed, using a between-subjects design with two conditions: a virtual human either nodded during listening or did not. To isolate nodding optimally, participants watched a video of a customer interaction: a virtual human advised a customer on a wardrobe. While watching, participants used a slider scale to keep updating their temporal trust in the virtual human. Afterwards, participants answered questionnaires on trust and perceived responsiveness. Results showed that nodding did not increase trust or perceived responsiveness, nor did nodding build temporal trust. Temporal trust was built throughout the customer interaction, mostly when the virtual human was speaking. Exploratory analysis found that nodding increased anthropomorphism. Possibly, nodding did not influence trust because other social cues already caused trust-building. Virtual human developers should therefore be aware that nodding does not necessarily build customer trust. The temporal trust scale was useful for visualizing trust-building throughout customer interaction videos. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Qualitative Versus Quantitative Risk Assessment in Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) Audits: How European-Based Auditors Interpret Probability Under International Council for Harmonisation Guideline (ICH) Q9 (R1)
Abstract: Purpose: Under ICH Q9 (R1), risk is defined as a function of probability and severity of harm. Although probability may be expressed quantitatively, little empirical evidence exists regarding how EU GMP auditors assess probability in practice. This study explored probability assessment approaches among auditors and the use of qualitative and quantitative methods. Methods: A descriptive cross-sectional questionnaire was administered to 52 EU-based GMP auditors with at least two years of auditing experience. Participants (21 in total) completed structured multiple-response questions on probability and optional free-text comment fields addressing probability assessment practices (response rate: 40.4%). Data were analysed using descriptive statistics and cross-tabulation; no inferential analyses were performed. Results: Qualitative probability assessment approaches were the most frequently reported method (14/21), while 8/21 respondents reported using quantitative approaches (multiple responses permitted). Probability assessment was commonly described as context-dependent and informed by professional judgement rather than purely numerical models. Qualitative approaches were reported across all experience categories and levels of English proficiency. Participants highlighted limited availability of robust historical data, contextual complexity, and reliance on prior audit experience as key factors influencing probability assessment. Respondents (4/21) suggested that no single clear definition of probability assessment was consistently applied in practice. Conclusion: Although some participants reported using quantitative approaches, probability assessment remained predominantly qualitative and experience-based in audits. Participants frequently described using structured risk matrices and categorical probability scales (e.g., High/Medium/Low) to support probability assessments. The findings highlight variability in how probability is operationalised and suggest that additional practical guidance may be useful. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Building sustainable influencer partnerships within the creator economy
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Influencer marketing has become an integral part of retail branding strategies. As the creator economy continues to expand, influencer collaborations are now viewed as strategic partnerships rather than promotional activities. Despite this transition, sustaining authentic and long-term brand-influencer partnerships remains a significant yet underexplored challenge. Combining Social Exchange Theory (SET) and Self-Determination Theory (SDT) into a unified motivational-exchange framework, this research focuses on how brand practices operate simultaneously as relational exchange resources and as psychological need-satisfying inputs within influencer–brand partnerships. With a mixed-methods two-phase approach, this study exmains how brand ethical–purpose alignment, autonomy support, and AI co-creation are linked to influencers' sense of ownership and thriving, as well as citizenship behaviours and partnership continuity. In Study 1, 22 semi-structured interviews were conducted with professional influencers across four regions, intended to understand their lived partnership experiences. In Study 2, responses from 422 influencers were analysed using structural equation modelling and moderation analysis. The study also examines serial indirect pathways through which brand practices are associated with voluntary citizenship behaviours and partnership continuity via Collaboration Ownership and Influencer Thriving. The findings suggest that autonomy support, purpose alignment, and AI co-creation enablement are positively associated with influencers' ownership and thriving. These again are associated with higher levels of voluntary advocacy and intentions to continue partnerships. Therefore, the research positions influencer collaboration as relational rather than transactional and highlights the significance of autonomy, ethical-purpose congruence, and relational fairness in understanding sustainable relationships between influencers and brands. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Why skilled migrants stay or leave host countries: A belongingness theory perspective
Abstract: While skilled migrants have a high propensity to quit their jobs and leave host countries, little is known about why some skilled migrants leave while others stay. This paper draws on belongingness theory to examine the mediated effects of work and non-work sense of belonging between skilled migrants’ local language proficiency and host country exit, and the moderated effects of work and non-work social support from locals between local language proficiency and both belonging types. Regression analyses of time-lagged, multisource data collected from 159 foreign academics in Japan suggest that local language proficiency was positively related to work sense of belonging, which was subsequently negatively related to host country exit. Furthermore, the positive relationship between local language proficiency and work sense of belonging was stronger when work and non-work social support were high. This paper contributes to the literature by providing a novel perspective on skilled migrants’ host country experiences, shifting the focus from withdrawal cognitions to belongingness and host country exit, and integrating language proficiency into the theory of belongingness. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: The impact of consumer culture positioning on multinational brand premium: The moderating role of global identity
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Multinational brands often charge higher prices in emerging markets than in their home markets. Although such multinational brand premiums can improve profitability, they may also invite consumers to compare prices across countries and evaluate the premium as unfair. This research examines how consumer culture positioning (CCP) shapes consumers' willingness to pay a multinational brand premium through price fairness perceptions, operationalized as perceived price unfairness, and how this process depends on consumers' global identity. Across a pretest and three experiments in China, we compare Global Consumer Culture Positioning (GCCP) with Local Consumer Culture Positioning (LCCP) in a multinational restaurant-brand context. Experiment 1 establishes the main effect of CCP and the mediating role of perceived price unfairness. Experiment 2 replicates this pathway and examines chronic global identity as a boundary condition. Experiment 3 further tests the moderation through situationally activated global versus local identity. The results generally show that GCCP, relative to LCCP, reduces perceived price unfairness and increases willingness to pay a premium. The fairness-based indirect effect becomes stronger as chronic global identity increases and when global identity is situationally activated. The findings integrate global branding and pricing research by showing when cultural positioning can make a higher price appear more acceptable rather than merely enhance brand image. The study also provides managerial implications for multinational and local brands operating in emerging retail and service markets. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Li S.; Li X.; Du X.; Xin Z.
Title: How local–global identity shapes physical-digital preferences through convenience preference
Abstract: Despite the functional advantages of digital products, consumers’ preferences between digital and physical formats remain highly heterogeneous in a marketplace where globalization and renewed localism coexist. Drawing on identity-based motivation theory, this research examines how local versus global identity influences consumers' preferences for physical versus digital products through convenience preference. Across three studies (five sub-studies), we demonstrate that a relatively stronger local-over-global identity is associated with greater preference for physical over digital consumption formats. Further analyses reveal an asymmetric effect that local identity drives stronger preferences for physical products, whereas global identity does not produce a corresponding increase in preference for digital formats. We further identify convenience preference as the underlying mechanism, showing that stronger local identity reduces convenience preference, thereby increasing preference for physical products. These findings reconceptualize physical versus digital preferences as identity-consistent choices rather than purely functional evaluations. By identifying convenience as an identity-contingent motivational preference, this research advances identity-based motivation theory and provides timely insights into how identity orientations shape consumer preferences amid ongoing digital transformation and heightened societal attention to globalization–localism dynamics. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Geopolitical risk and tourism firm resilience: Global evidence
Abstract: This paper analyzes how geopolitical risk affects the performance of tourism firms and identifies the conditions under which its adverse effects are mitigated. Using a global panel of 1438 firms across 39 countries from 2007 to 2021, we find that heightened geopolitical risk significantly reduces firms’ market valuations. Drawing on risk perception theory, network theory, and institutional theory, we show that this effect is conditional rather than uniform. Specifically, firms located in countries with stronger international tourism network embeddedness experience weaker negative effects, as network connectivity facilitates demand diversification and adaptive responses. Similarly, higher institutional quality reduces the adverse impact of geopolitical risk by enhancing stability and policy credibility. These findings are robust to alternative measures and estimation methods. Title: Beyond wear scar diameter: A multi-technique investigation of lubricity enhancement and tribofilm formation in biodiesel blends with ultra-low sulphur diesel and bio-hydrogenated diesel
Abstract: Bio-hydrogenated diesel (BHD) and ultra-low sulphur diesel both exhibit poor intrinsic lubricity owing to the absence of polar functional groups. Addition of 2% v/v biodiesel restored compliance in all blend systems, yet film formation data, wear depth profiles, and ATR-FTIR analysis collectively suggested that this concentration does not sustain reliable surface protection, with intermittent film breakdown and peripheral wear debris deposits persisting throughout the test. A minimum of 5% v/v was required for stable film formation, and 10% v/v for effective suppression of disc material loss. At 2% v/v, SBME produced a significantly lower wear scar diameter than PME in the diesel system (p = 0.001), consistent with earlier and more persistent ester tribofilm formation confirmed by ATR-FTIR, while no statistically significant difference was observed in the BHD system (p = 0.072). Title: Imperfection in motion: Implied motion reduces negative associations of imperfect produce
Abstract: Food waste remains a major sustainability challenge, with imperfect fruits and vegetables often rejected due to their appearance. Prior studies suggest that food choices are mostly automatic, implicit, and habitual, rather than made through deliberated choice. Such insights suggest why explicit messaging to increase consumers' imperfect food purchasing has shown limited effectiveness and highlight opportunities for behaviour change via less mindful means. This study investigates the extent to which negative implicit associations for “imperfect” (vs. “perfect”) exist, and whether implied motion (e.g., fruit splashing into water) can mitigate these evaluations. In a pre-registered study, participants (N = 145) completed an in-person multi-dimensional Implicit Association Test (IAT) to examine their implicit attitudes in static and motion contexts. Results showed that participants' implicit associations were positive for perfect produce and negative for imperfect produce, suggesting an “Ugly = Bad” association. However, exposure to implied motion imagery significantly reduced this negativity effect toward imperfect fresh produce, while having no significant effect on perfect produce. Our findings link implicit attitudes to sustainable food acceptance and demonstrate the potential of visually-based interventions, such as implied motion, to reduce negative aesthetic biases and support behaviour change aimed at increasing acceptance of imperfect produce and reducing food waste. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Examining the layered veil of pay transparency: Implications for perceived ambiguity, sensemaking, and negotiation
Abstract: In the last decade, pay transparency—making pay information more accessible and understandable—has become a defining workplace reform. We examine the common assumption that pay transparency reduces pay disparities by improving negotiation outcomes. Our cross-disciplinary review suggests that pay transparency's effects on negotiation hinge on three factors: (1) how transparency is operationalized (i.e., what type of pay information is shared); (2) how people interpret the information provided; and (3) whether transparency alone can motivate and equip individuals to leverage that information to negotiate effectively. Title: Predicting the future of retail services: Trends, technologies, and strategic imperatives for 2025–2035
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: The rapid convergence of digital platforms and shifting consumer behaviors is driving an unprecedented structural transformation across the global retail landscape. This paper examines the systemic evolution of retail channel revenue distributions and operational capabilities, establishing the critical strategic imperatives required to navigate market disruption over the 2025–2035 horizons. The primary objective of this study is to empirically model the longitudinal shifts between traditional physical retail, e-commerce, and physical channels, while concurrently diagnosing the capability gaps across diverse corporate scales. Methodologically, this research deploys a mixed-methods empirical framework, integrating a quantitative survey of 418 retail industry professionals with qualitative interviews from 32 senior executives across six countries, analyzed using Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) and Two-Way Repeated Measures ANOVA. The empirical findings reveal a definitive market polarization: traditional physical retail is projected to contract significantly from 54.3% to 30.8%, while e-commerce expands to claim a dominant 52.7% revenue share by 2035. Our multi-method analysis validates that digital-physical integration and AI-driven personalization (β = 0.38, p < .001) directly resolve post-pandemic operational vulnerabilities, emerging as the primary drivers of future performance outcomes. Longitudinal analysis confirms a steady decline in traditional commodity metrics, while scenario simulations warn that small and medium-sized enterprises face a severe (66.5%) market share loss under unmitigated polarization. To address this structural market polarization, this study provides a rigorous, data-driven defense by establishing the Retail Evolution Framework (REF) to explain how systemic retail survival requires aligning operational tools with shifting institutional norms. The study bridges the dynamic capabilities gap under the Resource-Based View while offering actionable strategies for ethical data governance. Practically, these insights provide an actionable investment roadmap for corporate managers to redirect capital allocations from physical footprint expansion into automated data ecosystems and cloud-based logistics architectures to maintain long-term competitive viability. © 2026

Title: How homophily and sociality propensity influence stakeholder diversity in wildfire risk management networks: an ERGM analysis
Abstract: Recent wildfire management strategies emphasize stakeholder engagement in risk management and prevention as a means of enhancing systemic safety and operational reliability. Despite its growing importance, guidance on how to effectively implement such engagement remains limited. This study addresses this gap by combining Social Network Analysis (SNA) and Exponential Random Graph Models (ERGMs) to examine a sample of 256 stakeholders across seven wildfire management networks in different European countries. The objective is to identify the propensity of stakeholders to form ties, network diversity and structural dependency within wildfire risk management networks. The results make two key contributions to risk and resilience in crisis and emergency management body of knowledge. First, we show that sociality – the propensity of stakeholders to establish connections – is shaped by stakeholder profiles. Second, we find that homophily – the propensity of stakeholders to connect with similar others – emerges across multiple categories alongside structural network effects. We discuss the dual role of these mechanisms that facilitate engagement while simultaneously constraining the diversity of stakeholder types. Title: Survival of Contractor Consortiums in the Road Construction Industry during Economic Crisis
Source title: Journal of Legal Affairs and Dispute Resolution in Engineering and Construction
Abstract: Road construction industries worldwide are periodically exposed to economic crises, which are cyclical in nature and often characterized by high inflation, currency depreciation, resource shortages, and institutional inefficiencies. In such conditions, traditional procurement methods frequently struggle to maintain project continuity, prompting the emergence of local contractor consortiums as a more resilient alternative. This study examines how contractor consortiums in the road construction sector adapted to recent economic crises and sustained operations amid unprecedented challenges. A qualitative research approach was adopted, involving 14 semistructured interviews with industry experts. Manual content analysis identified key adaptive measures, including financial pooling, shared equipment and labor, agile internal coordination, and proactive engagement with public authorities. These mechanisms enabled many consortiums to continue project delivery despite severe economic and operational constraints. However, the effectiveness of these measures was constrained by rigid legal and contractual frameworks, limited digital integration, fragmented stakeholder collaboration, and delayed institutional responses. To enhance future resilience, the study recommends modernizing contractual systems, strengthening digital adoption, and improving public-private coordination. Title: Institutional resilience and land-acquisition governance: Participation and conflict-management mechanisms in the Jakarta–Bandung High-Speed Railway project

Title: Perceived control and stress reactivity in algorithm-supported hiring decisions

Title: Models for risk management in the procurement process within organizational contexts: A systematic literature review
Abstract: Over the past decade, supply chain management has faced extreme volatility, culminating in the unprecedented disruptions of the COVID-19 pandemic. Consequently, resilience in procurement has transitioned from a secondary attribute to an indispensable requirement for operational continuity. This study classifies the state of the art in procurement risk management within the post-pandemic landscape (2021–2025). It analyzes the transition from reactive approaches toward predictive and prescriptive perspectives to address supply chain volatility. A Systematic Literature Review (SLR) was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 protocol. Based on a structured search in the Scopus and Web of Science databases, an initial pool of 1,109 records was screened. This resulted in a final sample of 107 high-impact peer-reviewed articles. These studies were evaluated using thematic content analysis and classified into ten technical categories based on their functional orientation. The evidence reveals a fragmented methodological ecosystem where Hybrid Models (21.5%) and Multi-Criteria Decision Making (MCDM, 16.8%) techniques predominate. A shift is observed from static approaches toward the integration of robust optimization, tail risk metrics like Conditional Value at Risk, and Machine Learning. However, a gap is identified between algorithmic complexity and corporate adoption. The study establishes that Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) and Blockchain are indispensable governance requirements to overcome the black box problem in strategic decision-making. This research contributes a functional classification of tools based on their diagnostic, predictive, or prescriptive orientation. Title: The persuasive power of video in hospitality: How guest-generated video reviews influence customer engagement
Abstract: Guest-generated video reviews are increasingly prevalent on online travel platforms, yet their effects and mechanisms remain underexplored. Drawing on media richness theory, this study is among the first to examine whether and how such reviews enhance customer engagement, measured by subsequent review volume. We adopt a multimethod approach that combines econometric analysis with a controlled experiment to establish causal inference and uncover underlying mechanisms. Using a 24-month panel of 4471 hotels on Ctrip.com, difference-in-differences results show that guest-generated video reviews significantly increase customer engagement, with stronger effects for higher-tier or large hotels. Experimental evidence further demonstrates that these effects operate through increased information diagnosticity and social presence. Title: How to move you? The persuasive effects of influencer narrative styles in recommending tourism activities
Abstract: Influencers exert significant promotional effects in tourism marketing; however, few empirical studies have examined how different types of tourism activities can strategically leverage these effects through influencer narrative style. Title: The Symmetric and Asymmetric Impacts of Foreign Capital Inflows and Trade Openness on Africa’s Economic Growth: Evidence from Linear and Nonlinear Panel ARDL Models
Abstract: This study investigates the symmetric and asymmetric impacts of foreign capital inflows and trade openness on economic growth in 37 African countries from 2000 to 2021 using linear and nonlinear panel autoregressive distributed lag (ARDL) models. To examine the dynamic panel threshold effect, the study employed dynamic panel threshold estimation for each of the independent variables. The results indicated that trade openness, foreign direct investment, and official development assistance have significant threshold levels at 24.24%, 23.44%, and 23.21%, respectively. This suggests that the effects of foreign capital inflows and trade openness operate across two regimes—base and high—defined by these thresholds. Comparative analysis of symmetric and asymmetric effects without threshold considerations showed that trade openness consistently exerts positive long- and short-term influences on economic growth, both symmetrically and asymmetrically. Conversely, foreign direct investment (FDI) does not demonstrate a significant symmetric effect but exhibits an asymmetric long-term impact on growth. Additionally, official development assistance (ODA) shows an asymmetric effect that surpasses its symmetric influence on economic growth, highlighting the vulnerability of African economies to financial shocks. Negative shocks in the interaction between FDI and ODA have a more pronounced effect on growth than positive shocks. In the long run, variables such as capital, the globalization index, and political stability positively and significantly impact economic growth, while the labor force has a negative effect. Title: The road to hell is paved with good intentions: How does the construction of low-carbon cities affect corporate low-carbon technological innovation in manufacturing?
Abstract: Low-carbon technological innovation (LCTI) is crucial for decarbonization and global climate change mitigation. Taking China's Low-carbon City Pilot (LCCP)—a pioneering exploration for low-carbon development through policy innovation—as an exogenous policy shock, this study utilizes a staggered difference-in-difference-in-differences model and the data of China's manufacturing firms to examine the causality between the voluntary carbon regulation and LCTI. For the first time, the results indicate that the LCCP enactment significantly hinders corporate LCTI, contradicting the predictions of the Porter hypothesis. Mechanism analysis reveals that under the LCCP framework, local governments are authorized to design innovative policies tailored to their specific conditions and are responsible for their own assessment. Using a two-stage LLM-based approach to construct a climate policy uncertainty perception index, we confirm that this “bottom-up” approach introduces significant policy uncertainty faced by firms and weakens their motivation for LCTI involvement. Furthermore, the compliance costs associated with the policy crowd out the funds for LCTI, further hindering firms from engaging in LCTI. Heterogeneity analysis indicates that the adverse impact is more evident among firms exhibiting high risk aversion, ones with high artificial intelligence (AI) technology exposure, ones situated in non-resource-based cities, and state-owned ones, and that the adverse impact is significant for emission reduction technologies and zero-carbon technologies, but not for negative-carbon technologies. Additionally, all three pilot batches negatively impact corporate LCTI, suggesting that institutional modifications have not led to intended positive outcomes. This empirical research offers novel evidence regarding the efficacy of the LCCP and yields valuable policy insights—stable policy expectations and robust supervision mechanisms are crucial for achieving policy goals. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Context matters in just culture: Translating formal just culture into lived near-miss reporting experience in maritime transportation
Abstract: In onboard environments characterised by high operational risk, near-miss reporting is an important mechanism for identifying latent risks, preventing accidents and supporting organisational improvement. However, there remains limited empirical understanding of whether the just culture advocated in formal systems can be translated into the lived reporting experience of seafarers who are willing, able and motivated to report near-miss incidents on a sustained basis. To address this issue, this study draws on semi-structured interviews with seafarers and shore-based managers. Six interrelated themes are identified: ease of reporting, motivation to report, trust, reporting independence, feedback and acknowledgement. The findings indicate that near-miss reporting is more likely to occur in organisational contexts where reporting is accessible, safe and worthwhile. Complicated procedures, paperwork burdens and hierarchical pressure weaken seafarers’ willingness to report, whereas simplified procedures, fair management, low exposure communication channels, timely feedback and positive acknowledgement help strengthen reporting willingness and promote experience sharing. Title: Not naive, just gullible: psycho-cognitive vulnerability and fraud victimization in Italy
Abstract: Fraud represents a growing and complex threat in contemporary societies, with consequences that extend beyond economic losses. Gullibility emerged as the only statistically significant predictor, indicating that higher gullibility was associated with a greater likelihood of victimization, whereas sociodemographic characteristics, personality traits, financial literacy, and financial self-efficacy were not significantly associated with victimization. Title: Anger regulation scale for adolescents (ARS-A): Psychometric properties of the Portuguese version and its associations with emotion regulation, depression, and anxiety
Abstract: Adolescence is marked by difficulties in anger regulation, which are linked to internalising and externalising problems. All subscales demonstrated acceptable internal consistency and fit indices, confirming the original three-dimensional structure after two items were removed. Pearson correlations with other measures of behavioural and cognitive emotion regulation were consistent with theoretical expectations, although not all associations were as expected. Title: When health labels increase indulgent food purchase intention
Abstract: Health labels are widely used in front-of-package communication and are generally expected to facilitate healthier decisions. Title: Trade-offs and transitions: A scoping review of structural and discursive power in post-growth interventions

Title: Empowering leadership in educational contexts: A bibliometric analysis to guide management in the framework of SDG 4
Abstract: Empowering leadership (EL) has emerged as a critical leadership approach in educational contexts, particularly in response to increasing demands for innovation, teacher autonomy, and sustainable institutional development. China and Indonesia emerge as major international collaboration hubs, while Indonesia shows the strongest author–keyword linkage. Keyword analysis identifies dominant themes related to psychological empowerment, teacher autonomy, innovative work behavior, job satisfaction, and distributed leadership. Notably, 74 out of 84 publications (88.1%) are aligned with SDG 4, highlighting the strong integration of EL research with global educational sustainability agendas. Title: Modality effects in human–technology interaction
Abstract: This paper reviews emerging research on how different interaction modalities influence information processing and behavior when using new technological devices. Title: Intersectional justice as a guiding principle for feminist ecological economics
Abstract: Ecological economics focuses on provisioning for a good life for all within planetary boundaries. Feminist ecological economists have long highlighted the relevance of unpaid care work, times beyond linear clock time, and social-ecological provisioning towards this same end. In this article, we explore why and how intersectional justice should be a guiding principle for (feminist) ecological economics. Intersectional justice involves recognizing and redressing the discrimination that individuals or groups face due to overlapping social identities, which give rise to structural injustices that undermine the provisioning for a good life for all within planetary boundaries. Through three examples (global care chains, hidden ableist assumptions about ‘work’, and inequitable water access in India) we show that while many areas of feminist ecological economics lend themselves to intersectional analysis, operationalizing intersectional justice as a guiding principle is far from easy in practice. Learning from Black feminisms, disability studies, and feminist standpoint theory, we show how intersectional feminist perspectives can help challenge power structures and institutions that sustain injustices on both epistemic and material levels. This enables the kinds of collaborative action that can bring (feminist) ecological economics into broader acceptance, uniting struggles against various forms of oppression while building economic systems that prioritize the sustainability of life. Title: Self-built or retailer-based? Online direct-to-consumer channel introduction strategies for the fresh producer under retailer competition and disruption risk
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: The sharing of logistics resources among competing retailers provides a new avenue for fresh producers to introduce online direct-to-consumer (OD) channels. However, differences in operational cost and stability create a strategic trade-off between two approaches. Producers may either build the OD channels by themselves, accepting exposure to disruption risk, or rely on retailers, which ensures consistent operational stability. This study develops game-theoretic models of a fresh supply chain comprising one producer and two competing retailers across three scenarios: no OD channel, a self-built OD channel, and a retailer-based OD channel. The results show that, once an OD channel is introduced, higher operational costs lead the producer to reduce direct-sales quantities and lower wholesale prices to stimulate retailer orders. In the self-built OD channel model, the producer must adopt a “conservative,” “aggressive,” or “balanced” operational strategy, depending on the delivery cost, to mitigate profit losses from rising disruption risk. The retailer-based OD channel model becomes the producer's equilibrium strategy only when the logistics service fee falls below a threshold. This threshold increases when the delivery cost is low and exhibits a U-shaped pattern when it is high, as disruption risk rises. Additionally, the retailer-based OD channel model expands the range of equilibrium strategies as disruption risk increases and weakens the moderating effect of wholesale prices on retailers' order quantities. This leads to an asymmetric competitive landscape in which the producer is constrained, the logistics-sharing retailer benefits, and the non-sharing retailer is disadvantaged. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Hu J.
Title: Hero products and the value of position in live streaming commerce evidence from Douyin
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Every livestream sales session has one product that sells best, and the minutes in which it is shown are when the broadcast's audience peaks. This paper asks what that moment is worth to the products around it: can the items that follow the hero, or those shown just before it, turn the traffic it attracts into sales of their own? Using 260,252 product–session observations from 8123 Douyin sessions and an event-study design with session fixed effects, we find conversion highest in the slot immediately after the hero, exceeding products more than five positions away by 0.0177. The advantage is not borrowed traffic. It appears before the hero as much as after it, and only the adjacent slot breaks that symmetry; when the same product is compared with itself across sessions in which it sat at different distances, most of the advantage disappears except beside the hero. The running order therefore reveals mainly which products a streamer places near the featured item, and we report a positional association rather than an attention spillover. What survives is conditional. Scoring each product's own listing title with a large language model, we find that credibility signals attenuate the advantage while informativeness moves it in both directions, and the advantage exists only where the hero appears in the first third of the running order, vanishing when it is held until the end. Title: EXPSO: A PSO-based ensemble gene expression classifier for plant species using histone and chromatin accessiblity data
Abstract: Gene expression in plants is regulated by complex interactions among chromatin features, including histone modifications and chromatin accessibility. Accurate prediction of gene-expression states from epigenomic information can provide insights into transcriptional regulation and facilitate functional genomic studies. However, the nonlinear and high-dimensional nature of epigenomic data presents challenges for conventional statistical approaches. Here, we developed EXPSO, a PSO-assisted ensemble learning framework for classifying plant genes into high- and low-expression states using integrated histone modification and chromatin accessibility data. The framework uses Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) to optimize Random Forest hyperparameters within an ensemble comprising Random Forest, Support Vector Machine, and XGBoost classifiers. The framework was developed and evaluated independently across five plant species, including Arabidopsis thaliana, Hordeum vulgare, Phaseolus vulgaris, Setaria viridis, and Sorghum bicolor. EXPSO achieved an AUROC of 0.904 for Arabidopsis thaliana and demonstrated competitive predictive performance across the independently evaluated species. Model benchmarking against DeepChrome, ShallowChrome, and PatternChrome was performed using stratified five-fold cross-validation, with performance reported as mean ± standard deviation and 95% confidence intervals. Paired two-sided t-tests were used to assess fold-wise differences between EXPSO and the benchmark models. Comparative benchmarking included DeepChrome, ShallowChrome, and PatternChrome under the evaluation framework used in this study. Feature-attribution analyses using SHAP, LIME, and PDP consistently identified H3K36me3 and H3K56ac as important predictive features, consistent with their reported associations with transcription-associated chromatin states. To facilitate practical application, we developed the freely accessible EXPSO web server, which enables users to submit gene IDs together with histone modification and chromatin accessibility data as individual entries or CSV files and obtain gene-expression predictions with associated prediction probabilities and downloadable results. EXPSO provides an accessible and interpretable computational framework for plant gene-expression prediction from epigenomic features and a practical web-based implementation for supported plant datasets. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Multi-scale design and techno-economic optimization of copper-mesh reactors for methanol steam reforming
Abstract: Structured copper-mesh catalysts offer axial heat conduction for endothermic methanol steam reforming (MSR), yet deployment requires optimizing geometry, operating conditions and economics. We present a multi-scale Python framework integrating (i) Peppley-type Langmuir-Hinshelwood kinetics calibrated on 36 points (R2 = 0.955; the lumped Ea = 37.1 kJ mol−1 is an empirical coefficient; the model-free apparent value is 89–96 kJ mol−1). (ii) Finite-volume modeling of the plain-weave unit cell, giving 3-fold radial-to-axial conductivity anisotropy. (iii) A 1-D plug-flow reactor justified by a 270-point dimensionless analysis. (iv) A techno-economic model across 1575 configurations on the measured voidage. Because the dry reformate contains 75–8090 ppm CO, LCOH is route-dependent: 7.7–8.7 $ kg−1 with vacuum-swing adsorption, 2.9–3.5 $ kg−1 feeding a high-temperature PEM directly, and 3.3–3.9 $ kg−1 with two-stage preferential oxidation to 10 ppm for a stationary low-temperature PEM with anode air bleed, each dominated by methanol and electricity. Against two commercial Cu/ZnO/Al2O3 pellets within the same system boundary, the mesh meets the same hydrogen duty in one third of the volume at about 10 % lower cost and 18–28 % lower cost at equal reactor volume, with the gap arising from heat transfer and packing density, not activity. Electricity price is the principal cost driver (S1 = 0.77–0.81), a ranking that is range-dependent, heater efficiency leading under normalized ± 25 % ranges and the methanol price held fixed in the index set; geometry remains decisive for pressure drop, productivity and scale-up. Title: Digitalising the intensive care unit diary: mapping users' perceptions in healthcare settings – a scoping review
Abstract: Aim: To map literature on perceptions of patients, relatives, and healthcare professionals regarding the use of digital diaries in healthcare, to inform pre-implementation of an ICU diary by identifying factors relevant to feasibility, acceptability, and integration into ICU workflows. Methods: The review followed the Joanna Briggs Institute (JBI) methodology and PRISMA-ScR reporting guidelines. Studies including patients, relatives, and healthcare professionals with experience of digital diary use in healthcare settings were eligible. Included studies reported perceptions of digital diaries. Data were synthesised using inductive content analysis. Findings: From 679 identified records, 13 studies (2014–2025) were included, covering symptom diaries (n = 7) and ICU diaries (n = 6). The synthesis generated three overarching categories across user groups: relational connectedness and person-centred care; empowerment and meaning-making; and implementation and technological readiness. Across contexts, digital diaries were described as shaping communication, participation, and continuity of care, while also enabling reflection and meaning-making during illness and recovery. However, their perceived value was highly context-dependent and shaped by implementation conditions. Conclusions: Digital diaries were perceived by patients, relatives, and healthcare professionals as influencing communication, continuity, and engagement in care. Patients highlighted reflection, increased awareness, and participation, while relatives emphasised connection and involvement. Healthcare professionals focused on usability, workflow integration, and organisational conditions shaping use. They were perceived as valuable when they supported communication and made patients' experiences more visible, but as less useful when poorly integrated into clinical routines. Their perceived value depended on how they were embedded in practice and shaped by interactions between users, technology, and organisational context. Implications for Clinical Practice: Digital diaries have the potential to support communication, involvement, and continuity of care. However, realising this potential requires deliberate integration into clinical workflows, role definition, and user-centred design. Title: Deep-QLP and Spline based Quadrature Rules for Fredholm Integral Equations of the First Kind
Source title: Journal of Computational and Applied Mathematics
Abstract: In this paper, we propose a numerical method to construct an approximate solution to Fredholm integral equations of the first kind. These equations are common in image processing, spectroscopy, and other engineering sciences but are often ill-posed. Moreover, the right hand side of such equations could be error-contaminated. To effectively tackle the mentioned challenges, we propose suitable quadrature rules to discretize the continuous problem. The resulting discrete system is solved in a regularized least-squares framework by adopting the Deep-QLP factorization: a novel algorithm that automatically computes an approximate truncated singular value decomposition based on a user-defined tolerance. Additionally, two regularization approaches are introduced. In the first one, given a perturbed right-hand side, a Hankel matrix is constructed and then, the so-called de-Hankelization is performed by adopting the same Deep-QLP algorithm. In the second approach, we rely on locally refined discretization spaces to increase the accuracy of the computed approximate solution, by keeping low the number of the used degrees of freedom. Numerical experiments are conducted on some famous Fredholm integral equations available in the literature. © 2026 The Author(s)

Title: The dual impact of cap-and-trade policies on innovations and the moderating role of accumulated resources
Abstract: While the cap-and-trade policy is a widely adopted mechanism for addressing climate change, its impact on firms' innovation portfolio remains underexplored. To balance regulatory compliance with profitability, firms must strategically allocate limited resources across different technology innovations based on their existing resource endowments. This study examines how the cap-and-trade policy alters firms' innovation resource allocation across different types of technologies with a combination of theoretical analysis and empirical validation. Our theoretical model suggests that while the policy encourages firms to invest more in green technology, it may crowd out resources from more profitable conventional innovation. This effect is less pronounced for firms with substantial stocks of green innovation resources, but stronger for those with extensive conventional innovation stocks. Using a difference-in-differences approach and firm-level patent data covering enterprises affected by China's regional cap-and-trade pilots, we find that the policy reduces the share of conventional patents by 5.951 percentage points on average, confirming the crowding-out effect. Our moderating analysis further reveals that each additional accumulated green patent mitigates this negative impact by 0.018 percentage points, whereas each additional accumulated conventional patent amplifies it by 0.002 percentage points. Additional significant heterogeneity is also observed, conditional on industry characteristics (pollution intensity, competition intensity, and SOE dominance) and firm-level attributes (R&D intensity, profitability, and governance structure). These findings underscore the importance of guiding highly regulation-sensitive firms toward a balanced innovation transition while encouraging less regulation-sensitive firms to engage more actively via well-targeted and supportive policies that foster both green and conventional innovation. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Negotiation across the social sciences: An interdisciplinary review
Abstract: Psychological investigations have generated numerous insights into how two parties bargain. To build on this literature, we review recent research across multiple disciplines, focusing on aspects of negotiation that have received relatively little attention, namely individual differences, multiparty negotiations, and contextual factors. Insights into individual differences are observed in the developmental psychology, artificial intelligence, and social psychology literature. Investigations in these domains show that young children can think strategically about exchange, that individual differences shape the information negotiators obtain and how they utilize information, and that situational factors can constrain or facilitate the expression of individual differences. Insights into multiparty negotiations emerge from the social networks and political science literature. Investigations in these domains explore novel multiparty dynamics, highlighting the importance of structural position in bargaining, and demonstrating that relationship history can shape coalition formation. Insights into contextual factors emerge from the economic and public health literature. Investigations in these domains challenge assumptions about core negotiation concepts such as power and alternatives. Overall, an interdisciplinary perspective on negotiation complements and enriches psychological understanding, and provides implications for interventions, future theoretical development, and empirical research. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Folklore in learning and its implications for cultural literacy: A bibliometric study and systematic literature review
Abstract: The forces of globalization and digital transformation have intensified attention toward the need to strengthen cultural identity through education, including the use of folklore as a meaningful learning resource. However, existing studies on folklore in learning remain fragmented. While much of the literature focuses on either cultural preservation or specific educational applications, the gap lies in a systematic exploration of folklore's pedagogical role across different contexts and educational levels. This study addresses this gap by examining the development of research on folklore in learning and its implications for cultural literacy through a bibliometric approach combined with a systematic literature review. For the bibliometric analysis, metadata records of articles published between 2015 and 2025 were processed from the Google Scholar database. Data for the systematic literature review were collected from Scopus, Web of Science, and Google Scholar, and the article selection process followed PRISMA procedures. A total of 41 articles met the inclusion criteria and were included in the final review. Bibliometric mapping was conducted using VOSviewer, while article identification and screening were supported by Publish or Perish. The bibliometric findings indicate a significant increase in publications over the past decade, accompanied by a thematic shift from cultural heritage preservation toward the integration of cultural values within educational contexts. The SLR findings show that the research is predominantly qualitative in nature, with folktales and legends as the most frequently used forms of folklore, and books and e-modules as the main learning media employed to strengthen cultural literacy. The findings suggest that folklore-based learning fosters students’ cultural awareness, internalizes values, strengthens identity formation, and deepens the understanding of local culture. This study contributes by providing a more integrated understanding of folklore as a pedagogical tool for cultural literacy, emphasizing its role in curriculum design. Title: Nonlinear river distance effects on housing prices: Integrating XGBoost and GeoShapley for spatially explicit valuation
Abstract: Urban river landscapes not only provide recreational and aesthetic benefits but also generate tangible market value. Focusing on Tianjin's six central districts, this study integrates conventional spatial models with interpretable machine learning, to identify the nonlinear influence of river water systems on housing prices in Tianjin and the threshold effect. Using 2020 data from the early pandemic period captures pre-regulation market conditions while avoiding structural distortions from post-pandemic policy interventions during 2021–2022. Spatial heterogeneity across river segments further indicates that uniform zoning is suboptimal, with eastern and northern corridors warranting targeted investment and western and southern segments requiring functional repositioning. Title: Brand stereotypes, information processing, and consumer acceptance of Chinese automobiles: The moderating roles of perceived brand globalness and brand credibility in an emerging market
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Stereotypes about Chinese products persist in many developing economies, even as Chinese manufacturers have substantially upgraded their technological capabilities and product quality. However, the cognitive pathways linking systematic and heuristic information processing to consumers’ stereotype-based perceptions of brand warmth and competence remain underexplored in the evaluation of high-involvement foreign products. Drawing on the heuristic-systematic model, stereotype content model, and signaling theory, this study develops and tests a process-based framework explaining how information processing routes shape stereotype-based brand perceptions, which in turn influence product evaluations and purchase intentions toward Chinese automobiles in Vietnam. A sequential mixed-methods design was employed. A qualitative phase with 20 in-depth interviews was conducted to explore consumers' cognitive processes and refine the theoretical framework. Subsequently, survey data from 638 Vietnamese consumers were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling. The findings demonstrate that systematic information processing strengthens perceived brand competence and warmth, whereas heuristic processing weakens both dimensions, thereby reinforcing brand stereotypes. Perceived brand competence and warmth enhance product receptivity, judgment, and quality, which collectively drive purchase intention. Perceived brand globalness weakens the negative effects of heuristic information processing and amplifies the positive effects of systematic information processing on stereotype-related perceptions. Brand credibility strengthens the conversion of product-level evaluations into purchase intention. Theoretically, this study integrates HSM, SCM, and ST to clarify the sequential relationships linking information processing, stereotype-based brand perception, product evaluation, and purchase intention. Title: Efficiency and vulnerability in natural monopoly ferry infrastructure under peak load

Title: Beyond data disclosure: A health system transparency framework informed by evidence and Iranian insights
Abstract: Objectives: Although transparency is widely recognized as a cornerstone of good health governance, existing studies have often addressed individual dimensions of transparency, with limited integration of these dimensions into a comprehensive conceptual framework for health systems. This study aimed to develop a conceptual framework for health system transparency by integrating evidence from Iran. Methods: This qualitative study was conducted in six sequential phases between 2021 and 2024. Three systematic scoping reviews synthesized existing transparency frameworks, implementation principles, and the applications, benefits, risks, barriers, and opportunities of transparency in health systems. Results: The resulting framework conceptualizes transparency as a multi-level governance system comprising strategic contexts and infrastructures, stakeholder interactions, implementation drivers and constraints, transparency application domains, and tactical and technical implementation principles. Rather than viewing transparency as information disclosure alone, the framework emphasizes dynamic interactions between governance conditions, data users, feedback mechanisms, and potential contributions to organizational learning and system improvement. Conclusion: The proposed framework provides an integrated conceptual foundation for designing, implementing, and evaluating transparency reforms in health systems. Although informed by evidence from Iran, its governance-oriented architecture may be transferable to other health systems, provided that context-dependent components are adapted to local institutional, political, legal, and socio-cultural conditions. This study developed a framework showing how transparency can become part of everyday health system governance. It identifies the political, administrative, economic, and social conditions needed to support transparency, the role of citizens, researchers, media, and other data users in creating demand for information, and the factors that can either support or hinder implementation. The framework also identifies key areas where transparency is needed, including governance, finances, medicines, workforce, research, and healthcare services, and provides practical and technical principles for implementation. Title: How certification credibility and benefit framing shape heterogeneous consumer responses to sustainable products in e-commerce

Title: Under pressure: High-Stakes exams and media-reported student suicides in India
Abstract: We estimate the temporal association between high-stakes exam timing and media-reported student suicides in India using geocoded news data. Student suicides are 17.5 percent higher during months in which NEET-UG or JEE-Mains examinations are held, with no comparable pattern around lower-stakes board exams or among adults. The association is concentrated when national entrance exams coincide with board exams, suggesting the salience of cumulative exam burden. These patterns are stronger among girls, in states with higher exam participation, and in urbanised districts. Event-study estimates show suicides increasing immediately before and during exams, while movements around result announcements are weaker and less precisely estimated. We find no evidence that broad shifts in media attention during cyclone or election months account for the pattern, although exam-specific reporting bias cannot be ruled out. In the absence of mental health data, we generate an alternative database to address a policy question and spur future research. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: A fairness-aware TabTransformer framework for credit scoring with high-cardinality regional bias
Abstract: This study examines whether fairness constraints must come at the expense of performance in credit risk models. We introduce a deep learning framework rooted in the TabTransformer architecture, integrating a Normalized Covariance Penalty into the loss function to mitigate regional bias over a high-cardinality sensitive attribute, the 27 Brazilian states. A real-world mortgage dataset of 1,529,211 contracts, under a strict unawareness-at-inference protocol and calibrated using Platt scaling, is benchmarked against industry standards and against fairness-aware alternatives from the pre-, in-, and post-processing families. The fairness-constrained model achieved an AUC of 0.751, above its unconstrained counterpart (0.745; DeLong p < .001) and Random Forest (0.735), while reducing the maximum True Positive Rate (TPR) gap across states to 0.445, against 0.499 for XGBoost, and reaching the lowest Demographic Parity difference among all evaluated models. XGBoost retains a statistically significant advantage in raw discrimination (ΔAUC (Formula presented)); among models that keep inference blind to the regional attribute, however, the proposed framework offers the most favorable fairness–performance profile and dominates the equity-constrained region of the empirical Pareto frontier. A decomposition across the 27 states shows that the penalty compresses the regional TPR distribution in both directions, raising the mean TPR of the three worst-served states, and a leakage audit confirms a measurable reduction in the regional information carried by the scores. Sensitivity analyses over the penalty weight and training seeds, module ablations, and replications on public credit datasets support the robustness of these findings. © 2026 The Authors. Title: Evaluating LLM–NACE divergence in firm classification: A multi-metric analysis in the experience industry
Abstract: This study examines whether patterns of divergence between large language model (LLM) firm classifications and the Statistical Classification of Economic Activities in the European Community (NACE) are more consistent with between-model inconsistency, information-availability effects, or taxonomic ambiguity. Using a registry dataset of 43,931 Finnish firms, of which 29,565 received at least one Experience Industry classification, we compare GPT-3.5, GPT-4, Gemini 1.5 Flash, and Llama 3 70B. LLMs were prompted using company name and identifier only, and the resulting keywords were mapped to sector profiles, enabling comparison between model outputs and formal taxonomic assignments without external descriptive text. We evaluate agreement with Krippendorff’s α, cosine similarity, and normalized HHI-based concentration measures, and examine variation by firm revenue, size, and sector-level keyword reliability. Using raw LLM-derived profiles, inter-LLM similarity is high (cosine 0.89–0.95), whereas LLM–NACE alignment is substantially lower (0.19–0.24). Confidence-level adjustment increases LLM–NACE similarity, as expected, because adjusted profiles partly incorporate NACE information. Agreement increases in revenue-weighted and larger-firm analyses, but declines in sectors with low keyword reliability and diffuse boundaries. Across all weighting schemes and size classes, inter-LLM similarity exceeds LLM–NACE similarity. The findings suggest that LLM–NACE divergence is more consistent with information-availability effects and taxonomic ambiguity than with large between-model inconsistency. The study contributes a multi-metric framework for evaluating classification under unstable category systems and shows how LLM-based profiling can complement formal industry coding in hybrid sectors. © 2026 The Author(s). Authors: Narayan P.; Kar S.; Jha K.N.
