Title: Paving the Way toward Sustainability and Improving Performance in Renewable Power Projects Through Risk Management Practices
Source title: Journal of Legal Affairs and Dispute Resolution in Engineering and Construction
Abstract: Risk management (RM) is an integral and essential component of project management. Addressing two vital aspects is critical: improving project performance and enhancing sustainability. Past studies have illustrated several RM practices without revealing their actual impact on these aspects, especially in addressing the unique characteristics of renewable power project development. This study fills the gaps and aims to explore critical RM practices and examine their influence on project performance and sustainability in developing renewable power projects. The present study identified 25 risk management practices from the existing literature and publicly available documents of 32 leading enterprises in the renewable sector in India. Furthermore, data were collected through a questionnaire survey from 104 renewable sector experts. An underlying structure of these practices was established, and factors were extracted using exploratory factor analysis (EFA). A partial least squares structural equation model (PLS-SEM) was then developed to evaluate their influence on the project's performance and sustainability parameters. The analysis revealed that RM practices such as systematic risk assessment, recording, and training (F1), inclusive and long-term planning (F2), engaging dedicated risk officers (F3), and identifying, documenting, and updating RM policy (F4) significantly and positively influence the performance and sustainability of renewable power projects. Moreover, the study provides a comprehensive insight into the current RM practices in the renewable power sector. The study enhances the body of knowledge by identifying critical RM practices and quantifying their impact on improving the performance and sustainability of renewable power projects. Adopting these crucial practices would help practitioners enhance the success of the power project, paving the way for achieving the sustainable development goals (SDGs).  © 2026 American Society of Civil Engineers.

Title: Caffeine in sugar-sweetened beverages: A silent amplifier of preference and intake
Abstract: Sugar-sweetened beverages remain a major source of dietary sugar exposure, yet the behavioural contribution of caffeine within these products is often treated as secondary to sweetness, branding and convenience. This commentary argues that caffeine in cola-style sugar-sweetened beverages is better understood as a behavioural and nutritional amplifier than as a benign flavour adjunct. Although caffeine is a bitter tastant in water, psychophysical evidence indicates that caffeine at commercial concentrations is largely imperceptible within cola matrices because sweetness, acidity, carbonation and flavour complexity mask low-intensity bitterness. Its post-ingestive effects may nevertheless reinforce learned preference, support habitual intake and contribute to higher voluntary consumption. Product level evidence also suggests that caffeine-containing variants can carry slightly higher sugar concentrations than their caffeine-free counterparts. Integrating sensory science, flavour-nutrient learning, caffeine pharmacology and consumer behaviour provides a more complete account of how caffeine may silently increase sugar exposure. This framing has implications for formulation, labelling, dietary guidance and future research on beverage choice. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Authors: Sha X.; Xu Z.; Park K.-S.; Su M.
Title: Urban economic resilience and low-altitude logistics industrial agglomeration: Implications for reliable deployment
Abstract: Low-altitude logistics (LAL) is a complex urban cyber-physical freight system comprising uncrewed aerial vehicles, eVTOL aircraft, airspace management, and ground infrastructure. Reliable deployment requires technical validation, regulatory compliance, and commercially sustainable operations, while urban socioeconomic conditions may provide supporting resources. This paper develops an interpretable causal learning framework to evaluate how urban economic resilience influences LAL industrial agglomeration, measured by the log-transformed stock of registered LAL-related enterprises. Utilizing panel data from 296 Chinese prefecture-level cities over 2010–2024, we quantify urban economic resilience via an improved entropy-weighted TOPSIS model and integrate panel fixed-effects, double machine learning, causal forests, and SHAP attribution to estimate average effects under identifying assumptions and examine spatial heterogeneity and nonlinear predictive contributions. The results indicate that urban economic resilience significantly fosters LAL enterprise concentration, yet reveals a distinct resilience saturation pattern: mid-resilience cities exhibit the largest estimated effects on LAL industrial agglomeration, whereas marginal returns diminish in highly resilient metropolitan centers. SHAP decomposition reveals that household wealth accumulation, income levels, and fixed-asset investment are primary contributors to industrial presence. These findings identify urban economic conditions associated with LAL industrial agglomeration and offer implications for the economic foundations supporting reliable deployment. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: How social media content shapes enrollment intention: Distinguishing firm-generated and user-generated effects through TPB and self-identity
Abstract: The increasing reliance on social media has transformed how prospective students gather and evaluate information when selecting universities. This study examines how firm-generated content (FGC) and user-generated content (UGC) influence students' behavioral intention to enroll in private universities through psychological mechanisms grounded in the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) and self-identity. Specifically, the study investigates both direct and indirect effects of FGC and UGC on behavioral intention, mediated by attitude toward behavior, subjective norms, perceived behavioral control, and self-identity. A quantitative, cross-sectional design was employed, with data collected from 295 final-year high school students in Banten, Indonesia. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The results indicate that FGC has a significant direct and indirect effect on behavioral intention, whereas UGC does not have a significant direct effect but appears to operate primarily through indirect pathways. Among the mediators, subjective norms emerge as the strongest predictor of behavioral intention, followed by attitude toward behavior and self-identity. In contrast, perceived behavioral control does not significantly influence behavioral intention. The findings suggest that FGC and UGC function through distinct mechanisms. While institutional content can directly shape behavioral intention, user-generated content primarily influences intention through social and psychological processes. These results highlight that the effectiveness of social media communication depends not only on information exposure but also on how information is cognitively evaluated, socially validated, and integrated into individuals' self-concept. This study contributes to the literature by distinguishing between different types of social media content and extending the TPB framework with self-identity in the context of higher education decision-making. The findings provide insights for understanding how digital communication influences complex behavioral decisions in contemporary educational environments. © 2027 Malque Publishing, All rights reserved.

Authors: Chen Y.; Zhang B.
Title: Predictive basket steering and shopper choice sovereignty in AI-enabled retailing: A self-determination theory perspective
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: As artificial intelligence becomes embedded in online retailing, personalization systems increasingly shape consumers’ shopping baskets rather than merely recommend products. Drawing on Self-Determination Theory, this study examines how predictive basket steering is associated with shopper choice sovereignty and retailer reliance comfort among Chinese online grocery shoppers. Predictive steering is conceptualized through three mechanisms: option pruning convenience, preference reflection accuracy, and commercial intent transparency. Survey data from 483 shoppers were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling, with post-stratification calibration to national demographic benchmarks. The results indicate that predictive steering is positively associated with all three mechanisms, and each mechanism is positively associated with shopper choice sovereignty. Preference reflection accuracy and transparency are also directly associated with retailer reliance comfort, whereas option pruning convenience has no direct association with reliance comfort. Shopper choice sovereignty, in turn, is strongly associated with retailer reliance comfort. The study contributes to AI-enabled retailing research by highlighting that convenience alone is insufficient for comfortable reliance; rather, perceived decision authorship (sovereignty) is the central mechanism. It suggests that effective basket steering should combine convenience and personalized relevance with transparent, revisable, and consumer-controlled choice architecture. © 2026

Authors: Fei X.; Yu Y.; Li Y.
Title: Sharing blame with me: How AI anthropomorphism encourages individual unethical behavior
Abstract: Anthropomorphism is increasingly incorporated into AI agent design to enhance human–AI interaction. However, prior research has largely emphasized its benefits, leaving unclear how anthropomorphic AI shapes moral behavior when AI actively participates in decision-making. Across six studies (N = 1680), including a real-time human–AI interaction experiment, we show that highly (vs. lowly) anthropomorphized AI increases individuals’ tendency to engage in unethical behavior. We identify a responsibility-attribution process underlying this effect: AI anthropomorphism increases perceived AI moral agency, which shifts perceived responsibility for decision outcomes from the self toward AI and, in turn, increases unethical behavior. Further, this effect is attenuated when personal responsibility is made salient or when AI service psychological ownership is high. These findings reveal a potential dark side of AI anthropomorphism by showing how humanlike AI design reshapes moral agency perceptions and responsibility attribution, with implications for the responsible design and use of AI agents. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: THE POWER OF FACIAL EXPRESSIONS IN SALES AVATARS: ELEVATING CONSUMER INTERACTION IN METAVERSE COMMERCE
Abstract: Metaverse commerce is reshaping e-commerce by offering immersive and interactive shopping experiences. Sales avatars, defined as digital representations of firm frontline employees in metaverse commerce, play critical roles in delivering real-time and interactive experiences. Drawing on the theory of affordances and the needs-affordances-features framework, this study investigates how the facial expressions of sales avatars (smiling vs. crying) influence consumer avatars’ interaction outcomes and the underlying mechanisms through subcultural appeal. Further, we test when the mechanism by which sales avatars’ facial expression leads to consumer interaction outcomes via subcultural appeal is amplified or weakened depending on sales avatar’s anthropomorphism. We conducted four experiments in which consumers were exposed to virtual commerce contexts that we built on the VRChat metaverse platform. The results reveal that unlike real-world interactions, crying sales avatars compared to smiling sales avatars elicit higher intentions to interact with the sales avatar, purchase a virtual item from the sales avatar, and spread positive WOM about the experience. This counterintuitive effect is driven by consumers’ heightened perceptions of subcultural appeal in the crying sales avatar context. However, when sales avatars exhibited high anthropomorphism (human-like vs. cartoon-like), the positive effect of the crying expression weakened. These findings provide actionable insights into how to strategically leverage sales avatars’ facial expressions in highly immersive metaverse commerce, where consumers’ desire for subcultural values is relatively high. © 2027 California State University, Long Beach. Authors: Ma C.; Shi J.; Zhang L.; Fan A.
Title: Green by association? Restaurant presence on food-waste reduction platforms as a hybrid sustainability signal for brand equity
Abstract: Food-waste reduction platforms allow restaurants to redistribute surplus food, but their branding implications remain unclear. Drawing on signaling theory, we conceptualize restaurant presence on these platforms as a hybrid sustainability signal that embeds sustainability and commercial meanings within the same marketplace cue. Across three experiments, we examine whether this hybrid signal enhances restaurant brand equity through green brand image and whether consumer residence and restaurant type condition its effects. Study 1 shows that platform presence enhances brand equity, partially through green brand image. Study 2 replicates the main effect and provides directional evidence that the premium of platform presence may be stronger among urban than rural consumers. Study 3 shows that this effect depends jointly on consumer residence and restaurant type, and that mediation through green brand image is evident primarily for full-service restaurants. These findings identify platform presence as a hybrid, context-dependent sustainability signal with branding implications. © 2026 The Authors

Title: VPP-Based Park-Level Integrated Energy Scheduling System with Carbon Emission and Integrated Demand Response Mechanism Using Data-Driven Distributionally Robust Optimization
Abstract: This paper investigates the effective management of distributed Renewable Energy (RE) sources in multi-user Park-level Integrated Energy Systems (PIESs), aiming to coordinate power supply, cooling, and other forms of energy through a Virtual Power Plant (VPP) while enhancing environmental and economic benefits in regulation markets. Beyond the uncertain influence of solar PhotoVoltaic (PV) power on VPP operation, the challenge exists in establishing carbon trading and Integrated Demand Response (IDR) mechanisms to enable internal regulation of VPP. To address the above problem, a data-driven two-stage Distributed Robust Optimization (2-DRO) model is proposed. The overall goal is to minimize the operating costs of VPP by maintaining a supply-demand balance in PIESs along with protecting the electricity for production tasks. A case study of an actual PIES in eastern China reveals that our model is more practical and cost-effective. It integrates the deployment of both electricity and cooling energy under the mechanism of IDR and carbon emissions, realising flexible scheduling for multi-scenario operation of PIES. © The author(s) 2027.

Title: Optimising construction health and safety training: the role of training design and firm size
Abstract: Background The construction industry is one of the most hazardous sectors globally, responsible for a disproportionate share of work-related injuries and fatalities. Construction health and safety (H&S) training is widely recognised as a critical component for improving workers’ H&S competence and reducing accident rates. Despite extensive investment in training programmes, research indicates that learning effectiveness varies across construction firms and may be associated with differences in training design and organisational context. However, empirical understanding of whether firm size moderates the relationship between specific training design dimensions and learning effectiveness is limited. Objective This study investigated the relationships between training design dimensions (training content relevance, facilitator competence, opportunity for practice, and learning environment) and learning effectiveness in construction H&S training while assessing the moderating role of firm size. Methods A cross-sectional study was conducted with 80 construction professionals from medium- and large-scale firms. Data were collected using 5-point Likert scales to measure training design dimensions and learning effectiveness. Correlation analysis, multiple regression analysis, and moderation analysis using PROCESS were performed to test the hypothesised relationships. Results Multiple regression showed that the four training design dimensions jointly explained 64% of the variance in learning effectiveness ( R2 = 0.64, adjusted R2 = 0.62), with all four dimensions showing significant positive associations. Moderation analysis showed that firm size significantly moderated the relationship between training design quality and learning effectiveness (interaction B = 0.19, p = 0.033), with a stronger conditional effect among large firms ( b = 0.62) than medium-sized firms ( B = 0.43). Conclusions This study extends the training effectiveness literature by showing that the relationship between training design quality and learning effectiveness varies according to organisational context, with firm size representing a potential boundary condition. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: The Type III realisation conjecture of Kirkland and Šmigoc
Abstract: Kirkland and Šmigoc constructed a family of stochastic matrices realising the Type III boundary polynomials of the Karpelevič region and conjectured that, conversely, every stochastic realisation of such a polynomial must come from their construction. We prove this conjecture for the full nonzero parameter range 0<α≤1, for the reduced Ito polynomials fα(x)=xy(xq−(1−α))d−αd,n=qd+y, associated with Type III Farey-neighbour arcs of order n. For 0<α<1, the boundary theorem of Dmitriev and Dynkin restricts the possible nonzero entries of a realising matrix. After relabelling the vertices, its directed graph consists of the edges i→i+n1 and a selection of edges i→i+n(n+1−q), with indices taken modulo n. Coates' coefficient formula and a weighted form of Turán's theorem then show that the directed cycles of length q fall into d classes. Any two cycles in the same class share a vertex, while cycles in different classes have no vertices in common. Each class has the same sum of cycle weights, where the weight of a cycle is the product of its edge weights. The positions of these cycles along the n-cycle then yield the product condition required by Kirkland and Šmigoc. The case α=1 is treated separately, and an explanation is provided for the failure when α=0. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Choice set expansion and dual-domain loss aversion in food delivery platforms: Evidence from price-time trade-offs
Abstract: This study examines how delivery-tier expansion shapes online food delivery choices when price-time trade-offs are held constant. Drawing on context-dependent choice theory and prospect theory, we conducted a between-subjects discrete-choice experiment with 438 South Korean consumers assigned to either a two-tier menu (Free and Economy) or a three-tier menu (Free, Economy, and Single-order). Paid options offered the same price per minute saved, isolating choice-set structure from economic efficiency. Adding single-order delivery significantly reduced free delivery selection and captured 30.49% of choices. Economy delivery's incumbent-relative share increased slightly but not significantly, indicating no reliable canonical compromise effect. Across logit and cross-nested logit models, price loss aversion was associated with free delivery selection, whereas time loss aversion was associated with faster paid tiers, especially single-order delivery. Title: Organisational capability for digital health transformation in long-term care: development of a conceptual framework
Abstract: Background: Digital health transformation in long-term care (LTC) involves more than the adoption of digital technologies. Organisations must coordinate leadership, workforce capability, infrastructure, governance and implementation processes to sustain digital systems within continuing care environments. Existing implementation and digital maturity approaches address important aspects of digital transformation but provide less explanation of how organisational capabilities interact as a system within LTC. Objective: This study develops an evidence-informed organisational capability framework for digital health transformation in LTC and proposes relationships among capabilities potentially relevant to sustained digital system use. Methods: An evidence-informed framework development approach was used. Published evidence from digital health, healthcare management, implementation and organisational research was examined to identify recurring organisational mechanisms associated with digital transformation. Related mechanisms were grouped into capability domains, and proposed relationships among the domains were conceptualised. The resulting domains were integrated into the Long-Term Care Digital Capability and Alignment (LTC-DCA) framework. Results: LTC-DCA comprises seven interdependent organisational capability domains: strategic digital leadership, organisational readiness, workforce development systems, technology and data infrastructure alignment, governance and ethical oversight, implementation and integration mechanisms, and performance and learning systems. The framework conceptualises these domains as a connected capability system in which changes in one domain may influence others. Performance and organisational learning are proposed as feedback mechanisms that may support continued adjustment and alignment. Conclusions: LTC-DCA shifts attention from technology adoption towards the organisational capabilities potentially involved in integrating, sustaining and adapting digital systems within long-term care. The framework is evidence-informed and conceptually specified rather than empirically validated. Future research could examine its domains, proposed relationships and indicators across different LTC settings and investigate whether they are associated with sustained digital system use and organisational performance. © 2026 Fellowship of Postgraduate Medicine

Authors: Yin T.
Title: The paradox of withdrawal: How managerial turnover intention and attitudes shape performance appraisal quality in high-contact service
Abstract: Purpose: Performance appraisal quality depends on the discretionary effort of the rater. This study examines rater-side psychological antecedents of appraisal rigor among hospitality managers, focusing on how managers’ positive attitudes toward the job and the organization drive appraisal quality and whether that relationship is disrupted by the managers’ own turnover intention. Design/methodology/approach: Data were collected from 318 U.S. hospitality managers through a multi-stage screening protocol on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Because job satisfaction and organizational commitment were empirically indistinguishable in the sample (r = .976), a higher-order Managerial Attitudes factor was specified to test the two attitudinal hypotheses jointly. Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) was used to estimate direct and moderating effects. Common method variance was addressed procedurally and through a marker-variable technique combined with an unmeasured latent method construct. Findings: Managerial Attitudes had a strong positive relationship with self-reported appraisal quality (β =.71 in the method-adjusted model). Contrary to the “withdrawal–negligence” prediction of Conservation of Resources (COR) theory, turnover intention showed a small but significant positive direct association with appraisal rigor, and its interaction with attitudes was not statistically significant. The pattern is consistent with a “Lame Duck Objectivity” account in which anticipated exit releases managers from certain political constraints on evaluative candor, but reverse causality, statistical power, and measurement limitations remain plausible alternatives that the design cannot rule out. Originality/value: The study reframes managerial withdrawal as a scope condition of COR rather than a uniform trigger of task disengagement, and it demonstrates the utility of a higher-order attitudinal factor for handling discriminant-validity breakdown in hospitality data. Boundary conditions on generalizability — including racial and gender homogeneity of the sample, single-source measurement, and cross-sectional design — are discussed in detail, and a program of multi-source, longitudinal, and gender- and race-balanced replications is proposed. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Exploring the role of green human resource management in enhancing employee well-being and job satisfaction in the it sector
Abstract: Green Human Resource Management (GHRM) has received a growing academic interest with organizations starting to incorporate the sustainability of the environment into their strategic human resource management. The present paper offers a synthesis and systematic review of the existing body of literature to identify the impacts of GHRM practices on employee well being, job satisfaction as well as environmental performance, especially in the IT industry. A systematic literature review was conducted. The sources of records were Google Scholar (n = 317) and Scopus (n = 312), which returned 629 preliminary studies. After applying inclusion criteria based on peer-review, relevance and timeframe criteria, 156 articles were selected for detailed analysis. Literature was grouped based on the Ability-Motivation-Opportunity (AMO) framework to assess the performance of GHRM practices in the main HR functions. The results show that green training and development (80% implementation impact; 90% environmental impact) and reward management (85% implementation impact; 90% environmental impact) have the greatest correlation with the employee engagement and sustainability outcomes. Title: Leaning into risk: How slanted typeface logos increase perceived risk of efficacious products
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Marketing practice commonly uses slanted typeface logos on product packaging to convey movement and vitality, yet existing research has paid limited attention to the potential conflict between this low-level visual feature and the core claims of specific products. Drawing on the elaboration likelihood model (ELM), this research examines when and why slanted typeface logos on packaging increase consumers' perceived risk of efficacious products, revealing the underlying mechanism and boundary condition. Study 2 supports the mediating role of design instability: a slanted typeface logo triggers a visually perceived sense of imbalance, which further induces consumers’ risk inferences about the product; meanwhile, arousal, perceived movement, and perceptual fluency do not emerge as significant mediating mechanisms. Title: How contribution streaks form and their role in long-term retention in OSS projects
Abstract: Contributor turnover is a major challenge in open-source software (OSS) projects, affecting project sustainability, quality, and many other dimensions of project performance. Although turnover has been widely studied in the OSS context, the importance of sustained contribution periods to long-term contributor survival remains poorly understood. In this context, contributor survival refers to the probability of sustained activity over time. We investigate the effect of contribution streaks, defined as consecutive months of contribution, on long-term survival, and analyze what kind of engagement, at different levels of ownership, predicts short-term contribution streaks. Using five years of data from 14 open-source projects, we applied landmark analysis to understand long-term survival based on peak streak lengths and logistic regression to identify the activities supporting short-term streaks. In both cases, we identified a three-month contribution streak to be an important threshold for sustained contributions. We found that development and communication related activities across ownership levels are important predictors of whether contributors continue their streaks, even though the relative importance shifts over time. In addition, we found that prior experience plays a stronger role early on, but its effect diminishes during later streak months. These findings suggest that contribution streaks are important predictors of long-term survival and provide practical insights for open-source practitioners on how to improve the retention of new and existing contributors through supporting short-term contribution streaks. © The Author(s) 2026.

Title: Hard-work orientation as an individual difference: Passion and subjective vitality as sequential mechanisms of student engagement

Title: Mathematical and computational fluid dynamics (CFD) investigation of thermo-hydraulic behaviour and cooling performance of an air-cooled server rack under steady information technology (IT) loads
Abstract: This study presents mathematical and three-dimensional computational fluid dynamics (CFD) assessments of an operational 42U air-cooled server rack under five steady information technology (IT) loads from 10 to 20 kW. The principal contribution is not a new CFD algorithm, but a load-dependent integration of rack-scale thermal, hydraulic, turbulence, convective heat-transfer and facility-energy indicators within a single validated framework. Increasing IT load raised the maximum rack temperature from 307.6 to 328.8 K and the pressure drop from 35.2 to 68.1 Pa, while rack-average cooling effectiveness decreased from approximately 0.91 to 0.74, corresponding to an 18.7% reduction. Although the inlet condition remained unchanged, the Reynolds number remained approximately 1.92 × 105, whereas the Grashof number increased from 1.64 × 1010 to 3.76 × 1010 and the Richardson number from 0.45 to 1.02, demonstrating a progressive shift from predominantly forced convection toward mixed-convection behaviour. The resulting buoyancy-assisted redistribution promoted upper-rack recirculation, hotspot expansion and increasingly localized turbulence and convective cooling. Numerical energy closure remained above 97% for all cases. In contrast to the deteriorating rack-level thermal performance, facility Power Usage Effectiveness (PUE) improved from 1.61 to 1.42 as IT utilization increased. Title: Environmental qualities in green and natural spaces: Fresh air / peace and tranquillity and feeling closer to nature as pathways to perceived visit-related health benefits
Abstract: Rising levels of stress and mental ill-health have intensified interest in nature-based public health approaches, including green social prescribing and nature as medicine. However, it remains unclear whether different environmental qualities are associated with different aspects of visit experience, and how these experiences relate to perceived visit-related health benefits. This study examined direct associations of biodiversity, safety, accessibility and cleanliness problems with perceived visit-related health benefits, and indirect associations involving fresh air / peace and tranquillity and feeling closer to nature. Cross-sectional data from 19,814 adults in England who reported a recent visit to a green or natural space in the People and Nature Survey (PaNS) were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling (PLS-SEM). In the direct-effects model, biodiversity, safety and accessibility were positively associated with perceived visit-related health benefits, whereas cleanliness problems showed a negative association. Most of these direct associations were substantially attenuated when the two visit experiences were included, and both experiences were positively associated with perceived benefits. The pathway model also revealed differentiated associations across experiences, with safety most closely associated with fresh air / peace and tranquillity, biodiversity with feeling closer to nature, and cleanliness problems showing a negative indirect association through fresh air / peace and tranquillity. By considering qualities of the setting alongside experiences during the visit, the findings highlight the value of a quality-experience-benefit perspective in which different environmental qualities may show different patterns of association with perceived visit-related health benefits through particular visit experiences. Authors: Shi W.; Jin Y.
Title: THE VALUE OF RECOMMENDATIONS FROM SOCIAL MEDIA ANALYSTS IN ONLINE INVESTMENT COMMUNITIES
Abstract: This study examines the informational value of stock recommendations issued by social media analysts through the lens of Self-Determination Theory (SDT). Using comprehensive data from Seeking Alpha, we demonstrate that these recommendations significantly predict abnormal stock returns over a two-month horizon, with no subsequent reversal, suggesting that they convey incremental information not captured by sell-side analysts or textual sentiment. Guided by SDT, we further show that predictive accuracy varies systematically with analysts’ motivational contexts. Recommendations are more informative when issued by analysts identified as traders, whose direct financial stakes deepen the internalization of extrinsic incentives, and by analysts with high comment-section engagement, where interactive feedback supports needs for competence and relatedness. Conversely, predictive ability declines with longer platform tenure, consistent with motivational saturation as psychological needs become satisfied, and with higher posting frequency, where cognitive overload undermines need satisfaction. Finally, we find that both editorial selection and user-driven engagement effectively identify recommendations with greater ex-post informativeness. In an era of information abundance in online investment communities, our SDT-grounded analysis offers investors guidance for signal extraction and provides platform designers with principled insights for fostering higher-quality content ecosystems. © 2027 California State University, Long Beach. Title: Predictive maintenance for aero-engine fleets integrating uncertainty-aware remaining useful life estimation and maintenance decisions
Abstract: Prognostics and health management plays a critical role in improving flight safety and reducing lifecycle costs in aero-engine systems. However, existing predictive maintenance studies generally focus on individual engines or treat remaining useful life (RUL) estimation and maintenance scheduling as separate processes, limiting their applicability to fleet-level operations under uncertain degradation conditions. To address this limitation, this study develops an end-to-end predictive maintenance framework that couples uncertainty-aware RUL estimation with multi-objective maintenance optimization for aero-engine fleets. First, an integrated deep learning model based on Transformer and Monte Carlo dropout is constructed to estimate the RUL and quantify its predictive uncertainty. The resulting uncertainty information is subsequently propagated into a multi-objective mixed-integer linear programming model through risk-related constraints, thereby establishing a closed-loop connection between the prediction and scheduling layers. The model simultaneously minimizes the total maintenance completion time and operating cost under maintenance-resource and sequencing constraints. An iterative ϵ-constraint method is employed to obtain exact Pareto solutions for small-scale fleet instances. For large-scale instances, a tailored multi-objective artificial bee colony algorithm integrated with Q-learning, termed MOABC-QL, is developed by redesigning the search operators, constraint-handling mechanism, and learning-based strategy selection. Unlike iterative methods that repeatedly invoke commercial solvers, MOABC-QL directly approximates the Pareto front with reduced computational overhead. Title: The prompt-response paradox: A cybernetic perspective of generative artificial intelligence usage and corner-cutting behavior

Abstract: The emergence and proliferation of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) have transformed workplace interactions, reshaping many of them into dense “Prompt-response (P-R)” cycles characterized by a structural imbalance between the effort employees invest in crafting prompts and the quality of AI-generated feedback. Using a scenario-based experiment and a three-wave field survey, we demonstrate that: (i) performance pressure mediates the nonlinear relationship between GenAI usage and CCB, such that this nonlinear indirect effect shifts from positive to negative as GenAI usage intensifies; (ii) workplace status moderates the inverted U-shaped relationship between GenAI usage and performance pressure. Specifically, high status sharpens this curve, whereas low status flattens it, with a complete reversal to a U-shaped relationship occurring only under conditions of extremely low status. Title: Beyond the noise: Early identification of emerging technologies through weak signal prediction in higher-order networks
Abstract: The early identification of emerging technologies from weak signals is a critical strategic imperative. Existing network-based methods remain largely confined to lower-order representations and static, snapshot-based conceptualizations of weak signals, emphasizing retrospective detection over prospective prediction. Therefore, this study constructs a multi-source heterogeneous hypergraph with higher-order semantics, spanning the “Science-Technology-Industry” dimensions. Using a dataset of 145,316 papers, 79,050 patents, and 5941 project records from the New Energy Vehicle (NEV) fuel cell domain (2015–2024), we identify 226 candidate nodes exhibiting this trajectory. A two-round Delphi expert evaluation confirms 193 of these nodes as expert-confirmed weak signals, establishing Delphi-validated reference labels for subsequent model evaluation. We then employ Multi-Layer Perceptron (MLP), Dynamic Hypergraph Convolutional Network (DHCN), and Large Language Models (ZS-LLM and ICL-LLM) to prospectively predict weak signals with disruptive potential. The ICL-LLM achieves the best predictive performance among the tested models, with a Macro-F1 score of 61.25%, outperforming the MLP (49.76%), DHCN (56.84%), and ZS-LLM (46.35%). Title: Where AI enters the product development process: Task orientation, human identity threat, and purchase intention

Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly moving beyond analytical retail functions into product development, raising new questions about how consumers respond depending on where AI is positioned within the process. Title: THE OTHER SIDE OF THE COIN: CLICKBAIT’S INFLUENCE ON CONSUMER PURCHASE INTENTION IN SOCIAL MEDIA

Title: Institutional co-development cues in retail food choice: Reducing perceived risk in alternative protein acceptance
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Alternative proteins are increasingly available to consumers through retail and online food channels, yet their unfamiliarity often heightens perceived risk at the point of product evaluation. Study 2 showed that the cue increased acceptance by reducing perceived risk. Study 3 showed that this risk-reduction pathway was stronger among consumers with greater food neophobia. Study 4 demonstrated that the cue reduced risk and increased acceptance when trust in the named institution was high, but not when it was low. Title: Conceptualising a scale to measure customers’ off-premise dining experience (OPDineX) with third-party food delivery services
Abstract: Third-party food delivery services (TPFDs) have reshaped how consumers experience restaurant meals. The resulting OPDineX scale comprises eight dimensions and demonstrates strong reliability, convergent, discriminant, and predictive validity, as well as measurement invariance across contexts. Title: Ethics practices in ai development: An empirical study across roles and regions

Title: Unpacking the pathways from green intellectual capital to green recovery performance: The power of employee voice and intrinsic motivation

Title: When service environments signal ideology: Customer responses to ideological cues
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Service environments increasingly contain visible cues that communicate political engagement, religious identities, LGBTQ + affiliation, environmental advocacy, and other collective values. Although servicescape research has traditionally emphasized atmospheric, aesthetic, and functional cues, less is known about how customers interpret ideological cues embedded within routine service encounters. Drawing on servicescape research and social identity theory, this research examines how ideological servicescape cues are associated with customer discomfort, avoidance intentions, and stated store-choice decisions. Authors: Qi X.; Huang Z.; Chang W.
Title: Employee-led disclosure of anthropomorphism in tourism GAI failure recovery: A mind perception model from tourists and employees
Abstract: Generative AI (GAI) is increasingly mediating tourism service encounters, reshaping GAI failure recovery within a broader tourist–employee–GAI service configuration, in which GAI serves as the failure source, employees act as recovery agents, and tourists are the end recipients. Drawing on Mind Perception Theory, we theorize and test a post-failure recovery tactic in which employees intentionally foreground anthropomorphic aspects of the failing GAI during recovery interactions. Across six scenario-based experiments and two on-site simulation studies ( N = 2061), results provide convergent evidence that employee-led disclosure of GAI anthropomorphism (vs. control) improves recovery outcomes for both tourists and employees through mirrored mechanisms. Specifically, it increases tourist forgiveness by elevating perceived GAI experience and increases state employee satisfaction by elevating perceived GAI agency. These benefits weaken under high tourist anger or employees' perceptions of tourist anger and are further contingent on tourists' AI expertise and employees’ competitive versus collaborative mindset. The findings advance tourism research by offering parallel dyadic evidence on GAI failure recovery beyond a tourist-centric lens, extending Mind Perception Theory through stakeholder-contingent effects of perceived experience and perceived agency, and repositioning anthropomorphism in recovery as a co-produced mechanism jointly enacted through employee framing and available GAI interface affordances. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd.

Title: Invisible data infrastructure and cross-domain digital innovation: Evidence from data groups in China
Abstract: This study examines whether and how formalized data governance reshapes firms’ digital innovation by exploiting the staggered establishment of municipal data groups in China. Using a difference-in-differences design and Chinese A-share listed firms from 2008 to 2024, we find that municipal data group establishment significantly expands firms’ cross-domain digital innovation. This effect is stronger among state-owned enterprises, regulated industries, firms in cities with lower technological complexity, and regions with more developed market and factor environments. Additional analyses provide evidence consistent with several potential pathways: municipal data groups are associated with changes in R&D uncertainty, managerial innovation expectations, interregional collaboration, and innovation activities. Further analysis reveals a quantity–quality divergence: data group establishment increases patent output but is associated with lower average measured patent quality, particularly among firms receiving stronger innovation incentives. This pattern is consistent with multiple explanations, including incentive responses and innovation composition changes. Title: Balancing productivity and safety: a risk-aware framework for human-robot collaborative workflows
Abstract: This paper addresses the Assembly Line Balancing Problem (ALBP) in the context of Human-Robot Collaboration (HRC), integrating task failure risks through Process Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (PFMEA)-inspired framework. The framework captures multiple categories of failure effects including safety and translates them into an Alternative Risk Priority Number (ARPN). Unlike existing research focused mainly on design-phase risk assessments or dynamic operational level controls, this study embeds ARPN directly into the tactical ALBP model, enabling a bi-objective optimization of Cycle Time (CT) and failure risk. Computational experiments across diverse assembly configurations reveal the role of human skills and cobots in objectives trade-off. They also demonstrate the model's ability to reduce hazardous task overlaps, especially under limited worker skill availability. Title: From LinkedIn to labor statistics: Using Revelio microdata for labor market research in developing economies
Abstract: We explore the use of Revelio data—obtained primarily from LinkedIn profiles—as a source of labor force microdata in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where large-sample, high-frequency, employer-linked alternatives are largely unavailable. Title: Market-driven or state strategic-driven? A hybrid driving paradigm and evolution of mission-oriented innovation ecosystems in aerospace engineering
Abstract: How national strategies and market forces jointly organize innovation for complex and uncertain space missions, such as deep space exploration, and why distinct driving logics retain their differences while incorporating governance mechanisms from one another remain important questions for research on mission-oriented innovation ecosystems. This study develops the Drive–Organization–Adaptation–Value (DOAV) analytical framework and conducts a longitudinal comparison of SpaceX's deep space exploration program and the China Manned Space Program, tracing stage-specific mission demands, local task gaps, mechanism entry, and coupling at task interfaces. The findings reveal a sequence of conditional relationships. First, mission mandates and resource conditions shape initial driving relations and produce distinct configurations of organization, adaptation, and value. Second, when stage-specific demands reach the configuration performance boundary, the leading actor can address local task gaps through internal adjustment or admit heterogeneous mechanisms when complementary capabilities and executable interfaces are available. Third, coupling at task interfaces links organization, adaptation, and value, encouraging convergence in governance mechanisms while leadership relations retain identifiable continuity at the defined long-term mission level. On this basis, the study distinguishes instrumental hybridization, asymmetric structural hybridization, and mission co-shaping according to mechanism embedding depth and the reach of governance feedback. Mission co-shaping is retained as a conditional theoretical extension within the process explanation of the DOAV dynamic adaptation mechanism. The findings inform the coordination of public objectives and firm innovation capabilities in major scientific and technological missions, including space exploration, and the design of collaborative rights, responsibilities, and verification arrangements in response to stage-specific tasks. © 2026 IAA. Title: How should conversational recommendation agents organize candidate products? Matching recommendation set granularity with time pressure
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: With the widespread application of conversational recommendation agents (CRA) on e-commerce platforms, an increasing number of consumers use a CRA to support product choices. Existing research has mainly focused on the accuracy of CRA recommendations, with limited attention paid to how candidate products should be organized and whether this organization should be adapted to consumers' current decision contexts. Drawing on the product set granularity perspective and the heuristic–systematic model, this study examines the matching effect between recommendation set granularity (coarse vs. fine) and time pressure (high vs. low) on consumers' intention to adopt CRA recommendations and investigates the underlying psychological mechanisms. The results of three online scenario experiments reveal that consumers show higher adoption intention toward CRA recommendations featuring coarse recommendation set granularity under high time pressure and toward those featuring fine recommendation set granularity under low time pressure. The two matching effects operate through perceived fluency and perceived attractiveness, respectively. Furthermore, consumer knowledge affects the relative effectiveness of the two matching strategies: the match between coarse recommendation set granularity and high time pressure is more effective for consumers with low product knowledge, whereas the match between fine recommendation set granularity and low time pressure is more effective for consumers with high product knowledge. Title: The automation paradox: Efficiency gains vs. workforce concerns in human-AI collaboration
Abstract: Human-AI collaboration (HAC) has attracted growing attention in operations and supply chain management due to its potential to enhance decision-making and organisational performance. Despite this promise, automation preferences remain uneven across organisations. This study examines preferences for full, partial, and no automation using a discrete choice experiment. Data were collected from 398 managers, generating 1592 choice sets and 4776 alternative-level observations. Alternative-specific conditional logit results show that automation preferences are primarily shaped by a trade-off between performance gains and workforce concerns. Anthropomorphism generates positive but context-dependent utility, while social interaction and investment cost are not statistically significant in the overall model. Managers prefer collaborative human-AI arrangements, choosing partial automation in 55.7% of scenarios and selecting no automation in only 3.4% of choice scenarios, indicating that the central decision concerns the degree of automation rather than its adoption. Further subgroup analyses reveal context-specific patterns across gender, sector, and organisational size, indicating subgroup-specific associations between socio-technical attributes and automation preferences. By identifying subgroup-specific patterns in the utility of AI attributes, this study extends socio-technical systems and contingency perspectives on technology adoption and highlights the need for context-sensitive automation strategies that balance efficiency gains with workforce security. © 2026

Title: Good listening as a wise negotiation tactic
Abstract: Listening is a foundational interpersonal skill. Effective listening is central to managing the dual demands of negotiation: competing over limited resources while sustaining cooperation and trust. Nevertheless, limited research has shed light on how to listen effectively in negotiation. Integrating research from psychology, communication, and negotiation, we identify three common listening traps that undermine negotiation effectiveness: negotiators tend to focus too much on: (1) the self (and too little on others); (2) resolving disagreement (and too little on exploring it); and (3) what is said (and too little on what remains unspoken). We propose three approaches for effective listening in negotiations: (1) listening to understand rather than persuade; (2) listening for movement and change; and (3) making listening observable through concrete verbal and nonverbal behaviors. We argue that high-quality listening improves both informational and relational outcomes by facilitating deeper information exchange, increasing trust, and supporting integrative agreements. By highlighting high-quality listening as a wise negotiation tactic, this article illustrates how negotiators can better navigate the tension between cooperation and competition in mixed-motive interactions. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: When and why women ask (or do not): Taking stock of research on gender differences in negotiation propensity, behavior, and outcomes
Abstract: Evidence first emerged several decades ago that women are less likely than men to initiate negotiations and perform less competitively than men in negotiations. Researchers also have discovered moderators of these effects, including structural ambiguity, representation role, and gender salience and relevance. Furthermore, the anticipation of backlash has emerged as a potential mechanism to explain gender differences in negotiations. Yet, more recent research has revealed varied findings concerning whether gender differences, underlying mechanisms, and moderators have shifted, as well as the role of intersectionality. We review the research in this area and find that the nature of gender differences in negotiation is complex, with some recent research replicating certain past findings (e.g., gender gaps in negotiation behavior) but not others (i.e., gender gaps in negotiation propensity or moderation by representation role). Still other recent research has even revealed a reversal of gender gaps in negotiation propensity, with women being more likely than men to negotiate in certain cases, and that female negotiation counterparts are liked more than male negotiation counterparts, leading to greater counterpart satisfaction. We also consider the role of statistical power given the small-to medium-sized effects typically reported: Sample size may be another important reason for inconsistent findings in the gender and negotiation literature. Finally, we consider the potential for changing gender roles. Overall, we conclude that gender differences in negotiation performance outcomes persist and are influenced by situational nuances, but that these differences have been mitigated for propensity to initiate negotiations. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Unveiling the effects of multidimensional urban shrinkage on urban flood resilience: A case study of the Yangtze River Basin, China
Abstract: Climate change poses growing flood-management challenges for cities undergoing economic, demographic, and spatial decline. (1) Both UFR and subsystem coordination improved significantly, with Sen slopes of 0.0023 and 0.0059 per year, respectively. (2) Drainage infrastructure, economic activity, and fiscal capacity made the largest predictive contributions, whereas the associations of population and spatial shrinkage were smaller, more heterogeneous, and more dependent on local context. (3) The mechanism tests further indicate partial pathways through population density and impervious surface. (4) The expansion scenario produces the highest projected coordination level, followed closely by SSP1, whereas SSP3 yields the lowest trajectory. Economic shrinkage remains below the baseline, whereas population- and spatial-shrinkage trajectories are not clearly separated from it in several comparisons. These findings identify robust associations and scenario-dependent pathways rather than causal effects. Title: Capability, opportunity, and motivation for healthy eating: Exploring gender-specific pathways

Title: What makes human service distinctly human in the AI era? Conceptualizing and measuring authentic relational service competency
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) service agents increasingly simulate human interaction, the basis for distinguishing human service has become theoretically ambiguous. While prior research consistently identifies authenticity as a key limitation of AI-enabled service, authenticity remains underdeveloped as a uniquely human service capability. Title: Affordances and paradoxical engagement in virtual immersive learning platforms: A configurational analysis across demographic groups
Abstract: Virtual immersive learning platforms (VILPs), integrating immersive technologies, gamified design, and learning tools, enable meaningful engagement in learning while also creating possibilities for compulsive engagement. The findings show that meaningful and compulsive engagement are associated with distinct combinations of affordances and these configurational patterns vary across demographic conditions. Title: Synergy or backfire? Adding virtual influencers to advertisements featuring human influencers: The roles of sensory cues and temporal framing
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: In recent years, virtual influencers (VIs) have emerged as a salient presence in brand communication. Firms are increasingly featuring them alongside human influencers (HIs) in advertising campaigns. Yet whether such HI–VI co-endorsement creates synergy or instead backfires remains unclear. Drawing on cue utilization theory and the elaboration likelihood model, this research examines how endorsement format, defined as advertisements featuring only HI(s) versus HI–VI co-endorsement, and advertising sensory cue type (distal vs. proximal) jointly shape consumers’ purchase intentions, and how this relationship varies across temporal frames (past vs. future). Results from four experiments (total N = 1293) show that advertisements featuring both an HI and a VI are more effective than advertisements featuring only HIs when distal sensory cues are emphasized, but less effective when proximal sensory cues are highlighted. These effects operate through two distinct mechanisms: perceived novelty explains the synergy associated with HI–VI co-endorsement under distal sensory cues, whereas perceived authenticity explains the advantage of advertisements featuring only HIs under proximal sensory cues. Moreover, future-oriented framing strengthens the novelty-based effectiveness of HI–VI co-endorsement, whereas past-oriented framing favors advertisements featuring only HIs through authenticity-based evaluations, particularly when proximal sensory cues are emphasized. By identifying when HI–VI co-endorsement succeeds or fails, this research extends endorsement theory from a source-substitution perspective to a hybrid co-endorsement perspective and provides practical implications for advertising strategy. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Developing instrument to measure the glass ceiling phenomenon among female academics in Indonesia
Abstract: The persistence of the glass ceiling phenomenon in academia indicates the necessity of developing a contextually valid and reliable measurement instrument, particularly within Indonesian higher education institutions. Instruments developed in different cultural settings are often unable to fully capture the structural and sociocultural dynamics influencing female academics' career advancement in Indonesia. This study aims to develop and validate a comprehensive measurement instrument that reflects these contextual specificities and improves measurement accuracy in assessing career advancement barriers. A quantitative research design was employed using a survey approach. Instrument development was conducted through the integration of two established questionnaires originating from India and Europe, followed by contextual adaptation. Data were collected from female lecturers employed at Catholic universities in Indonesia. The two preliminary questionnaires were administered to the same initial group of female academics. For the final validation, the integrated instrument was administered to the initial respondents together with additional participants, resulting in a larger validation sample. The measurement model was evaluated using confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) with SmartPLS. Reliability and validity were assessed through composite reliability, Cronbach's alpha, average variance extracted, and discriminant validity criteria. The findings indicate that the newly developed instrument demonstrates strong reliability and validity across all dimensions, with acceptable thresholds achieved for composite reliability and convergent validity. Compared to the adapted international instruments, the final instrument exhibits higher cultural relevance and improved measurement precision. Several dimensions were more accurately captured, particularly those related to organizational culture, informal networks, and discriminatory promotion practices, indicating a stronger alignment with the Indonesian academic environment. The study contributes to the refinement of measurement approaches in gender-related research by providing a robust and context-sensitive instrument. The instrument is expected to support future empirical studies and institutional policy evaluations aimed at reducing gender disparities in academic career advancement and leadership positions in Indonesia, while also enabling more accurate diagnosis of structural and cultural barriers. Title: ST-AHM: a soft-threshold sparse-attention hypergraph model with contrastive learning for session-based recommendation
Abstract: Session-based recommendation (SBR) predicts the next interaction from anonymous, short-lived behavioral sequences. A central challenge is to capture higher-order dependencies within sessions and collaborative information across related sessions while limiting weak contextual relations. We propose ST-AHM, a dual-channel model that jointly represents within-session and cross-session information. In the within-session channel, hypergraph convolution captures higher-order item dependencies. Hypergraph-specific sparse attention (HSPA) then averages scaled compatibility scores across attention heads before applying Sparsemax. This operation creates a consensus-based sparse support while retaining head-specific value projections, thereby reducing the propagation of weakly supported relations. An identity-free blank node summarizes the enhanced sequence and produces a context-dependent session-intent representation without relying directly on the last item. In the cross-session channel, Jaccard similarity between session item sets defines a relational graph. Relational graph convolution propagates collaborative information, and the blank-node representation acts as a blank-node-derived query for aggregating relevant cross-session context. A contrastive objective aligns valid interaction representations with the blank-node-augmented view of the same session and distinguishes them from shuffled representations. Across Tmall, Diginetica, and 30Music, ST-AHM outperformed the evaluated baselines, including DCL-BPM, DiffSBR, and MSGAT. Its average improvements were 19.23% for HR@10, 12.71% for HR@20, 23.19% for MRR@10, and 24.28% for MRR@20. These results support the joint modeling of within-session and cross-session information while reducing the influence of weak relations. Title: Non-intrusive appliance classification in smart grids using swin transformer mixtures
Abstract: As smart grids evolve, non-intrusive appliance classification has become an important enabler of demand-side energy management and grid intelligence. However, accurately identifying appliances from aggregate low-resolution power measurements remains challenging due to concurrent appliance operation, temporal variability, and similar consumption signatures across appliances. To address these challenges, we transform consumption windows into complementary time-series images to provide richer spatiotemporal representations and enable robust image-based learning and classification. We propose a Mixture of Swin Transformers (MoST) in which a pretrained Swin backbone extracts features from stacked multi-modal images while a mixture-of-experts transformer head performs adaptive appliance classification. To improve sample efficiency and accelerate convergence, we fine-tune ImageNet-pretrained Swin weights via transfer learning. For resource-constrained deployment, we further optimize MoST using Neural Architecture Search (NAS). Authors: Munir K.; Nand A.
Title: Circular economy approaches to sustainable food waste management in the hospitality and food services sector
Abstract: The Circular Economy (CE) as a model has become a widespread approach to promoting sustainability through the restoration and regeneration of products and materials within production and consumption. Despite the plethora of work done, research on the application of CE principles for food waste management in the hospitality and food services (HaFS) sector remains scarce. This study adopts a conceptual review approach and follows the PRISMA-ScR guidelines to address this gap through exploring the role of CE in reducing and managing food waste in the HaFS sector through a review of papers between 2015 and 2026. The findings indicate that collective efforts of both actor-internal (hospitality managers and staff) and actor-external (customers, local authorities and government) stakeholders are essential to achieve sustainable and circular practices. Additionally, a framework that supports managerial decision-making by aligning with external stakeholders to enable circular food waste management is proposed for adoption in the HaFS sector. Title: Why (not) subscribe? Drivers and barriers of grocery replenishment subscriptions
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Subscription models are gaining importance across retail sectors, yet a picture of consumers’ evaluations of replenishment subscriptions for regularly needed products, particularly groceries, is still lacking. Drawing on perceived value theory and technology acceptance research, this study proposes a value-risk framework for replenishment subscription adoption. It contrasts four value-related drivers (time efficiency, supply reliability, cognitive relief, and cost efficiency) with four corresponding risk-related barriers (time concerns, supply mismatch concerns, lock-in concerns, and financial concerns) and examines their effects on perceived usefulness, attitude, and ultimately usage intention. Two structural models, a ‘drivers model’ and a ‘barriers model’, were estimated using quota-representative surveys in Germany (N = 493) and the UK (N = 339), complemented by multigroup analysis. The results show that subscription evaluations are inherently ambivalent: positive and negative evaluations coexist, but drivers account for considerably more variance in perceived usefulness and attitude than barriers, while financial and supply mismatch concerns still exert strong negative effects. Convenience proves multidimensional: while cognitive relief outweighs time efficiency as a driver of perceived usefulness, distinct barrier facets also show different relevance. The cross-country comparison reveals common patterns alongside differences. Retailers are advised to communicate the benefits of subscriptions more concretely rather than through generic convenience claims. However, relying just on benefit communication is insufficient: adoption also hinges on actively mitigating perceived risks, with messaging tailored to a market's maturity and familiarity. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Personalized assignment of UAV rescue tasks: an integrated framework of content-based filtering and two-stage robust optimization
Abstract: This paper presents a novel integrated framework approach of content-based filtering and two-stage robust optimization for personalized assignment of UAV rescue tasks. Our approach differs from traditional UAV task assignment method in that (1) The personalized assignment of UAV task is established on the mining of “fine-grained” attributes such as hovering capability, payload capacity, wind resistance, and rainproof capability, etc; rather than simply considering “coarse-grained” attributes like cost, time, and capacity. (2) Pre-disaster airport positioning and UAV allocation are integrated with post-disaster task assignment into a single model, accounting for the uncertainty of disaster scenarios. In our approach: Text mining techniques are first employed to identify the “fine-grained” attributes of UAVs and rescue tasks. Subsequently, content-based filtering method is utilized to calculate the matching degree between UAVs and rescue tasks. Finally, a two-stage robust optimization model, incorporating constraints based on the matching degree parameters, is applied to optimize both pre-disaster UAV deployment and post-disaster task assignment plans. Title: When products speak: The effects of product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication on consumer responses to carted products
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: Shopping cart abandonment is a pervasive challenge in e-commerce, with more than 70% of online shopping carts failing to convert into purchases. Across five experiments, we find converging evidence that product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication enhances consumers' purchase-related responses to carted products. Study 1 shows that product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication generates stronger responses than both non-anthropomorphic and brand-as-subject anthropomorphic communication, while Study 2 demonstrates that these effects are robust across different levels of pity conveyed in the message. Study 3 identifies state empathy and perceived interestingness as parallel mediators. Study 4 further demonstrates that these indirect effects are stronger among consumers with an emotional (vs. rational) decision-making style. Finally, Study 5 extends the findings to behavioral responses, showing that product-as-subject anthropomorphic communication increases behavioral cart re-engagement and reduces consumers’ reported likelihood of cart abandonment. Title: Exploring the determinants of student loyalty in islamic higher education: An empirical study from Indonesia
Abstract: This study investigates the determinants of student loyalty in the context of Islamic higher education in Indonesia, focusing on the role of religiosity and student satisfaction. As competition among higher education institutions intensifies, particularly in Yogyakarta, understanding the drivers of student loyalty becomes essential for institutional sustainability. Drawing upon relationship marketing theory and the service-dominant logic perspective, this research examines whether religiosity directly influences student loyalty and whether student satisfaction mediates this relationship. A quantitative approach was employed via a structured questionnaire distributed to 190 respondents, consisting of final-year students and alumni from private Islamic universities in Yogyakarta. The data were via structural equation modelling-partial least squares (SEM-PLS). The findings reveal that religiosity significantly influences student satisfaction, which in turn positively affects student loyalty. However, religiosity does not directly influence loyalty, indicating that satisfaction plays a critical mediating role. These results underscore the importance of cultivating religiosity-based values in higher education service delivery, as well as ensuring continuous improvement in student satisfaction to strengthen loyalty. The study contributes to the literature by integrating religiosity into the service quality and loyalty framework, offering both theoretical insights and managerial implications for Islamic universities in Indonesia. Despite its notable contributions, this study is constrained by its focus on private Islamic universities within a single regional context, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. Future investigations are encouraged to employ longitudinal designs or comparative analyses encompassing diverse types of higher education institutions and broader geographical areas to enhance the external validity of the proposed model. Title: Safety concepts through a memetic lens
Abstract: Within safety practice and science there are countless ideas, approaches and concepts to manage safety. Some of these safety concepts are picked up, discussed widely and spread, while others do not. Little is known about this subject. This paper provides a unique perspective on the development and adoption of safety concepts by using an evolutionary framework to explore reasons why. As a case, this paper traces the historic development of one of safety’s most influential and iconic safety concepts, the accident triangle, over nearly a century through successive cycles of replication, variation, and selection. Knowledge of factors that influence the adoption of safety concepts can contribute to the design of more effective concepts that attract attention and of social and organisational environments that are receptive of these concepts. In the end, provided the concepts in question are useful, this can contribute to enhancing safety and reducing harm. In addition, the insights gained in this paper can help safety professionals and academics to critically reflect on the development of safety concepts, to help them better understand how safety concepts evolve and can change meaning leading to various interpretations and reflect on what this means for their own adoption of concepts and eventually their practice. © 2026 The Author(s).

Authors: Zhou D.; Gong Z.
Title: Organizational responsibility attribution: Public responses to AI versus human failures in government services
Abstract: Existing research provides only limited insights into whether, compared to traditional human service failures, artificial intelligence (AI) failures in government services lead the public to attribute more responsibility to the service organization, and whether outsourcing necessarily alleviates organizational responsibility attribution. To advance this debate, this study conducted three pre-registered survey experiments. Study 1 (N = 1112) reveals that citizens attributed more responsibility to the service organization for AI service failures than to human service agents. The effect was mediated by the perceived service provider's controllability, rather than by counterfactual thinking. Study 2 proposed and tested two distinct pathways, namely the responsibility-transfer and controllability-transfer pathways. The objective was to explain how diminished controllability perceived at the individual service provider level increases the attribution of responsibility to the organization. Empirical evidence (N = 1084) supports the responsibility-transfer pathway. When citizens perceive that AI agents have less control over services than humans, they assign less responsibility to the AI agent and transfer more responsibility to the service organization. Study 3 (N = 1007) examines whether disclosing that the AI agent was externally developed mitigates the attribution of organizational responsibility. Compared to in-house AI systems, outsourcing to either a state-owned enterprise or a private enterprise, rather than to other government organizations, reduced organizational responsibility. In this study, this reduction was substantial enough to eliminate the disparity between AI and human service failures. This study advances theories of responsibility attribution in the digital era, highlighting the nuanced role of outsourcing transparency and the responsibility-transfer mechanism. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Pharmaceutical Import Forecasting for Supply-Chain Decision Support: A Comparative Evaluation of Fuzzy, Statistical, and Machine-Learning Models
Abstract: Purpose: Pharmaceutical supply-chain planning in import-dependent economies is sensitive to macroeconomic shocks, currency volatility, and global supply disruptions. This study evaluates a Dynamic Fuzzy Time Series (DFTS) candidate together with statistical and machine-learning benchmarks for annual pharmaceutical-import forecasting. Methods: Azerbaijan’s annual pharmaceutical-import observations for 2012–2023 are used for model development; the 2024 observation (USD 507.50 million) is reserved as an untouched external holdout. Model comparison uses a common rolling-origin/expanding-window protocol beginning with a 2012–2017 initial training window. RMSE is pre-specified as the primary loss, with MAE and sMAPE as complementary measures. The DFTS recency parameter rho is selected from {0.70, 0.80, 0.90, 1.00}, and an optional log-space long-term blending weight alpha is selected from {0, 0.25, 0.50, 0.75, 1.00}, using pre-2024 rolling-origin RMSE only. The best DFTS setting was rho = 0.70 with RMSE = 120.17 million USD; adding the long-term log-trend component did not reduce RMSE, so the selected alpha was 0 and the hybrid candidate collapsed to the DFTS component. Its frozen 2024 forecast was USD 591.91 million, corresponding to a 16.63% absolute percentage error, compared with 10.51% for the naive benchmark. Conclusion: The revised evidence does not support a claim that the hybrid/DFTS candidate outperforms simple benchmarks on this short annual series. Title: Wireless mobile charging for emergency electric vehicle routing: A mixed-integer and metaheuristic framework for in-motion energy transfer
Abstract: As electric vehicles (EVs) become central to decarbonization efforts, the need for uninterrupted power supply in time-critical logistics, particularly in medical transportation, poses unique challenges for power systems integration. Title: Nature sells: How visual biophilia influences promotional effectiveness of service firms

Abstract: Amidst the crowded media environment and growing consumer disconnection from nature, leveraging biophilia - the innate human tendency to connect with nature - offers a compelling way for service firms to attract and engage consumers. Title: Comparing applicants’ self-presentation in artificial intelligence versus human interviews: The role of opportunity to perform and contingency-based interactivity
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming increasingly embedded in employment interviews. Although AI interviewers may enhance the efficiency and standardization of personnel selection, their effects on applicants’ authentic and inauthentic self-presentation remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on impression management theory, this study examines how AI interviewers, relative to human interviewers, shape applicants’ self-presentation and why differences arise. Across four studies, we find that applicants facing AI interviewers perceive fewer opportunities to perform than those facing human interviewers. This reduced opportunity to perform, in turn, weakens not only exaggerated self-enhancement but also authentic self-presentation and authentic self-enhancement. These findings indicate that AI interviewers do not constrain deceptive impression management. They also dampen the expression of genuine strengths and self-relevant information. The results also show that contingency-based interactivity can mitigate this disadvantage by enhancing applicants’ perceived opportunity to perform and narrowing the gap between AI and human interviewers.
