Title: Exploring Metadata in Enterprise Architecture by Applying Conceptual Graphs—Formal Concept Analysis (CGFCA) to Moregraph
Abstract: Enterprise Architecture (EA) is increasingly driven by heterogeneous metadata drawn from cloud-based APIs, ERP systems, and platform reference architectures. This paper revisits Moregraph, a metadata-driven EA platform that combines OData API metadata parsing, force-directed graph visualisation, and extends its specification with Conceptual Graph – Formal Concept Analysis (CGFCA). Title: Process Binoculars: Resilient Log Generation from Multi-video Sources

Abstract: Process mining links event data to process models, typically assuming structured logs. However, many actual processes do not leave digital traces and need to be discovered in the field. Abstract: This paper evaluates the impact of a pilot innovative project aiming at promoting a replicable model to create access to distributed electricity in rural areas where grid extension is economically infeasible. The experimental dimension of the paper is based on a treatment implemented at the locality level. A dozen of comparable localities had been initially selected after a common pre-feasibility study as suitable for the project, and the project has been randomly implemented in only half of them. Findings reveal notable improvements in household access to electricity, particularly in the use of modern energy services like lighting and phone charging. The project has also triggered nascent new economic activities, especially secondary income-generating occupations, though the overall impact on household wealth remains limited. Authors: Wang H.; Sun Y.; Rao Z.; Gong R.; Zhao Y.
Title: Driving low-carbon technology diffusion in heterogeneous steel enterprises through carbon emissions trading: An evolutionary game analysis
Abstract: Subjected to the carbon neutrality goal, the carbon emissions trading scheme (CETS) has become an essential market-oriented tool for carbon emission reduction in high-emission sectors like the steel industry through the diffusion of low-carbon technologies. However, the heterogeneous responses to CETS across enterprises of different scales remain unclear, limiting the differentiated policy design. This study presents a tripartite evolutionary game model involving the government, large-scale steel enterprise (LSE), and small-scale steel enterprise (SSE) to investigate the low-carbon technology diffusion driven by CETS. By incorporating enterprise-scale heterogeneity like innovation capacity, financing constraints, risk preferences, and policy responsiveness, the model examines the evolutionary pathways of technology adoption under various policy and market conditions. The results show that the evolutionary trajectory of low-carbon technology adoption follows a staged framework but a non-sequential progression, encompassing four distinct scenarios including low-incentive, government-driven promotion, multi-stakeholder collaborative adoption, and industry self-regulation. Shifts between these scenarios are contingent on the interplay of carbon price, quota allocation and other policies considering scale heterogeneity. LSE is highly sensitive to carbon price, while SSE requires relatively light quota constraints combined with sufficiently high carbon price to overcome the barriers for technology diffusion. Furthermore, when collaboration costs fall below a certain threshold, it can effectively shorten the cycle of corporate strategic adjustments, prompting businesses to swiftly transition from partial adoption to comprehensive implementation of low-carbon technologies. This study provides the theoretical understanding of CETS-induced technology diffusion and targeted policy insights for advancing the low-carbon transformation of the steel industry. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: From standards to patent pools: SEP-owner heterogeneity and the staged formation of collective licensing
Abstract: Patent pools enable owners of standard-essential patents (SEPs) to coordinate licensing for standards-based technologies, but doing so requires agreement among firms with divergent competitive positions, technological capabilities, and commercialization interests. We develop a staged governance framework in which SEP-owner composition is associated with patent pool formation through theorized stage-contingent mechanisms. The conditions that increase the governance necessity and coalition feasibility of collective licensing in Stage 1 need not be the same conditions that enable rapid agreement in Stage 2; in some cases, the same compositional feature can operate in opposite directions across the two stages. Using a new dataset covering nearly 1000 ICT standards, of which 57 became viable pool candidates, we estimate a two-stage survival-selection model that jointly examines whether a standard enters the pool-formation process and, conditional on entry, the time required to launch a pool. We find that greater heterogeneity in SEP owners' knowledge domains increases the likelihood of pool candidacy but slows formation, suggesting that fragmented technological ownership raises governance necessity while impeding execution. Business-domain heterogeneity is associated with slower formation but has no detectable association with candidacy, a pattern consistent with an execution-stage friction. SEP-quality dispersion is associated with lower candidacy and slower formation, a pattern consistent with asymmetric outside options weakening coalition feasibility and bargaining efficiency. The findings provide ex ante observable indicators of licensing-coordination delay risk and suggest that standard establishment alone is insufficient for timely commercialization when IP ownership is fragmented across heterogeneous SEP owners. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Developing and Configuring Artificial-Intelligence Systems in Manufacturing: Adoption Insights from a Practitioner Survey

Abstract: Artificial-Intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly regarded as key enablers of smart manufacturing, offering benefits such as reduced downtime, improved efficiency, or enhanced quality. Yet, the adoption of scientific approaches in practice remains limited due to persistent challenges in appropriate transfer, implementation, deployment, and configuration. In this article, we report on a survey with 26 AI-system practitioners from the manufacturing domain, focusing on their opinions and experience regarding three pillars: development, configuration, and perceived value. Our results show that development is primarily hindered by data quality and integration barriers, while configuration problems, such as version conflicts or unintended feature interactions, occur frequently and lead to business-critical impacts, including downtime and vulnerabilities. Nevertheless, practitioners perceive clear value in AI systems, especially in predictive maintenance, although broader applications, such as real-time optimization or advanced quality control, remain underexploited. Overall, the study provides valuable insights into how AI systems are currently adopted in manufacturing practice. Title: Supply chain digitalization and ESG greenwashing: A signal reliability perspective
Abstract: Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) greenwashing is often attributed to firm-level opportunism, yet less is understood about how the broader information environment systematically shapes the reliability of ESG signals. We address this gap by examining how supply chain digitalization (SCD) curbs greenwashing by reducing two distinct information asymmetries and enhancing signal reliability. We argue that digitalization enhances supply chain transparency, thereby improving signal fit by reducing supply chain vertical information asymmetry, and strengthening signal honesty by reducing ESG disclosure information asymmetry. Title: When AI ads backfire: Deconstructing consumer backlash to GenAI advertising

Title: An adaptive defense generation method for mimic honeypots based on Minimax-Q game theory
Abstract: Honeypots serve as powerful tools for protecting critical internal assets by deploying resources without real value as decoys to attract, capture, and analyze attacker behaviors, and have been widely applied in enterprise-level advanced network defense systems. However, as the cybersecurity landscape evolves, attackers are increasingly developing anti-honeypot techniques that can identify and bypass deception mechanisms, or even exploit honeypots as stepping stones to compromise other hosts, thus escalating overall network risks. Consequently, maintaining both strong deception capability and intrinsic security has become a key challenge in network defense. To address this issue, we propose an adaptive defense generation method for mimic honeypots based on Minimax-Q game theory, which effectively enhances both deception and security in honeypot defense systems. Specifically, building upon the multi-level adjudication mechanism, we design mimic honeypots composed of multiple business executors and further define the reward evaluation function of each executor to quantify its defensive effectiveness. Subsequently, an attack–defense game model for mimic honeypots is constructed, and the Minimax-Q reinforcement learning algorithm is employed to solve for the Bayesian Nash equilibrium, enabling the adaptive generation of optimal defense strategies. Furthermore, a dynamic scheduling mechanism is integrated to replace suspicious executors in real time, thereby preventing attackers from further compromising other hosts. Finally, experimental results show that compared with existing methods, the proposed mimic honeypot demonstrates significant advantages in both deception capability and intrinsic security, offering new insights for building more robust network defense systems. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Finding green start-ups at scale: Automating selection through Natural Language Processing algorithms
Abstract: Research and policy interest in green entrepreneurship is growing, but identifying green start-ups remains a major challenge because the concept of “green” is inconsistently defined across studies, and existing identification strategies often rely on costly, non-scalable, or discretionary procedures. The results show that automated text-based identification can capture a broad and policy-relevant landscape of green start-ups while preserving thematic heterogeneity across environmental domains. To illustrate the analytical value of the framework, we compare the resulting distribution of these green start-ups across topics with Italy's National Recovery and Resilience Plan investments and with SDG performance indicators. This application reveals both areas of alignment and mismatch between entrepreneurial emergence, policy priorities, and environmental sustainability challenges. Title: Voluntary sustainability standards and industrial fisheries: Roles of friend of the sea certification on occupational safety and working conditions in Nigeria, Gulf of Guinea
Abstract: Fishing, especially within industrial sectors, is widely recognized as one of the most dangerous occupations in the world, as fishers are exposed to adverse physical and environmental risks. While legal frameworks in Nigeria provide occupational safety and labor protections for industrial fishers, inconsistencies in enforcement and compliance persist. Voluntary sustainability standards (VSS) have been promoted as market-based mechanisms to reduce risks, increase safety compliance, and improve working conditions. Despite their relevance, evidence of their impacts on industrial fisheries remains unclear. This study examines the effects of the Friend of the Sea (FOS) certification program on the occupational safety and working conditions of industrial fishers in Nigeria's Gulf of Guinea, Atlantic Ocean. A mixed methods approach was employed, integrating quantitative surveys with semi-structured interviews with key informant to facilitate triangulation among participants recruited from FOS-certified and Business as Usual (BAU) fishing companies. Title: Privacy‑by‑Design Customer Data Platform for Hyper‑Personalized, Cost‑Efficient B2B‑SaaS Lead Acquisition

Abstract: Escalating privacy regulations and siloed customer signals drive up acquisition costs for Business-to-Business (B2B) Software as a Service (SaaS) firms, yet most Customer Data Platform (CDP) still treat consent, identity resolution, and segmentation as disconnected tasks. This paper introduces a privacy‑by‑design CDP that unifies explicit‑consent capture, hybrid deterministic-probabilistic identity resolution, and combined behavioural and psychographic‑based segmentation into a single event‑driven pipeline that feeds automated multichannel campaigns. Deployed for 28 live campaign‑days at a mid‑market SaaS provider, the platform lowered cost‑per‑lead by 84% and lifted budget‑normalized lead volume by 6.4 to 7.0 times, relative to the incumbent batch process. Title: The mediating role of information security efficiency in the relationship between digital transformation and banking service quality
Abstract: This study examines the mediating role of Information Security Efficiency (ISE) in the relationship between Digital Transformation (DT) and Banking Service Quality (BSQ) in Yemen, a developing economy characterized by institutional and operational challenges. Understanding how digital initiatives translate into service improvements is particularly important in such contexts, where infrastructure constraints and security risks may limit the benefits of transformation efforts. The study adopted a quantitative descriptive-analytical design. Data were collected through a structured questionnaire distributed to managerial employees in 17 banks operating in Sana'a city. A total of 401 valid responses were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings reveal that DT exerts a positive and statistically significant direct effect on BSQ ( β = 0.861, p < 0.001 ) and on ISE ( β = 0.848, p < 0.001 ). In addition, ISE has a significant positive effect on BSQ ( β = 0.608, p < 0.001 ). The mediation analysis further confirms that ISE significantly mediates the relationship between DT and BSQ ( β = 0.516, p < 0.001 ), indicating that part of the influence of digital transformation on service quality is transmitted through stronger information security capabilities and controls. At the dimensional level of ISE, confidentiality demonstrated the strongest mediating contribution, followed by timeliness, availability, and integrity. Practically, the results suggest that banks in Yemen and comparable emerging markets should integrate digital transformation strategies with effective information security systems, with particular attention to protecting customer data and ensuring timely information access. The study concludes that, in economically fragile environments, information security efficiency should not be viewed merely as a technical requirement, but a strategic condition for sustaining trust and improving banking service quality. Title: Beyond Correlation: Integrating Process Mining and Causal Inference for Root Cause Analysis
Abstract: The increasing digitalization of business processes has made Root Cause Analysis (RCA) essential for diagnosing Service Level Agreement (SLA) violations. While recent process mining and machine learning techniques automate the extraction of actionable features from event logs, they predominantly frame RCA as a predictive classification task. However, predictive classification is insufficient for identifying root causes because it merely highlights variables that frequently co-occur with anomalies, failing to distinguish between a harmless symptom and an actionable driver. This approach inherently conflates correlation with causation, leaving decision-makers without rigorous proof that intervening on identified bottlenecks will actually mitigate process deviations. To address this gap, this paper proposes a novel, automated framework that bridges predictive process mining with the formal Potential Outcomes framework. Our methodology utilizes global and contextual decision trees to automatically discover candidate treatments and specific operational sub-populations from enriched event logs. Subsequently, we deploy the X-Learner, an advanced causal meta-learning architecture, to rigorously estimate the Conditional Average Treatment Effect (CATE) of these process behaviors. Evaluated on a real-world telecommunications event log, the framework successfully moves beyond correlational analysis to explicitly quantify cause-and-effect relationships. It successfully pinpointed both causal drivers of SLA breaches, such as specific high-risk activities under high workloads, and critical operational mitigators. By providing a scalable and mathematically robust mechanism to rigorously estimate the impact of process attributes, this approach empowers organizations to deploy highly targeted interventions and optimize resource allocation for continuous process improvement. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: A Static Approach to Android Malware Detection Using Ensemble Techniques and SMOTE-Based Data Balancing

Abstract: Android devices are widely used in various activities, including social, business, and communication. Malware, malicious code designed to disrupt or damage computer systems, networks, and devices without user knowledge, is growing exponentially. Traditional signature-based malware detection systems are not effective for detecting obfuscated and encrypted malware, as they lack advanced and updated datasets. To overcome the above challenges, a novel fusion based ensemble technique is proposed to combine with static approaches employing five different classifiers like Extra Tree (ET), Logistic Regression (LR), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Decision Tree (DT) and Random Forest (RF) for the android malware detection to enhance security. Moreover, some classifier gives more accuracy for a particular set of features but not for another set of features. So, the fusion of different classifiers covers all features and gives more accuracy. Prediction accuracy of model also depends on the proportion of different samples. That is why Synthetic Minority Over Sampling Technique (SMOTE) is used to make dataset homogeneous. For prominent feature selection, Variance Threshold (VT) statistical approach is used to train the model. The eminent features like Application Program Interface (API), permissions and network traffic are passed as input to the model. The proposed Android Malware Detection System (AMDS) has been tested on three different datasets namely, TUANDROMD, MALGENOME and DREBIN-215. The outcome of the proposed model demonstrates that our approach successfully detect malware with the accuracy 99.54% along with F1 score of 99.56%. Title: Visual Comparative Analysis of Process Variants

Abstract: Data visualization plays a central role in process mining, particularly when analysts need to compare multiple process models, often representing different process variants, to assess changes, detect deviations, or benchmark performance. Title: The impact of CSR contracting on reputational risk: An expectancy violation theory perspective
Abstract: We focus on a fast-growing phenomenon in which firms link top executive compensation to corporate social responsibility (CSR) criteria, commonly referred to as CSR contracting. Title: Toward a Thai-Specific Generational Cohort Framework: A Basic Individual Values Perspective

Abstract: This study takes a step toward developing a Thai-specific generational cohort framework grounded in the country’s historical, economic, and social transformations. Title: Model-aware counterfactual explanations for transformer-based sequence prediction via attention-guided semantic search
Abstract: Counterfactual explanations for Transformer-based sequence prediction models should change model predictions while remaining semantically plausible and consistent with the underlying data manifold. Existing methods often rely on input-level distance metrics, externally specified constraints, or weakly guided perturbations, limiting their ability to exploit semantic dependencies encoded in neural representations. We propose SAGE, a Semantic Attention-Guided Explanations framework for model-aware counterfactual generation. SAGE formulates counterfactual generation as a constrained semantic optimization problem and transforms the predictive model's attention distribution into a structured probabilistic prior for guiding the search. The framework integrates three components: semantic-aware population initialization in the contextual embedding space, a confidence-aware hybrid fitness function that jointly optimizes target prediction confidence and semantic proximity, and an attention-guided evolutionary operator that perturbs model-relevant sequence elements under feasibility constraints. SAGE is evaluated in predictive business process monitoring, a representative heterogeneous sequence prediction setting involving static attributes and dynamic event sequences. Experiments on BPIC 2017, BPIC 2012, Helpdesk, and Sepsis show that SAGE maintains competitive prediction validity and achieves substantially higher manifold plausibility than most representative baselines. Ablation and controlled comparisons further demonstrate that semantic initialization and attention-guided mutation improve counterfactual quality and search convergence. Under the same evolutionary budget, attention-guided mutation discovers the first valid counterfactual 36.4% earlier in terms of generations than random mutation, although the complete framework remains more computationally expensive than simpler baselines. These results support model-internal attention as an operational search prior for reliable, feasible, and semantically plausible counterfactual explanations. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: Toward Digital Invoicing: A Layered Approach

Abstract: Automated invoice digitization presents substantial challenges due to extreme layout variability, degraded scan quality, and vendor-specific formatting conventions. Traditional approaches based on optical character recognition OCR or neural Intelligent Document Processing (IDP) models frequently fail to maintain structural consistency and logical validity under such heterogeneous conditions. Title: Designing Sustainable BMs for Testbeds in Industry 4.0: An Empirical 5G Testbed Study

Abstract: Testbeds play a critical role in supporting the experimentation, validation, and diffusion of emerging technologies within Industry 4.0. Title: Mechanisms and spatial effects of digital-financial co-agglomeration on urban digital entrepreneurial vitality
Abstract: Based on the panel data of 236 Chinese cities from 2005 to 2022, this study examines the impact of digital-financial co-agglomeration on urban digital entrepreneurial vitality. We measure digital-financial co-agglomeration with a modified E-G index and measure urban digital entrepreneurial vitality with a labor-market approach based on firm registration data. The results show that co-agglomeration significantly increases urban digital entrepreneurial vitality. The findings remain robust after addressing endogeneity and conducting multiple robustness checks. Mechanism tests indicate that venture capital activity and technological innovation mediate the effect. Spatial econometric results further show significant spillovers, and the indirect effect exceeds the direct effect. Threshold estimates reveal a non-linear effect that becomes stronger after the threshold is crossed. © 2026 The Authors

Title: The Rise of Agentic Analytics: Towards Autonomous Decision Intelligence Systems
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: The traditional data analytics value chain that spans the phases of description, diagnosis, prediction, and prescription, typically concludes before execution, leaving a critical gap between analytical insight and action. This “last-mile” gap is widely noted in the prescriptive analytics literature and contributes to unrealized value [1]. This gap often results in measurable value loss, particularly in data-rich and time-sensitive domains. The latency or cost of inaction manifests as millions of dollars in inefficiencies, suboptimal resource allocation, and diminished responsiveness to market dynamics, therefore establishing a critical need to use end-to-end AI enabled decisioning in supply chain This “last-mile” gap is widely noted in the prescriptive analytics literature and contributes to unrealized value [2]. This paper proposes a three-tier agentic architecture [3] for building an end-to-end, closed-loop Decision Intelligence (DI) system designed to significantly reduce decision latency. The framework integrates three purpose-built components: Diagnostic Engine – Automates and scales KPI driver analysis, performing fine-grained variance attribution and contribution analysis to precisely isolate performance drivers; Cognitive Engine – A Large Language Model (LLM)-based module that transforms structured diagnostics into contextual, natural language insights and analytical narratives [4]; Action Engine – An autonomous, LLM-based agent that distills actionable trends from these narratives and can recommend or execute corrective workflows such as rebalancing business volume, onboarding new partners, raising exceptions, or initiating financial recovery [5].The Action Engine operates under a principled, Human-in-the-Loop (HITL) governance framework [6] that ensures safety, accountability, and continuous human oversight. By tightly coupling diagnosis, interpretation, and action, this architecture advances traditional decision-support analytics into a truly autonomous decision-making system enhancing operational resilience and unlocking significant business value. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Beyond technological readiness: How financial benefit and top management support drive public electric vehicle charging station investment in Indonesia
Abstract: This study investigates what drives potential business partners in Indonesia to invest in public electric vehicle charging stations (PEVCS). Using the TOE framework and TPB, this study examines key determinants of investment decisions in a B2B context. Survey data from 242 organizational respondents were analyzed using PLS-SEM. Results indicate that Perceived Financial Benefit (PFB) is the strongest driver of investment intention, consistent with the economic logic that business decision-makers prioritize profitability and anticipated returns over other considerations. Top Management Support (TMS) also emerges as influential, directly affecting investment intention and reinforcing financial confidence among organizational stakeholders. A notable characteristic of the sample dominated by national private firms with highly centralized structures appears to meaningfully shape how decisions are made within organizations. One of the more striking outcomes of this study is that Government Support (GSP) showed no direct bearing on investment intention. Government incentives only drive investment when perceived as tangible financial gains via cost reduction or revenue growth confirming that policy instruments must translate into firm-level economic value to influence decisions. Perceived complexity, meanwhile, did not register as a meaningful obstacle within this sample, suggesting that surveyed organizations possess formalized capabilities to manage technical and integration challenges. On the other hand, perceived compatibility proved consistently relevant, particularly when the technology slots naturally into pre-existing systems such as parking facilities or customer loyalty programs, thereby amplifying perceived financial returns. From a practical standpoint, these findings carry important implications for policymakers, specifically the need to sharpen messaging on return on investment when engaging top management and to design incentive structures that speak directly to financial attractiveness. While contributing to the sustainable energy infrastructure literature, the cross-sectional design limits causal inference; future studies should examine how ownership type and competitive dynamics moderate investment decisions. Title: The Role of Smart Technologies in Sustainable Logistics: A Good Practice of Lithuanian Logistics Companies
Source title: Advances in Science, Technology and Innovation
Abstract: The implementation of smart technologies, including advanced robotics, artificial intelligence, autonomous vehicles, blockchain, drones, internet of things, etc., plays a crucial role in fostering sustainability within the field of logistics. These technologies enable cost reduction, enhanced productivity, increased adaptability, improved quality, reduced environmental impact, energy consumption mitigation, carbon emission reduction, and waste minimization. The purpose of the paper is to examine the factors determining the implementation of smart technologies toward sustainability in logistics companies from a theoretical and practical point of view. Systematic literature analysis and case study methods were used. Through analysis of 115 papers from 2011 to 2022, the factors determining the application of smart technologies toward sustainability in logistics companies were identified. Fifth case studies were used to investigate good practice implementing smart technologies. Analysis showed that implementation of smart technologies depends on internal factors, such as the size of the logistics company, business growth potential, organizational structure, culture, and complexity of internal processes. External factors such as the quality and price of smart technologies in market, user-friendliness, complexity, popularity and security, environmental competitiveness, legal regulation, availability and support of external expertise and services, and others also have a significant influence. Case analysis showed that business technology platforms were used, big data analysis and artificial intelligence solutions were actively applied, investments were made in warehouse technologies, and various robotic solutions were used. By managing information and data flows, companies not only create a better network between logistics companies, but also get an effective instrument that allows timely monitoring and control of all-important processes in the supply chain. Quick identification of problems and their solution allows us to avoid losses, reduce service costs, and increase customer satisfaction. At the same time, it indirectly contributes to reducing the negative impact on the environment. Despite the obvious benefits of smart technologies, their implementation is associated with challenges, such as high implementation costs, limited financial resources of companies, lack of qualified employees, employee resistance to digitization. To ensure the implementation of smart technologies in logistics companies toward sustainability, it is important to identify the factors hindering their application and to eliminate them. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Workplace Satisfaction and Organizational Culture in Thailand: An Explainable Machine Learning Approach Using SHAP
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Abstract: The study examines workplace satisfaction and organizational culture in Thailand by using SHAP-based feature selection within an explainable machine learning framework. The analysis uses survey data from 1,059 respondents from the Global Labor Market Status Survey. In response to concerns about model transparency and causal interpretation, this revised study explicitly treats SHAP as a variable-selection and prediction-interpretation method rather than as a causal estimator. Four predictive models were compared: linear regression, ridge regression, random forest, and XGBoost. XGBoost produced the strongest holdout performance among the compared models, with a test R2 of 0.381 and RMSE of 0.931. SHAP values were then used to identify the organizational culture items that most strongly contributed to the model prediction. The most important variables were respect for individual values, mutual understanding, and flexible thinking. Additional checks using permutation importance, SHAP-selected reduced models, and repeated random-seed stability analysis support the robustness of these variables as predictors. The strongest XGBoost model using the top 15 SHAP-selected variables achieved a test R2 of 0.436 and RMSE of 0.889, indicating that SHAP-based feature selection improved predictive parsimony. The findings suggest that workplace satisfaction in Thailand is increasingly associated with respect for individual values, mutual understanding, and organizational flexibility, while the results are interpreted as predictive associations rather than causal effects. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Unpacking the effects of pro-environmental attitudes on green eWOM from a big data– and LLM-driven perspective: moderating roles of product characteristics
Abstract: As consumers become more concerned about sustainable development, they increasingly share electronic Word-of-Mouth (eWOM) about products and services’ sustainability practices and environmental impacts. However, little research has investigated the drivers of green eWOM and their interactive effects with the product’s multi-dimensional characteristics. Grounded in attitude-behavior-context and theory, this study examines the effect of pro-environmental attitudes on green eWOM leveraging big data (512826 consumer reviews across 2000+ beauty products) and large language models. This study further investigates the moderating roles of the product’s internal characteristic (environmental disclosure) and the product’s external characteristic (popularity). The findings reveal that pro-environmental attitudes positively influence green eWOM behavior, while this positive effect is weakened by product environmental disclosure and popularity. This research contributes to the nascent green eWOM literature, with implications for digital marketing and sustainability strategies. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Author full names: Foss, Nicolai J. (7005282199); Klein, Peter G. (57210470692); Dorobat, Carmen Elena (57203124976); McCaffrey, Matthew (55180484000); Packard, Mark D. (57194398892)
Title: The judgment-based approach to entrepreneurship: The uncertainty–heterogeneity nexus
Abstract: The judgment-based approach (JBA) has emerged as an important contemporary perspective in management and entrepreneurship research. The JBA offers a distinctive theoretical account of entrepreneurship, centered on the formation and implementation of subjective theories of value creation under conditions of Knightian uncertainty, which highlights resource ownership, heterogeneous capital structure, organization and the firm, institutions, uncertainty, and the overarching need to appraise and coordinate all these factors using judgment. We present and develop the JBA by articulating the uncertainty–heterogeneity nexus, in which the joint presence of fundamental uncertainty and heterogeneous resources gives rise to the need for entrepreneurial judgment and makes its exercise economically consequential. Because judgment is subjective, tacit, and difficult to communicate or contract upon, entrepreneurs must rely on ownership and residual control rights to create value, linking judgment to the combination and deployment of resources, profit and loss, and organizational structure. The purpose of this article is threefold. First, we provide a systematic statement of the JBA as a theoretical framework, clarifying its core constructs, causal mechanisms, and domain of application. Second, we engage with key critiques and distinguish the JBA from related approaches, including opportunity-based, effectuation, and bricolage perspectives. Third, we outline directions for future research that build on the JBA's emphasis on judgment, ownership, and the organization and deployment of heterogeneous resources under uncertainty. By integrating these elements, we position the JBA as a coherent and distinctive theory of entrepreneurship with broad implications for research in management, organization, and strategy. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: Modelling barriers to green entrepreneurship in traditional MSMEs: Evidence from the Batik industry in Madura, Indonesia
Abstract: The global transition toward sustainable development has increased pressure on micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) to adopt environmentally responsible business practices. Although green entrepreneurship is widely promoted as a pathway to sustainability, its implementation remains challenging for traditional and culture-based enterprises. Existing studies largely emphasize performance outcomes, while empirical evidence on implementation barriers remains limited. This study examines the key barriers to green entrepreneurship implementation among batik MSMEs in Madura, Indonesia. A quantitative approach was employed using survey data collected from 200 respondents across four regencies. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) with SmartPLS to assess the relationships between government policy, technology adoption, environmental education, and implementation barriers. The findings reveal that technology-related constraints constitute the most significant barrier, followed by weak regulatory support and limited environmental knowledge. High costs of green technology adoption and insufficient access to education, information, and sustainable production inputs further constrain MSMEs' readiness to transition toward sustainable practices. This study contributes to the green entrepreneurship literature by shifting the analytical focus from sustainability outcomes to implementation barriers in traditional MSMEs and by providing a more robust empirical model using PLS-SEM. The findings offer policy-relevant insights for developing targeted regulatory frameworks, environmental education programs, and technological support mechanisms to facilitate sustainability transitions in heritage-based industries. Moreover, the results provide implications that may be applicable to traditional MSMEs in other developing economies. Title: Energy Efficiency Implementation: Driver–Barrier Analysis of the Macedonian Legislation
Source title: Advances in Science, Technology and Innovation
Abstract: As one of the energy transition pillars, energy efficiency (EE) holds significant untapped potential, not only via facilitating responsible energy use, but concomitantly, for achieving climate targets and environmental protection obligations. Unfortunately, in the Western Balkan countries, the game-changing power of EE is particularly underestimated due to the discrepancy between the by-instalments harmonization with the acquis communautaire of the corresponding country-specific legislation, on one side, and its actual implementation lagging behind, on the other. Though, in the latest Energy Community (EnC) Annual Implementation Report (EnC 2022), EnC notes Macedonian average annual progress of 67% in terms of EE, significant differences across sectors are evident. The lowest progress is achieved in buildings (52%) and in heating and cooling (54%), whereby the latter, is mainly because only the Macedonian capitol has a developed district heating system, while the majority of households across country use inefficient electrical heating appliances or firing wood. The European Commission (EC) annual accession progress report (EC 2022, Ch. 15) is significantly stricter in assessing country progress as ‘limited’. Considering the above, this study focuses on identifying and quantifying barriers and drivers relevant for implementing EE legislation in Macedonia (As of Feb 2019, the official name of R. Macedonia, has been changed to R. North Macedonia). Though the Law on Energy Efficiency (aligned with the acquis) is in force since 2020, its implementation—as per EC (2022), as well as the EnC (2022) is at a very early stage, while adoption of related by-laws is still pending. Numerous barriers and obstacles—e.g. institutional weakness at national and local level, lack of incentives and/or subsidies among business community, lack of cooperation between stakeholders in promoting innovative solutions, state intervention during crisis, bad governance and corruption, protectionism, etc.—contribute to this. Weighted driver-barrier analysis (DBA) is utilized to categorize and prioritize identified drivers and barriers in accordance to the adopted EE implementation categories—targets/policy measures, buildings, financing, product labelling, heating/cooling, industry—Further, possibilities for transforming certain barriers into drivers, based on country-specific aspects are elaborated and examined. The obtained results are categorized to enable effective assistance for decision-makers in fostering and improved implementation of the Macedonian EE legislation. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Authors: Phan H.-T.; Le X.-B.; Quan T.
Title: Uncertainty-Aware Forecasting and Inventory Optimization for ATM Cash Management in Vietnam
Abstract: ATM networks remain essential cash-distribution infrastructure in cash-intensive economies such as Vietnam, where cash still accounts for most consumer payments. Effective replenishment requires balancing the opportunity cost of idle capital against the risk of stockouts. We evaluate a forecast-then-optimize framework that integrates modern probabilistic deep learning models with a periodic-review base-stock policy. Thirty forecasting configurations are benchmarked, including statistical baselines (SARIMA, Exponential Smoothing, Prophet), tree-based ensembles (LightGBM, Random Forest), and global neural architectures (N-BEATS, Temporal Fusion Transformer), using daily withdrawal data from 84 ATMs over 3.7 years. Performance is assessed not only by forecast accuracy and calibration, but also by downstream inventory cost under a realistic replenishment policy. Global neural quantile models substantially outperform classical alternatives, reducing simulated total cost by roughly half while maintaining near-perfect calibration and 99% fill rates. Importantly, forecast accuracy alone proves to be an unreliable indicator of business outcomes, as models with similar error can yield markedly different costs. ATM-level heterogeneity further shows that no single model dominates across all locations, supporting a monitoring-based deployment strategy that adapts model assignments according to realized cost. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: HyProTwin: Hybrid Digital Process Twins for Predictive Simulation of Continuous Processes
Abstract: Business process management has mostly studied discrete processes with clearly identifiable process outcomes, e.g., the package delivery by an online shop. In contrast, continuous processes are characterized by real-time, discrete control of complex, continuous physical dynamics to maintain stable operating conditions, e.g., a sewage water treatment process with constant desirable chemical composition. Digital twins (DTs) of continuous processes provide simulation and prediction capabilities to enable real-time decision making that is key for efficient, proactive operations. However, implementation of DTs is greatly hindered by interoperability, communication, orchestration, and modeling challenges. Moreover, real-time decision making could be enhanced by predictive simulation, i.e., the ability to simulate future what-if scenarios to consider future changes and their impact on predictions. To realize DTs of continuous processes and enable predictive simulation, we propose hybrid digital process twins (HyProTwin) with their architecture and predictive simulation techniques. We demonstrate the feasibility and performance of HyProTwin on three real-world continuous processes. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Assessing industrial land-use efficiency at parcel scale: Actual vs. expected economic outputs across diverse parcel types and spatial conditions
Abstract: As urban development shifts toward the optimization of existing built-up areas, identifying inefficient industrial land is increasingly important for targeted land renewal and stock-oriented land governance. Although industrial land-use efficiency (ILUE) has been widely assessed at industrial-park and administrative scales, large-area parcel-scale evaluation remains constrained by limited fine-grained land use information and parcel-scale economic data. To address these limitations, this study develops a parcel-scale ILUE evaluation method by comparing actual economic output (AEO) with expected economic output (EEO), which refers to the reasonably expected output of a parcel given its functional type and spatial conditions. Firstly, using multisource spatiotemporal data, 13,510 industrial parcels in Beijing are classified into four functional types, i.e., technology office, commercial service, manufacturing, and warehouse & logistics, and characterized by built, socio-economic, and ecological conditions. Then, parcel-scale AEO is estimated by integrating gridded economic information with administrative industrial statistics, while EEO is estimated using cyclic random forest regression (CRF-R) to capture nonlinear spatial condition–output relationships. Our results reveal 3684 inefficient parcels, primarily concentrated in southern and eastern peri-urban districts. Compared with observed business revenue and documented renewal projects, the downscaled AEO better captures parcel-scale economic variation, while the inefficient parcels identified using CRF-R achieved a 76.7% project-level spatial correspondence rate. Based on feature importance analysis, the study gives type-specific governance recommendations, including improving transit accessibility for office and commercial land, supplementing residential and public service for manufacturing land, and increasing development intensity and road accessibility for logistics-oriented parcels, thereby providing a practical diagnostic tool for differentiated industrial land renewal. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Rewarding leadership: CEO compensation and growth outcomes in agricultural industry
Abstract: Performance-based CEO pay is becoming more popular as a way to align executive incentives with business growth. However, the research results are still not consistent, especially in emerging markets such as Malaysia. In some cases, CEOs continue to receive high compensation even when companies perform poorly, and many companies provide limited disclosure of executive pay. This raises concerns about whether CEO compensation truly supports sustainable company growth. The objective of this study is to examine the relationship between chief executive officer (CEO) compensation and company growth among Malaysian public listed companies. A sample of 25 companies in the agricultural industry from 2021–2023 was selected. All financial data were collected from Orblis and companies' annual reports. Fixed effects panel regression analysis was used to determine the relationship between the dependent and independent variables and control variables. The results reveal a significant positive relationship between CEO compensation and company growth. Title: De-risking equity investment for productive use integration in mini-grids: Designing a first-loss demand-risk guarantee for e-mobility in Kakuma refugee camp, Kenya
Abstract: Achieving commercially viable mini-grid operations in remote areas of sub-Saharan Africa remains constrained by uncertain electricity demand, contributing to investor hesitancy, particularly among equity investors. Productive use of electricity can improve asset utilisation and strengthen revenue generation, but its integration requires additional investment that remains exposed to revenue risk when early-stage demand uptake is uncertain. This paper designs and evaluates a first-loss demand-risk guarantee for electric two-wheeler battery-swapping integration into the solar mini-grid of Kakuma refugee camp, Kenya. Methodologically, the case study is grounded in design science research and combines system sizing, financial modelling, scenario analysis, and guarantee stress testing. The system analysis identifies a technically feasible configuration of 200 electric two-wheelers and 140 spare batteries without additional generation or storage capacity, which is used as input for the financial model. The financial model shows that the business case reaches the equity investor threshold, defined as a 15% equity internal rate of return, only under high vehicle utilisation and with a 25% capital subsidy on charging and swapping infrastructure. The proposed guarantee addresses the resulting utilisation-driven revenue risk through partial first-loss coverage, a utilisation-based activation window, annual payout caps, and a cumulative exposure cap. Scenario results show that the guarantee improves equity returns across all eligible utilisation-shortfall scenarios. It raises the base- and best-case scenarios above the investor threshold and substantially reduces the return gap in the worst-case scenario. The study contributes a project-level design framework for developing demand-risk guarantees as development-finance de-risking instruments for productive-use integration, while highlighting the need for case-specific calibration, robust verification, and further testing across additional mini-grid contexts. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Innovation Platform Activity and Scope: Case Evidence and Future Research Directions

Title: Consumers' servitization experience: Implications for perceived social value and preference for local brands
Source title: Journal of Retailing and Consumer Services
Abstract: This study examines how consumers’ servitization experience may reshape the symbolic and social meanings associated with local brands in sustainable consumption contexts. The increasing adoption of service-based consumption models in retail and consumer services is transforming how consumers interact with brands. While prior research has examined the functional and relational benefits of servitization, less is known about how service-based consumption experiences shape the social meaning of brand consumption and influence consumer preferences in sustainability contexts. The findings suggest that servitization experience may function as a double-edged mechanism: it enhances the social signaling value of local brands while simultaneously weakening direct brand preference. Drawing on a survey of 396 consumers in the automotive sector and using structural equation modeling, the findings indicate that servitization experience is positively associated with the perceived social value of local brands, which is strongly associated with brand preference. At the same time, a negative direct effect on brand preference is observed, revealing trade-offs between experiential benefits and reductions in ownership-based symbolic meaning. Additionally, sustainability-oriented consumers are more likely to engage with servitized offerings and perceive higher social value in local brands. These results contribute to retailing and consumer services research by showing that service-based consumption experiences may reshape not only functional and relational value, but also the social meaning of consumption. Title: The impact of pilot inland free trade zones on household income: Evidence from China
Abstract: Using data from the China Household Finance Survey (CHFS), we employ a staggered difference-in-differences design to examine the effect of the establishment of inland pilot Free Trade Zones (FTZs) on household income. We find that inland FTZs significantly increase household income through increases in wage income, business income, and property income. The income gains are larger for households engaged in leading industries and their supporting sectors, as well as for those with higher human capital and stronger risk tolerance. In addition, inland FTZs reduce both within-city income inequality and the development gap between inland regions and the economic frontier. Title: Impact of wind-assistance on the efficiency of a tramp fleet

Abstract: Wind assisted ship propulsion (WASP) is expected to be an important element for the decarbonization of the shipping industry. Title: A Heterogeneous Sharding Architecture for Privacy-Preserving Consortium Blockchains
Abstract: Consortium blockchains are increasingly used for collaboration between organizations such as supply chains and e-government. However, deployments must isolate sensitive business data across organizations while preserving global auditability, and confidentiality mechanisms based on heavyweight modules often incur substantial overhead. To address these issues, we conduct the following research. Firstly, we propose a heterogeneous “parallel privacy shard” architecture. In this architecture, each organization runs an independent Byzantine Fault Tolerance (BFT) in a privacy shard to maintain its private state, while a mainchain provides request scheduling, routing, and state anchoring. Secondly, we design a mainchain-coordinated execution protocol that enforces organization-level data isolation while preserving public verifiability for transaction confirmation. Finally, we implement a prototype on ChainMaker and evaluate it on AWS EC2. When scaling the number of privacy shards from 1 to 5, throughput improves by about 4.2× while latency increases by only 8.8%. With 5 shards, state-updating contract calls achieve 7.8030 ktx/s throughput with 1.1508 s latency. Results show that our system achieves high throughput and near-linear scalability with only marginal latency increase. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Mapping the evolution from incentives to insights: A bibliometric analysis of executive influences on corporate risk-taking (1996-2025)
Abstract: This bibliometric analysis examines 252 peer-reviewed publications (1996–August 2025) to map the evolution of research on executive influences on corporate risk-taking. By integrating data from both the Web of Science and Scopus databases, this study offers a more comprehensive view of the research landscape compared to previous analyses that often relied on a single source. Relying on a single database risks overlooking contributions published in niche-exclusive journals or regionally concentrated outlets, which disproportionately feature emerging-market research and interdisciplinary studies not uniformly indexed across repositories. Using Biblioshiny and VOSviewer for performance analysis, network construction, and clustering, we document three evolutionary phases: agency-dominated research (1996–2010), demographic integration (2011–2019), and theoretical synthesis (2020–2025). China leads in publication volume (186 articles) while the United States dominates citation impact (28.88 citations per article), reflecting different research priorities and institutional contexts. Keyword co-occurrence analysis identifies five thematic clusters, demonstrating the field's evolution from pure incentive-based studies to behavioral and psychological analyses. Temporal analysis shows compensation research maintaining consistent presence while psychological attributes such as CEO overconfidence and executive power gained prominence post-2020. The findings highlight the growing theoretical integration between agency and behavioral perspectives, with the most influential papers increasingly bridging internal attributes and external incentives. This synthesis provides critical insights for boards, compensation committees, and policymakers seeking to integrate behavioral considerations into executive selection, incentive design, and risk governance frameworks in contemporary complex business environments. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Title: Tobacco Retailer Perspectives on Potential Phase Out of Tobacco Sales in South Australia: An Exploratory Survey
Abstract: Issue Addressed: To examine tobacco retailers' perspectives on the potential phase out of tobacco sales in South Australia, a retail-based tobacco endgame strategy that directly targets product availability. Methods: A cross-sectional mixed-methods survey of licensed tobacco retailers conducted in South Australia in April 2025. The survey included 70 licensed tobacco retailers and assessed anticipated impacts of a retail phase out, strategies they might adopt in response and the support they would seek. Both quantitative ratings and open-text qualitative responses were analysed using descriptive statistics and inductive thematic analysis. Results: Retailers rated legal requirements, declining profitability and reduced consumer demand as the most important drivers for them to cease tobacco sales, while few highlighted public or community health considerations. One-third reported needing lead-in time to transition, citing financial compensation, business planning support and opportunities for product substitution as priorities. Concerns about illicit tobacco trade featured prominently, with many describing reduced legal sales, financial loss and security risks. Retailers held mixed views on phased transition to ending tobacco sales. Conclusions: Some retailers view tobacco as increasingly unprofitable, yet business sustainability concerns and illicit trade complicate retailer support for mandated phase out. Clear timelines and targeted transition support are critical to increasing retailer confidence and policy feasibility. So What?: By aligning tobacco retail phase-out policies with retailer support, governments may be able to reduce tobacco availability while limiting impacts on retailers' livelihoods; further research is needed to confirm how this approach would affect policy acceptability and business transitions at scale. © 2026 The Author(s). Title: A Fiat-Anchored Dual-Rail Triple-Entry Architecture for SSC-Based K-12 Financial Systems
Abstract: School Services Center (SSC) platforms increasingly support tuition and fee collection across multiple educational institutions, yet they often face a persistent separation between fiat settlement and cross-party payment-state visibility, leading to reconciliation delays and weak shared auditability. This paper is grounded in an existing SSC business system and proposes a fiat-anchored dual-rail architecture in which regulated fiat settlement remains off-chain, while payment evidence is normalized, batched into Merkle commitments, and anchored on Cardano as a tamper-evident third entry. In this design, blockchain is not used as the payment rail; instead, it functions as a public evidentiary layer that supports independent verification without exposing raw financial payloads. We evaluate a full-stack prototype using 10,000 synthetic payment events and report a maximum batch size of 1,681 events per anchoring transaction, 609 ms submission-to-receipt latency, 0.0735 ms local proof verification, and an estimated monthly anchoring cost of approximately $4.28 USD under the evaluated workload assumptions. These results indicate promising operational feasibility for extending real SSC deployments with publicly verifiable reconciliation evidence while preserving fiat-native compliance. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Behavioral nudges and feedback lead to improved pre-primary teacher practices in Kenya
Abstract: Many national pre-primary curricula call for classroom practices that support children’s autonomy and teacher-child dialogue, but these practices are observed inconsistently. Teachers in low-resource settings often lack affordable, scalable support and professional development to adopt these practices. This four-month, blinded, incomplete factorial randomized controlled trial evaluated whether low-cost, tech-enabled feedback and behavioral nudges can improve pre-primary teachers’ adoption of seven target practices in Mombasa, Kenya. Teachers (n= 129) were randomized into one of three intervention arms: (1) business as usual (control); (2) observation feedback and weekly WhatsApp nudges (feedback and nudge); or (3) observation feedback, weekly WhatsApp nudges, and two in-person meetings facilitated by early childhood trainers (feedback and nudge + cluster). The primary outcome was the number of target practices observed at endline, adjusting for baseline. Relative to control, teachers in the feedback and nudge arm implemented 0.92 additional practices (d = 0.45), and those in the feedback and nudge + cluster arm 0.94 (d = 0.45). The similar effects across arms suggest no statistically detectable incremental benefit of adding cluster meetings in this sample; the design does not permit conclusions about cluster meetings as a standalone component. Seventy-five percent of teachers reported that the nudges were helpful in improving their understanding of target practices and that they would recommend them to fellow teachers. Attrition was under 1%. Embedding feedback and behavioral nudges within existing early childhood quality assurance and professional development systems may therefore offer a scalable approach to strengthening classroom practice in low- and middle-income contexts. Title: Human-in-the-Loop Entity Linking Visualization and Refinement with KOALA-UI and the Crocodile Framework
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Abstract: Entity linking (EL) on tabular data often produces many ambiguous cell annotations that are costly to review. We present KOALA-UI, a lightweight web interface for inspecting and refining EL results on spreadsheets and CSV-like tables. KOALA-UI provides table navigation, cell-level candidate panels, color-coded scores, simple filtering, and in-place edits with export. To enable reuse across backends, KOALA-UI consumes a compact JSON schema and responses compatible with the W3C Entity Reconciliation specification, allowing integration with potentially any EL backend. We illustrate KOALA-UI with the Crocodile EL framework and demonstrate a human-in-the-loop (HITL) workflow. In addition, we report a preliminary user study, a real business use case, and a validation of pipeline execution through TAO–a workflow engine, where Crocodile was integrated as a module. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Predictive Dropout Research Through a Data-Based Value-Creation Taxonomy: Patterns and Blind Spots
Abstract: Predictive dropout research uses data-based, individual-level predictions for the early identification of at-risk students with the general aim of improving student retention. Yet it lacks a systematic understanding of the specific types of value that its data-driven approaches are expected to create. This study addresses this gap by applying Baecker et al.’s data-based value-creation taxonomy to a purposive sample of 23 predictive dropout studies in higher education contexts. Using the taxonomy as an analytical lens, this study examines how existing research conceptualizes institution-level value-creation through its data foundations, proposed value-creation approaches, and proposed business value. The findings reveal strong convergence, characterized by recurring data foundations and a dominant focus on targeted interventions. In contrast, financial value and institution-level strategic value are rarely articulated. The study contributes a precise conceptual vocabulary for analyzing prediction-based value-creation and clarifies structural patterns and blind spots within predictive dropout research, thereby supporting future empirical work beyond predictive accuracy. © IFIP International Federation for Information Processing 2027.

Title: Optimization of Energy Consumption in Battery-Operated Real-Time Systems
Source title: IFIP Advances in Information and Communication Technology
Abstract: Real-time applications emphasize worst-case scenarios due to their precise timing demands. However, many critical applications of embedded systems have other requirements, such as energy consumption. The results of this study can inform the e-commerce infrastructure, including payment gateways, online transactions, and data-driven logistics. This would be especially beneficial in terms of energy savings and improving operational costs for embedded systems in e-business. This study presents a model for work scheduling that minimizes energy usage by implementing a suitable scheduling algorithm for dynamic power management (DPM) and dynamic voltage scaling (DVS) and evaluating the effectiveness of power management approaches. Applying DVS leads to an 84.03% reduction in energy consumption, while using DPM reduces the total energy consumed by devices by 66.76%. Combining DPM and DVS yields similar energy savings to DVS alone (83.22%) but with the potential for more significant energy savings due to external device involvement. While this combination can lead to longer execution times, a significant reduction in energy consumption makes it a worthwhile trade-off for energy-efficient computing. © IFIP International Federation for Information Processing 2027.

Title: From symbolic gestures to substantive reform: how ethics shape the diffusion of gender quota responses
Abstract: Drawing on institutional theory and behavioral ethics, we investigate how firms interpret, enact, and respond to gender quota mandates within organizational networks. Based on 6038 firm-year observations from listed firms in France, Germany, and Italy, we find that symbolic compliance is widespread and positively associated with exposure to symbolic peer behavior. We further find that firms with stronger ethics-oriented compliance tendencies are less susceptible to symbolic peer influence and exhibit greater substantive compliance. Exploratory analyses indicate that this moderating effect is most pronounced in France and among larger firms. By integrating institutional diffusion with internal interpretive orientation, this study extends research on symbolic compliance and heterogeneous organizational responses to gender quota policies. The findings suggest that the effectiveness of institutional reforms depends not only on formal regulatory requirements but also on how organizations interpret and enact them within their governance practices. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Title: Buffer or burden? The role of corporate reputation in the market valuation effects of suppliers’ human rights controversies
Abstract: Does corporate reputation buffer firms from reputational spillovers, or can it backfire when controversies arise? This study examines how corporate reputation shapes the market-valuation consequences of suppliers’ human-rights controversies, recognizing that shareholders may hold focal firms accountable for upstream misconduct. Using an international panel of RepTrak® Pulse firms from 2011 to 2023, we show that supplier-related human-rights controversies are associated with lower market valuation and that corporate reputation amplifies this negative association, consistent with a reputational “boomerang” effect. We further theorize and test firm visibility as a boundary condition: the reputational burden is stronger when the focal firm receives higher media coverage, reflecting greater public visibility and stakeholder attention. We estimate interaction-based dynamic panel models using two-step System GMM to address endogeneity and complement coefficient estimates with marginal-effects analyses to facilitate interpretation of conditional relationships. Robustness checks using market-to-book yield qualitatively similar inferences. The findings suggest that highly reputed and highly visible firms need supply-chain governance mechanisms that can anticipate, detect, and respond to upstream human-rights controversies. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Title: Linking multiple sources of performance feedback to firm behavior: the combined effect of technological and financial performance on innovation
Abstract: The behavioral theory of the firm proposes that performance feedback based on aspiration gaps influences search behavior. Prior research has focused on testing this proposition predominantly using financial performance, with less consideration of other critical sources of feedback, such as technological performance. We argue that both types of performance feedback jointly influence subsequent innovative activities by providing distinct information regarding how firms should balance their degree of exploration and exploitation. We provide evidence that while financial performance feedback impacts the scope and nature of firms’ exploratory search across technological domains, technological performance feedback influences the types of knowledge leveraged and utilized in the search. In doing so, we contribute by developing theory and evidence for why multiple sources of performance feedback matter in decision making amid uncertain exploratory and exploitation processes and how these sources together affect the behavioral states and the innovation strategy of the firm. © 2026 Elsevier Inc. Title: Economic Diplomacy and Urban Innovation: Pioneering Smart Cities in Morocco
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: This article explores the concept of “smart cities” in Morocco, highlighting the pivotal role of economic diplomacy, innovation, and entrepreneurship in urban development. It begins with a review of the smart city concept and its key components from existing literature to frame the study. The research then analyzes smart city implementations in Morocco through case studies of Casablanca, Benguerir, and the Zenata Eco-City, illustrating practical applications and the significance of international partnerships in fostering technological and economic advancement. Additionally, the article investigates how economic diplomacy strategically supports innovation and entrepreneurship to drive sustainable urban growth. By examining Morocco’s diplomatic efforts, it reveals how collaboration and investment attraction enhance digital business ecosystems aligned with smart city goals. Using a qualitative approach, the study analyzes official reports, academic sources, and institutional publications, supplemented by detailed case study evaluations. The findings demonstrate that integrating economic diplomacy with innovation and entrepreneurship is essential for successful smart city initiatives, promoting sustainable economic development and positioning Morocco as a leader in digital urban transformation. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: A Systematic Literature Review of Approaches to Maturity Model Implementation in Public Bodies Using Agile Initiatives
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Abstract: For public bodies, implementing maturity models is vital for enhancing competitiveness and service quality. Adopting flexible and adaptable processes enables organizations to better meet the demands of a dynamic society. However, adopting agile methodologies requires careful planning. The variety of agile methodologies (e.g. Scrum, SAFe and Kanban) can be confusing, making it challenging to select the most appropriate approach. Poorly planned implementation can lead to process overload, team resistance and, ultimately, failure to achieve the desired outcome. To mitigate these challenges, public bodies should invest in a gradual, personalized implementation process and process models adopted by other organizations. When choosing an agile methodology, factors such as team size, project complexity, organizational culture, and strategic objectives must be considered. Additionally, strong support from senior management and engagement from all employees are crucial. A gradual, personalized approach increases the likelihood of successfully implementing a maturity model using agile methodologies. This work presents an extended Systematic Literature Review (SLR) aimed at identifying effective approaches to implementing maturity models in public bodies. The SLR analyzed 13 primary studies, revealing practices, recommendations, standards, implementation strategies, benefits, challenges, and considerations in these processes. The shared characteristics of the implementation processes reported in different bodies suggest that these findings could form the basis for other public bodies to adopt similar methodologies. This work makes a valuable contribution by consolidating recommendations that can streamline the implementation of maturity models, enabling managers and stakeholders to develop clearer implementation plans and ensure a smoother process. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: From perception to feasibility: Explaining AI adoption in SMEs through the TOE framework
Abstract: This study aims to examine the determinants of artificial intelligence (AI) adoption among small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in Central Java, Indonesia, by applying the Technology-Organization-Environment (TOE) framework with a focus on organizational readiness, financial capability, and perceived usefulness. Despite the growing availability of affordable AI-based applications, AI adoption among SMEs remains relatively limited, particularly in developing regions where resource constraints and uneven levels of digital readiness continue to hinder digital transformation. This study employs a quantitative approach using survey data collected from 117 SME owners and managers in Central Java. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM) to test the proposed relationships among the constructs. The findings reveal that financial capability, organizational readiness, and perceived usefulness all exert positive and significant effects on AI adoption. Among these determinants, perceived usefulness demonstrates the strongest influence, followed by organizational readiness and financial capability. These results indicate that both technological perceptions and organizational capabilities are important drivers of AI adoption decisions among SMEs, with perceived usefulness emerging as the most influential determinant. The study contributes to the literature by extending the application of the TOE framework to the context of AI adoption among SMEs in a developing economy and by providing empirical evidence from SMEs in Central Java, a regional context that remains underexplored in prior AI adoption research. The findings also offer practical implications for policymakers and SME owners in designing strategies that simultaneously strengthen organizational capabilities and enhance awareness of the benefits of AI technologies to accelerate digital transformation among SMEs. Title: Hybrid Leadership in the Age of the Metaverse: Navigating Between Physical and Virtual Workplaces
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: The swift advancement of digital technologies, propelled by worldwide disruptions including the COVID-19 pandemic, has transformed organizational operations and the dynamics of leader-team interactions. With businesses’ growing adoption of hybrid work models, a novel leadership paradigm is taking shape, necessitating the capacity to lead effectively in both physical and virtual environments. The emergence of the Metaverse introduces significant potential for enhancing workplace interaction, providing immersive and persistent digital environments that fundamentally alter collaboration, communication, and organizational culture. This study investigates the notion of hybrid leadership within the framework of the Metaverse, analyzing the strategies leaders can employ to adeptly manage the convergence of physical office environments and virtual work settings. This study synthesizes current literature, industry practices, and theoretical frameworks to delineate the essential competencies for effective hybrid leadership in an evolving context. The identified competencies encompass digital fluency, emotional intelligence, inclusivity, and sustaining trust and engagement within decentralized, technology-driven contexts. This study further examines the challenges leaders encounter, including digital fatigue, ethical considerations, and technological disparities, while emphasizing opportunities such as the integration of global talent, gamified learning approaches, and data-driven decision-making processes. Title: From quality to value: linking product and system perspectives in the plastic packaging ecosystem
Abstract: This study investigates value in the plastic packaging ecosystem. Previously, we identified the quality perceptions of technical actors, such as polymer producers, converters and recyclers. Using semi-structured interviews, we now extend this by focusing on value for broader ecosystem actors which influence and are influenced by technical actors, such as governments, investors, and academics. Two broad themes emerged from the data analysis which combined lead to the notion of value: quality and system performance. Quality is identified at the product level and consists of the nine previously identified categories: purity, uniformity, mechanical properties, physical properties, processability, functionality, regulations & safety, substitutability and circularity. System performance is defined at the system level and consists of four categories: sustainability, technology fit, multi-criteria performance, and market acceptance. While system performance categories are separate concepts, they do interconnect. This new understanding of value facilitates better alignment in the plastic packaging ecosystem and initiatives. © 2026 The Authors
