Title: Improving Environmental Quality in the Mediterranean: The Impact of Financialization, Human Capital, and Energy Efficiency
Source title: Advances in Science, Technology and Innovation
Abstract: Context/Purpose: Environmental quality is one of the cardinal goals of the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) of the United Nations. However, prior research has overlooked the necessity of energy efficiency, knowledge economy, and financial resources in achieving environmental quality. Thus, by capturing the contributions of financialization measured in terms of financial development, human capital in terms of returns on education, and energy efficiency in evaluating the environmental quality impact in the Mediterranean, this study offers a fresh perspective. The Mediterranean area is experiencing significant stability problems as a result of its higher rate of warming than the world’s average. Methods: Depending on the availability of data, the study makes use of a panel data covering ten Mediterranean countries between 1990 and 2018 on five variables, namely, ecological footprint, financial development, human capital, energy efficiency and economic growth. The sources of the data include Global Footprint Network (GFN), International Monetary Fund (IMF), Penn World Table (PWT), and World Development Indicators (WDI), respectively. The research utilizes the Cross-Sectional Autoregressive Distributed Lag (CS-ARDL) model. Results: The results showed that financial development and economic growth exert a decreasing impact on environmental quality by incrasing ecological footprint, while human capital and energy efficiency enhance environmental quality in the Mediterranean region by decreasing ecological footprint. Interpretation: The results imply that, in spite of their advantages, financialization and economic expansion contribute to environmental deterioration in the region. This is because growing economies frequently need more raw materials, which deepens extraction and the depletion of natural resources. Furthermore, increased production and consumption usually lead to increased waste and pollution, which degrades the quality of the air, water, and land. Financialization can also push companies to put short-term earnings ahead of long-term sustainability, which can result in environmentally harmful business practices. Conclusion: The findings suggest that financialization, human capital, and energy efficiency are significant factors that influence environmental quality in the Mediterranean region and ought to be taken into consideration when formulating policy decisions. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Structural and Algorithmic Limitations in LLM-Driven BPMN Generation: A Rapid Review of Empirical Evidence
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: Business Process Management (BPM) demands formalized models, yet manual BPMN construction remains labor-intensive and error-prone. Large Language Models (LLMs) present opportunities for automated text-to-model translation, though their effectiveness remains underexplored. This rapid review synthesizes 11 empirical investigations published from 2023 to 2025, revealing a nascent field dominated by GPT-4 (55% adoption) and prompt-based methodologies (64% prevalence). Our analysis uncovers critical structural deficiencies: LLMs demonstrate fundamental incapacity for graph-theoretic reasoning and set-theoretic spatial optimization required for valid BPMN layouts. Specifically, 55% of surveyed approaches fail with non-trivial process complexity, while 64% lack reproducible artifacts. Execution of all 4 available implementations (S4, S6, S7, S8) confirmed severe degradation when confronted with hierarchical structures, parallel gateways, or spatial coordinate systems (Diagram Interchange). We conclude that current approaches conflate linguistic pattern matching with algorithmic reasoning—a categorical error that mandates hybrid architectures combining LLM semantic extraction with specialized graph layout algorithms. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Defining family firms: A survey of empirical criteria
Abstract: We survey 153 empirical studies of family firms and document 192 operational definitions representing 25 distinct definition types. These definitions can be decomposed into five recurring, codable dimensions: ownership, management, board representation, embeddedness, and succession. We relate these dimensions to economic mechanisms including agency conflicts, residual control rights, transaction costs, and dynastic control. Alternative definitions select systematically different populations and yield materially different estimates of firm performance and innovation. Definition choice is largely unrelated to the research question, except in succession studies. Ownership thresholds track private enforcement of self-dealing rules, but not statutory shareholder rights or rule of law. We conclude that the family firm is a family of related constructs rather than a single latent construct. Definitions should therefore match the family-firm construct implied by the research question, and results should be reported across alternative classification rules. © 2026 Elsevier B.V.

Title: The Path to Venture Creation: A Moderated Mediation Model of Entrepreneurial Alertness, Intention, and Education on Entrepreneurial Behavior

Title: Method-level technical debt detection based on source code and comments
Abstract: Technical debt (TD) refers to suboptimal code resulting from compromises made by developers to meet business budgets or time constraints. Existing studies mainly focus either on code or comments, which restricts their applicability. Additionally, current research often overlooks the granularity of TD, which can lead to inaccurate identification and inefficient remediation of technical debt. To address these challenges, this paper introduces TDD-TCNN, a novel deep-learning approach for method-level TD detection through source code and comments from multiple perspectives. We first collect method-level source code and comments from nine open-source projects to construct a large method-level technical debt dataset, containing 103,006 validated Java methods, all of which have undergone thorough manual verification. Afterward, we use the dataset to train a deep learning model combining Convolutional Neural Network and Transformer for method-level TD detection, integrating local syntactic features with global contextual dependencies from code snippets to enhance accuracy and robustness. Experimental results demonstrate our approach achieves state-of-the-art performance, with precision of 83.26%, recall of 80.84%, and F1-score of 81.92%. This work provides developers with actionable code quality improvement suggestions through precise TD localization at the method level. Copyright © 2026. Published by Elsevier B.V.

Title: Determinants of Maternal Adaptation to Childhood Vaccination in 21st-Century Southernmost Thailand
Source title: Journal of Population and Social Studies
Abstract: This study investigates maternal behavioral adaptation toward childhood immunization within the sociocultural context of Southernmost Thailand, evaluating how individual capacities and contextual correlates influence vaccination completion. A quantitative cross-sectional survey was conducted among 1,200 mothers of children aged five years or older in Pattani, Yala, and Narathiwat. Using a three-stage, stratified, multi-stage random sampling technique, geographic and demographic representativeness was ensured. Data were collected via structured interviews using a validated instrument (IOC ≥ 0.60), and binary logistic regression was employed to identify significant predictors of immunization adherence. Results indicated a childhood vaccination completion rate of 63.7%. Multivariate analysis revealed that maternal adaptation was strongly driven by socio-economic stability and modern health literacy. Mothers with stable socio-demographic profiles, particularly government officials (OR = 7.98; 95% CI [2.67, 23.81]) and business owners (OR = 6.74; 95% CI [2.54, 17.87]), had significantly higher odds of completing. High service satisfaction (OR = 4.39; 95% CI [3.09, 6.23]) and maternal COVID-19 vaccination history (OR = 3.28; 95% CI [1.53, 4.22]) emerged as robust positive predictors. Conversely, specific contextual determinants, including paternal decision-making authority and vaccine safety anxiety, significantly hindered adherence, reflecting the enduring influence of traditional patriarchal structures. The persistent disparity in Southernmost Thailand is driven by a complex interplay between modern enablers and traditional constraints. Strictly medical or economic approaches are insufficient to address this variation in uptake, as barriers are deeply rooted in the region’s unique sociocultural and structural scaffolding. Title: SCOPE: Sequential Causal Optimization of Process Interventions
Abstract: Prescriptive Process Monitoring (PresPM) recommends interventions during running business processes to optimize key performance indicators (KPIs). In realistic settings, interventions are rarely isolated: organizations need to align sequences of interventions to jointly steer the outcome of a case. Existing PresPM approaches only partially address this challenge. Many focus on a single intervention decision, while others treat multiple interventions independently, ignoring how they interact over time. Methods that do address these dependencies depend either on simulation or data augmentation to approximate the process to train a Reinforcement Learning (RL) agent, which may create a reality gap and introduce bias. We introduce SCOPE (Sequential Causal Optimization of Process Interventions), a PresPM approach that learns aligned sequential intervention recommendations. SCOPE employs backward induction to estimate the effect of each candidate intervention action, propagating its impact from the final decision point back to the first. By leveraging causal learners, our method can utilize observational data directly, unlike methods that require constructing process approximations for RL. Experiments on both an existing synthetic dataset and a new semi-synthetic dataset show that SCOPE consistently outperforms state-of-the-art PresPM techniques in optimizing the KPI. The novel semi-synthetic setup, based on a real-life event log, is provided as a reusable benchmark for future work on sequential PresPM. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: When ethical signaling amplifies technological harm: Hypocrisy-based amplification of corporate digital responsibility on artificial intelligence hallucination and sustainable innovation
Abstract: Based on the social construction of technology perspective, we examine how generative artificial intelligence (AI) hallucination undermines sustainable business model innovation (SBI) and competitive advantage by weakening the transactive memory system. In Study 1, we analyze cross-sectional data from 201 hotels in Eastern China. In Study2, we analyze multiwave, multisource data from 205 hotels in Western China. After testing a hypocrisy-based amplification mechanism, we find that corporate digital responsibility is at a high level and that the negative indirect effect of generative AI hallucination on SBI and competitive advantage is significantly strengthened. This occurs because organizational members perceive a pronounced inconsistency between external digital ethics and internal knowledge integrity. Authors: Ro E.; Powell E.E.; Baker T.
Title: Who will I be? Refugee entrepreneurship and founder identity
Abstract: We conducted a 27-month field study of 23 North Korean Defector (NKD) founders. Founders responded in three different ways to the disparaging default social identities they encountered by self-categorizing into three “avowed” social identities, which served as aspirations for how they would build their ventures. Founders generated sensemaking narratives that explained their behavior – to themselves and to others – by anchoring on the past, present, or future circumstances and claiming individual capabilities to build their ventures. The resulting ventures were characterized by distinctive missions, branding, and hiring preferences and therefore by patterned differences in the roles founders played. We contribute to scholarly understanding of refugee entrepreneurship by showing that the ways in which refugee founders respond to being in a new country and constructing new identities is more varied – because it is embedded in their responses to local social evaluations – than prior research has portrayed. We contribute to the development of founder identity theory (FIDT) by expanding prior understanding of how social identities drive founder role creation. Overall, we show the extension of refugee founder agency as they move from self-categorizing into avowed social identities to embedding themselves in the concrete social relations required to perform a role. © 2026 Elsevier Inc.

Title: Cultural–relational identity in digital loyalty formation: Insights from fandom and the Korean Wave in emerging markets
Abstract: This study develops and empirically validates the concept of Cultural-Relational Identity (CRI) to explain how relational trust and cultural belonging interact in shaping e-customer loyalty within digitally mediated fandom environments. Drawing on Relationship Marketing Theory (RMT) and Social Identity Theory (SIT), the study proposes that loyalty in cultural communities emerges from the structural integration of engagement, identity, and relational commitment rather than from isolated psychological mechanisms. Within digital fandom ecosystems, repeated interactions, shared cultural meanings, and collective participation create a relational environment in which individuals develop a sense of belonging that reinforces loyalty toward digital platforms and cultural products. Data were collected from 350 Indonesian K-pop fans, representing one of the most active digital fandom communities in Southeast Asia. The data were analyzed using Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling (PLS-SEM), complemented by mediation analysis and multi-group analysis to assess the robustness of the proposed relationships. The results show that social media engagement and fandom participation significantly influence both cultural engagement and e-customer loyalty. Cultural engagement partially mediates these relationships, providing empirical support for the integrative mechanism proposed by the CRI framework. These findings indicate that loyalty in digital fandom environments is reinforced not only through interaction intensity but also through the shared cultural identity that develops through community participation. The structural model explains 57.3% of the variance in e-customer loyalty, indicating a moderate-to-substantial explanatory capacity. Multi-group analysis further reveals that gender and fandom intensity moderate several structural paths, highlighting boundary conditions in the CRI mechanism. Additional assessments confirm that common method bias does not materially affect the results. The study contributes theoretically by conceptualizing Cultural-Relational Identity as an ecosystem-based integration of relational and cultural processes. Managerially, the findings emphasize the importance of culturally resonant engagement strategies to sustain digital loyalty in emerging markets. Copyright (c) 2026 The Authors. Title: Environmental performance feedback and green innovation: The moderating role of organizational slack
Abstract: Prior research has highlighted a variety of external and internal drivers of green innovation (GI), yet much less is known about how firms interpret their own environmental performance and adjust GI strategies accordingly. Using panel data from Chinese publicly listed firms, the results reveal a U-shaped relationship between performance below aspirations and GI, and an inverted U-shaped relationship when performance exceeds aspirations. Title: Employee knowledge and smart technology adoption: Evidence from the E-waste sector
Abstract: Smart technologies are increasingly introduced in workplaces, yet employees do not always translate positive evaluations into technology adoption. This study examines how different forms of employee knowledge shape persuasion toward smart technologies and how employee engagement conditions the relationship between persuasion and technology adoption, an area that has received little attention. Drawing on the Diffusion of Innovation (DOI) framework, employee knowledge is conceptualised as a broader domain comprising four theoretically related but empirically distinct first-order dimensions: implicit, explicit, perceptual, and generational knowledge. Survey data from 279 employees in the Sri Lankan e-waste sector were analysed using covariance-based structural equation modelling (CB-SEM) with latent interaction modelling. The results show that implicit, explicit, and perceptual knowledge strengthen employee persuasion, whereas generational knowledge weakens it. However, persuasion alone does not directly lead to the adoption of smart technology in the e-waste sector businesses. Instead, employee engagement positively moderates the persuasion–smart technology adoption relationship, suggesting that engagement helps explain when favourable evaluations are more likely to translate into adoption behaviour. Therefore, mediation analysis indicates a more complex pattern: persuasion showed a negative direct association with smart technology adoption, and the indirect effects suggest a possible context-specific discontinuity between persuasion and reported adoption behaviour rather than a straightforward knowledge-persuasion-smart technology adoption pathway. These findings highlight that employee responses to smart technologies depend not only on knowledge but also on behavioural engagement and implementation conditions, providing new insight into human–technology interaction in workplace digitalisation. © 2026 The Authors

Title: Are corporate venture capital and R&D complements or substitutes? A process view of absorptive capacity
Abstract: While both corporate venture capital (CVC) and R&D are essential vehicles for innovation, the literature has largely overlooked whether and when they act as complements or substitutes in generating firm innovation outcomes. Title: An Unsupervised Contrastive Learning Approach for Cold-Start Question-Answering Systems
Abstract: In the current wave of digital transformation, Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) answering systems have become a key technology for replacing traditional manual customer service and efficiently handling high-frequency user inquiries. This paper focuses on the cold-start phase of FAQ question-answering systems, aiming to ensure that such systems can be effectively initialized under no in-domain labeled data conditions. To this end, we investigate an FAQ question-answering system based on question semantic similarity, specifically designed for the cold-start scenario. To mitigate the anisotropy problem commonly observed in pre-trained language models, we propose an unsupervised text augmentation method to construct high-quality positive samples for contrastive learning. This approach enables the learning of a improved embedding geometry, which serves as a strong foundation for subsequent fine-tuning in low-resource downstream tasks. We refer to this method as LACSE (Large-model Augmented Contrastive Sentence Embeddings). Experimental results demonstrate that LACSE produces higher-quality sentence embeddings and effectively adapts to cold-start requirements across different business scenarios, providing a more robust semantic representation basis for subsequent supervised fine-tuning. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Singapore Pte Ltd. 2027.

Title: Automatic AI-Based Extraction of Processes from Administrative Texts: The Case of Waste Management

Abstract: Public administrations produce large volumes of unstructured administrative documents that regulate operational procedures, responsibilities, and regulatory constraints. Title: BERT-Driven Deep Learning for Enhanced Spam Email Classification with Browser Extension Integration
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: Email volume continues to surge across business, education, and personal use, with spam composing nearly half of global traffic and driving financial and security risks. Classical filters (blacklists, rules, Naive Bayes, k-Nearest Neighbors) and even deep models like BiLSTM struggle to capture full semantics or resist modern evasion. Title: Capital structure adjustments of Hotel SMEs in Portugal's hospitality industry during the COVID-19 pandemic
Abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic triggered an unprecedented economic shock, disrupting business operations and demand across sectors. This study examines the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on the capital structure of small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) in the Portuguese hotel sector, a core segment of the hospitality industry and one of the most severely affected by the crisis. Using a panel dataset of private hotel firms in Portugal, we find a significant reduction in total debt during the pandemic. Decomposing debt by maturity reveals that firms reduced short-term borrowing while expanding long-term financing, indicating a recomposition of the debt structure during the pandemic. Furthermore, when firms are segmented by size, the reduction in total leverage was concentrated among smaller, financially constrained firms, while the expansion in long-term financing was observed among larger, financially unconstrained firms. A further decomposition of total liabilities into financial and operating components reveals that financial and operating liabilities responded in opposite directions during the pandemic: operating liabilities contracted, while financial liabilities, notably long-term financial debt, increased. This study contributes to the literature on capital structure, corporate finance, and crisis management by providing one of the first empirical assessments of COVID-19's effects on SME financing in a tourism-dependent, bank-reliant economy, a context that remains understudied. It also extends prior research by focusing on private rather than public firms. By examining a highly vulnerable sector, the findings offer insights into financial resilience during crises and provide policy implications for improving liquidity access and strengthening financial stability among tourism-dependent hotel SMEs. © 2026 The Authors

Title: An End to End Trustworthiness Evaluation Framework for Enterprise AI Systems
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are becoming integral parts of modern enterprise systems to facilitate intelligent automation, decision-making processes, and enterprise knowledge management at scale. Nowadays, transformer models, such as foundation models and instruction-tuned models, are being integrated into intricate business workflows routinely. While these practices are common, they are still primarily model focused, with a focus on individual measures of performance and a lack of transparency of the operational reliability, accountability, and systemic risk. This difference creates what we call the Fragmented Trust Evaluation Problem, in which existing assessment methods do not support the detection of in-win failures due to the interaction of modules, propagation of errors and lack of traceability. To meet this challenge, we propose a System-Level Trustworthiness Evaluation Framework whose key principles are the introduction of common reliability, provenance coverage, and failure containment metrics for end-to-end application pipelines. Title: Making Sense of Continuous Process Dynamics
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: Operating in dynamic and often unpredictable environments, business processes are exposed to changes that cause their execution to fluctuate over time. Since changes are inseparable parts of process execution, capturing them is crucial for gaining reliable insights into how they behave during their execution. Although prior research has studied continuous fluctuations of processes, most studies have focused primarily on visual representations of such changes. However, drawing more actionable insights requires a structured analysis approach that goes beyond visualization. To this end, this paper explores the potential of leveraging established time series analysis techniques—such as decomposition and correlation analysis—to derive meaningful insights into such changes. We evaluate our approach through backward-looking and forward-looking analysis: the former demonstrates the type of insights it can provide into continuous process dynamics by applying it to multiple event logs, while the latter examines whether the approach is beneficial for a downstream process mining task, the prediction of future process behavior. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Does AI Improve BPMN Modelling? Evidence from Iterative Assignments and Critical Verification Practice
Source title: Lecture Notes in Business Information Processing
Abstract: This paper investigates whether and under what conditions AI assistance improves BPMN modelling in higher education. Building on research in BPM education, active learning, and LLM-assisted modelling, authors designed an iterative two-stage assignment in which students first submitted an initial BPMN model (V1) and then refined it using a rubric-aligned verification checklist, scenario-based test cases, and a shortchange log (V2). A volunteer subgroup additionally produced an AI-assisted alternative final model (V2–AI), accompanied by an AI Usage Statement capturing intentions, verification behaviors, and reasons for accepting or rejecting AI suggestions. Results show substantial learning gains between V1 and V2, particularly in logic-intensive areas such as gateways and events. Error frequencies decreased across most categories, demonstrating the effectiveness of structured scaffolding for guiding iterative improvement. The comparison of V2 and V2–AI reveals heterogeneous outcomes: while some students benefited from AI support, others introduced new inconsistencies when relying uncritically on AI-generated suggestions. Qualitative analysis of AI Usage Statements indicates that critical verification, rather than intensity of AI use, is the key determinant of high-quality AI-assisted modelling. The primary contribution is empirical evidence on learning gains through iterative revision and structured verification. As secondary, exploratory contributions, the study provides: (2) a fine-grained error taxonomy for analysing student process models, and (3) the first paired comparison of human-refined and AI-assisted BPMN models in higher education. The proposed instructional design offers a scalable, responsible approach for integrating critical AI use into BPM education. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: What are the Challenges in High Maturity Organizations
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Abstract: This paper revisits a widely held assumption in the process improvement and maturity model literature: that high maturity organizations face a consistent set of persistent challenges. However, this study tests that assumption empirically through a survey of high maturity organizations, and contrary to expectations, the findings show that ten commonly cited challenges are largely absent in practice. Rather than struggling with rigidity, excessive bureaucracy, or diminishing returns, high maturity organizations report the opposite conditions: increased adaptability, stronger alignment with business goals, more effective use of data, and sustained capability for continuous improvement. These organizations appear to have resolved or transcended the issues highlighted in prior research. For academics, the results call into question the validity and continued relevance of challenges often mentioned in literature. For practitioners, the findings offer a more optimistic and actionable perspective: achieving high maturity may not introduce new systemic barriers, but instead enables more resilient, efficient and responsive ways of working. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Gender Equality in Governance and Social Topics of Italian Sustainability Reports. First Evidence Under the CSRD
Abstract: Gender equality is a key driver in addressing inequalities in business and society while creating value for the broader ecosystem. In governance and management literature, gender diversity is widely recognized as a mechanism that positively affects economic performance, earnings quality and disclosure transparency. However, research on gender equality disclosure within ESG reporting remains limited, despite its growing relevance for competitiveness and sustainability performance. Drawing on legitimacy theory, this study explores how gender equality is disclosed within governance and social topics of sustainability reports and examines whether increased disclosure reflects a genuine commitment to gender-related policies. The analysis is based on content analysis of hand-collected data from 420 nonfinancial reports issued by 105 Italian firms during the transition to the European Sustainability Reporting Standards (ESRSs). The findings reveal an overall improvement in gender equality disclosure related to both sustainable governance and social inclusion. Moreover, recent legislation appears to have enhanced the standardization and comparability of reporting and to have supported women’s participation in governance and social areas. Nonetheless, evidence of the effective implementation of gender equality programs remains limited. The study provides theoretical and practical insights into corporate approaches to gender equality and its integration into sustainability reporting, contributing to the debate on the role of gender equality in strengthening ESG performance in the post-ESRS context. © The Author(s) 2027.

Title: The Impacts on Malaysia’s Logistics, Ports and Shipping Companies in the COVID-19 Pandemic Situation
Source title: SpringerBriefs in Applied Sciences and Technology
Abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic affected global economics, and this economic shock has impacted logistics, ports, and shipping businesses. One of the measures introduced to curb the pandemic with implementation of quarantine that imposed by authorities, limiting the movement of people. This measure affected the operation of logistics ports and the shipping business. Quarantine measures resulted in a decrease in demand for cargoes, directly affecting the demand for logistics services, ports experiencing plunges in container throughput and shipping companies experiencing a reduction in chartering. The pandemic directly affected the performance of logistics, ports and shipping companies and the intention of this research is to rank the performance of Malaysia’s logistics, ports, and shipping companies before and during the COVID-19 pandemic. Conducting this research, it helps to evaluate and understand the impact of the pandemic on these companies’ performance. This research has identified eleven companies listed in Bursa Malaysia that are involved in logistics, ports, and shipping activities. Financial reports from each of these companies were gathered from 2017 to 2021. Data from these financial reports is then separated between the period before COVID-19, from 2017 to 2019, and the period of COVID-19 from 2020 to 2021. Eight financial ratios were identified for evaluation, consisting of current ratios, net profit margin, return on assets, total assets turnover, current assets turnover, debt to asset ratio, debt to equity ratio, and return on equity. The technique of order preference by similarity to ideal solution (TOPSIS) method has been utilised to rank the performance by using these eight financial ratios. Results of the ranking indicate that port operating companies were among top performer companies compared to shipping companies in the period before COVID-19 and during COVID-19. It also found that logistics companies that were involved with consumer logistics performed better compared to companies involved with project logistics within both periods. It was found that shipping companies were not performing in ranking compared to logistics and port companies. This research also found that shipping companies involved in the oil and gas energy sector performed better compared to those in other sectors. Future research is recommended to study the effect of Malaysia’s logistics, ports, and shipping companies in regard to the post-COVID-19 pandemic. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Commercial or relational cues: how information salience in project titles affects crowdfunding performance
Abstract: Scholars have paid considerable attention to factors that could influence crowdfunding performance. However, whether or how the salience of information in project titles may affect crowdfunding performance remains unknown. To address this research gap, we examine 2,064 startups that sought funding on the Kaishiba crowdfunding platform. We find that market validation information in a project title is positively correlated with crowdfunding performance, whereas low psychological distance information is negatively associated with crowdfunding performance. We reveal that the influence of project title information on crowdfunding performance is moderated by the gender of entrepreneurs. Specifically, projects will more (less) likely be funded when entrepreneurs provide information that is congruent (incongruent) with stereotypes associated with their gender. Title: Online Resource-Aware Process Configuration with Uncertain Arrivals and Stochastic Resource Consumption
Abstract: Business processes are often executed in multiple variants, which affect operational costs and the consumption of shared resource capacities. We study an online planning problem in which process instances arrive sequentially and must be configured irrevocably upon arrival under horizon-wide resource capacity constraints. For example, in a hospital, an unknown number of patients arrive sequentially during a shift. The patient’s diagnosis consumes capacity of available resources and the resources then chosen for allocation, in turn, affect the resulting control flow configuration for this patient. We formulate the problem as an online integer program (IP) with a fixed configuration space and model uncertainty through (i) a random number of arrivals and (ii) stochastic, positive resource consumptions revealed upon arrival; costs are modeled as a weighted sum of consumed workload, reflecting processing time, and thus are also stochastic. We assess rolling-horizon and resource-pricing (primal-dual) approaches and compare them with simple heuristics and the optimal ex post solution. We instantiate the framework for a hospital diagnostics data set. Using distribution estimates based on this data, we evaluate online decision policies under robustness perturbations. The findings show that optimization-based policies that account for remaining capacities and expected demand substantially improve throughput and resource utilization under uncertain arrivals. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Inside-out and outside-in: How digital capabilities and environmental dynamism shape AI adoption in SMEs
Abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly transforming the competitive landscape, yet small and medium enterprises (SMEs) vary considerably in whether and how they adopt AI technologies. While prior research has focused on the drivers of AI adoption, it has largely overlooked the interplay between internal capabilities and external pressures and has treated adoption behavior as homogeneous across firms. Addressing this gap, we develop and test a model that explains both the level and heterogeneity of AI adoption through the lenses of dynamic capabilities and strategic fit. Using survey data from 616 Russian SMEs across sectors, we find that digital capabilities and environmental dynamism independently promote AI adoption, but their interaction produces a stronger and more consistent response. Our heteroskedasticity-based analysis shows that each factor independently increases variability in adoption behavior. We also find tentative evidence that the alignment of digital capabilities and environmental dynamism is associated with lower heterogeneity in AI adoption, suggesting that capability–context congruence may promote more consistent adoption behavior. By showing that capability-context alignment may shape both the average level and the dispersion of AI adoption, this study moves AI adoption and digital transformation research beyond mean-centric explanations and clarifies when firms converge on similar AI responses versus diverge in how intensively they adopt AI. Title: Cognitive framing and affective expressions of green economic growth: Evidence from social media analytics
Abstract: Green growth has become an important pathway for reconciling economic development with environmental sustainability, increasing the need to understand how it is discussed and evaluated across digital communication environments. This study examines the cognitive and affective dimensions of stakeholder-related online discourse on green growth using social media analytics. The final analytical dataset comprises 1799 English-language posts collected from LinkedIn, Reddit, TikTok, Twitter/X, and YouTube. The methodological framework integrates lexicon-based sentiment and emotion analysis, Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) topic modelling, correspondence analysis, and non-parametric statistical testing. The sentiment analysis indicates a predominantly positive lexical orientation, although validation results suggest that individual-level sentiment classifications should be interpreted cautiously. LDA topic modelling, conducted on 1792 posts retained after vocabulary filtering, identifies three principal thematic domains interpreted as textual proxies for cognitive framing: Sustainable Development and ESG Transition (29.97%), Climate, Energy and Net-Zero Transition (44.64%), and Circular Economy and Sustainable Business Practices (25.39%). Emotion profiles differ significantly across thematic domains, while cross-platform analysis reveals systematic variation in sentiment, emotional expression, and thematic composition. Correspondence analysis further indicates platform-specific associations between social media environments and thematic domains. Overall, the findings demonstrate systematic associations between thematic framing and affective expression in green growth-related online discourse, while avoiding causal interpretation of these relationships. The study contributes to sustainability communication research by integrating cognitive and affective dimensions within a multi-platform analytical framework and provides practical insights for designing context-sensitive green communication strategies. © 2026 The Authors.

Title: BRIDGE: A Bayes-Risk-Informed Process Decoder for Suffix Prediction
Abstract: In Predictive Process Monitoring, activity suffix prediction predicts the remaining sequence of activities given a prefix. As a multi-step sequence prediction task with many plausible suffixes, decoding is critical to predictive accuracy. However, the performance of existing decoding strategies is highly dataset-dependent, and no method is consistently reliable. A key limitation is a recurring mismatch between how suffixes are selected during decoding and how prediction quality is evaluated: current approaches typically rely on likelihood to guide decoding, without explicitly accounting for sequence-level prediction error. In this work, we characterize this mismatch and propose BRIDGE, a Bayes-risk-informed decoding framework that samples candidate suffixes and ranks them by expected quality under the evaluation metric, thereby aligning decoding more closely with the task objective. As a post-training inference-time method, it can be applied across predictive models without retraining. We evaluate BRIDGE on eight real-life event logs against multiple decoding strategies and established suffix prediction models. BRIDGE is consistently competitive and often best-performing, with particularly strong gains on logs with long traces and for simple statistical models. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Co-designing Alternatives of Adaptive Reuse: The Case of the Church of the Holy Name of Jesus in Moncalieri
Abstract: This paper presents a participatory co-design process focused on the adaptive reuse of the Chiesa del SS. Nome di Gesù, a deconsecrated church in the historic centre of Moncalieri, Northern Italy, developed within the PRIN TREE 2022 research project on circular economy models for architectural heritage reuse. Title: Family ownership, performance below aspiration levels and signaling strategies in emerging markets
Abstract: Advertising and CSR constitute the two key signaling strategies for family firms in emerging markets to attract new stakeholders and investors and to retain existing ones. However, the preference of family owners for these strategies may shift based on firm performance. We combine Signaling Theory with the Behavioral Theory of the Firm to examine how family ownership influences these strategies and whether these preferences shift when firms perform below aspiration levels. Title: Serendipity and innovation in new ventures: The moderating role of primary investor type
Abstract: Rather than pure luck or a fully planned search, opportunities in new ventures frequently emerge from serendipitous discoveries. While research has emphasized the antecedents of serendipity, empirical evidence on its innovation outcomes remains scarce. Drawing on social cognitive theory, we argue that serendipity’s value depends on environmental conditions, which shape whether unexpected discoveries are recognized and translated into venture-level action. Analyzing survey data from 386 founders and CXOs of new ventures in Western and Northern Europe, we find that serendipity is positively associated with innovation radicalness and speed. These relationships are contingent on investor type: Compared with bootstrapped ventures, the positive associations are weaker in ventures backed by venture capitalists, business angels, or family and friends. These findings advance our understanding of serendipity’s contingent value in early-stage entrepreneurship and highlight investor dynamics as a boundary condition shaping innovation trajectories. Title: Reimagining Knowledge Management Education in South Africa for the Artificial Intelligence Era
Source title: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Abstract: Knowledge Management (KM) education in South Africa has developed unevenly across higher education institutions, frequently embedded within Library and Information Science, Information Systems, or Business disciplines rather than institutionalised as a coherent professional qualification. Building on the integrated five-perspective KM curriculum framework developed from a South African perspective [1], this paper argues that the rapid emergence of artificial intelligence (AI), particularly generative AI, has shifted the epistemic conditions of KM education from repository-centric management toward AI-mediated knowledge ecosystems. While the integrated model remains structurally foundational, it does not explicitly theorise AI as an epistemic co-actor in knowledge processes. The paper reconceptualizes KM education by treating AI as a mediator in knowledge processes, embedding governance and assessment integrity as core curriculum requirements, and positioning Indigenous Knowledge Systems as equal knowledge pillars rather than contextual additions. Anchored in South Africa’s higher education transformation landscape and AI governance trajectory, the paper proposes an AI-mediated KM epistemology framework, maps curriculum implications across the five perspectives, and presents a phased implementation roadmap for South African universities [5]. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Cognitive Effects of Using LLMs for Process Modeling: An EEG Study
Abstract: We investigate the cognitive effects of using large language models (LLMs) for BPMN process modeling. Participants were divided into two groups – a group with AI assistance (“LLM group”) and a group that had to model manually (“brain-only group”) – and were then asked to create a BPMN process model in the respective setting. Our results indicate significant differences in brain activities for the two groups, in particular, LLM users exhibited strongly reduced active cognitive engagement across multiple EEG measures such as theta power, alpha power and frontal alpha asymmetry. Furthermore, a post-experiment survey one week after the laboratory session also revealed that participants who used the LLM showed significantly lower memory and ownership of the model they had created. Title: An LLM-Based Agentic Framework for Industrial Forecasting Workflows
Abstract: Demand forecasting at Amazon Devices requires predicting demand for hundreds of ASINs (Amazon Standard Identification Numbers) across regions and channels to support inventory, supply chain, and pricing decisions under strong business pressure to reduce cost, increase sales, and react quickly to changes in consumer behavior. Existing workflows rely on manual, bespoke pipelines for data exploration, feature engineering, model selection, and evaluation, which limits experiment throughput and reuse. A central LLM-based orchestrator plans and executes end-to-end workflows by invoking MCP tools for profiling, EDA, feature engineering, model training, and evaluation, including specialized agent skills that compute the M5 competition metric and internal business metrics such as wMAPE and bias. On the M5 benchmark and analogous internal workloads, the agentic pipeline achieves forecast quality close to strong manual baselines while substantially outperforming an AutoML baseline, at a fraction of the expert effort required for manual pipelines. Title: Environmental values, climate awareness and willingness to pay for green savings: The direct and moderating effect of perceived greenwashing
Abstract: The transition to a low-carbon economy depends critically on mobilizing household savings toward green financial products. Using a survey experiment on a representative sample of 1061 French adults, we examine how perceived greenwashing shapes willingness to pay for a green savings account and whether environmental impact disclosures influence it. We find that individuals are, on average, unwilling to pay a premium to green their savings, and that willingness to pay does not increase when the stated environmental impact is scaled up. Perceived greenwashing plays a dual role: it directly reduces willingness to pay and moderates the relationship between pro-environmental attitudes and financial behavior. Green consumption values raise willingness to pay only when sustainability claims are perceived as credible; climate awareness follows the same pattern. When perceived greenwashing is high, these relationships become statistically insignificant, even among environmentally motivated individuals. At the individual level, willingness to pay declines with subjective financial literacy, whereas climate-related emotions play no robust role. These results suggest that impact disclosure alone is insufficient to shift household financial behavior, and that the perceived credibility of environmental claims is a necessary condition for translating pro-environmental values into green financial choices. © 2026 Elsevier B.V. Title: Shaping sustainable investment through digital technologies: Strategic perspectives for the transformation era
Abstract: This paper examines the importance of technological infrastructure in influencing sustainable investment, with particular reference to gross fixed capital formation (GFCF) and foreign direct investment (FDI). We use principal component analysis (PCA) and data envelopment analysis (DEA) to uncover the structural interdependences among digital readiness, innovation capacity and macroeconomic stability. Countries that are identified as DEA-efficient, with high internet penetration, extensive mobile uptake and strong high-tech exports, are consistently receiving greater investment. Inflation impacts economies in different ways, it prevents capital accumulation in less efficient economies and it helps promote investment in more efficient economies. This highlights the importance of context sensitive macroeconomic strategies. Unemployment is still a big hurdle to sustainable investment, limiting GFCF and FDI especially in economies with structural rigidities. The outlier analysis identifies Vietnam, China and Malta as examples of ICT-driven investment resilience, while Sudan illustrates how structural and labor-market constraints can impede capital accumulation despite moderate digital progress. A robust digital infrastructure, innovation capacity and a stable macroeconomic and labor-market are essential to sustain competitive investment strategies. This alignment of factors strategically promotes inclusive growth and long-term investment resilience in countries. It provides actionable guidance to policy makers and business leaders to advance sustainable economic development. © 2026

Title: Scale and space in industrial policy implementation: Geospatial evidence from urban Ethiopia
Abstract: Industrial policy in Africa has regained prominence, yet many registered manufacturing investments do not progress to production. This study examines the spatial patterning and correlates of implementation using a field-verified geospatial census of 2277 manufacturing projects in Shaggar City, Ethiopia. Projects were classified into five ordered implementation categories: Not Implemented, Abandoned, Under Construction, Construction Completed, and Operational. Ordered logistic regression was used to examine associations with network distance from Addis Ababa's central business district (CBD), firm size, industrial subsector, and distance to former town centers. In the primary specification, greater distance from the CBD was negatively associated in the primary ordinal specification with lower cumulative odds of being in a higher implementation category (OR = 0.921, 95% CI: 0.901–0.942, p < 0.001). The distance association was nonlinear in supplementary specifications, although its precise form varied across model formulations. Residual diagnostics, however, indicated substantial spatial autocorrelation across all four cumulative thresholds (Moran's I, p < 0.001), limiting the extent to which conventional model-based uncertainty can be interpreted as spatially independent inference. Distance to former town centers showed evidence of stage-specific association, concentrated at earlier implementation transitions. Firm size was also associated with implementation status in the primary ordinal model, with large projects having lower cumulative odds than small projects; this association weakened after adjustment for project timing and was directionally reversed in a binary multilevel sensitivity model. The latter model accounted for sub-city clustering but produced a non-positive-definite Hessian and is therefore treated as indicative rather than confirmatory. Missing firm-size information was spatially patterned, with missing records more common near the metropolitan core and among projects with higher operational rates. These findings show that manufacturing implementation is a spatially structured, multi-stage process and that observed associations depend on how implementation stage, project timing, missing information, and spatial dependence are handled. The study highlights the value of field-verified project-level data for distinguishing registered investment from actual implementation and for identifying where different stages of the implementation process may require closer monitoring and support. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd

Title: Copy That? The Influence of Process Model Representation Format on LLM Comprehension
Abstract: LLMs are increasingly applied across the business process management (BPM) lifecycle, e.g., for analyzing or documenting processes. How reliably they support these applications depends on how well they comprehend the underlying process model. In practice, the same process model may be provided to an LLM in different ways, e.g., as a structured serialization or a rendered diagram. However, it is unclear whether and to what extent the choice of representation format affects comprehension. We address this gap with a systematic study that assesses comprehension through interpretation quality, i.e., the graded correctness of task responses. We compare the representation formats of the same process model in three categories: natural-language text, rendered diagrams, and structured serializations. This yields four isolated formats (textual narrative, PNG, BPMN-XML, Mermaid) and selected hybrid combinations, all derived from a common set of BPMN models. We evaluate these format configurations across six LLMs, eight processes, and eleven task types. An LLM-as-a-judge scores responses against reference answers using a graded metric and an error taxonomy. The results show that the representation format substantially affects interpretation quality, with no single format being best across all LLMs. The isolated PNG is consistently the weakest, while hybrid combinations of natural-language text with BPMN-XML or Mermaid emerge as the strongest formats overall. These findings establish the representation format as a design variable for LLM-supported BPM tasks and yield implications for its selection. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Adoption of Battery Electric Trucks: A Review on Transport Companies’ Perspectives

Title: Bridging the AI Adoption Gap: A Practitioner Framework for Non-technical Decision Makers: The CREATE Framework for Strategic AI Implementation
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: Despite significant advances in artificial intelligence capabilities, organizational AI adoption remains considerably slower than technological readiness would predict. This study addresses the adoption gap—the disconnect between AI’s technical potential and its practical deployment in non-technical organizational contexts—and frames it as a problem of organizational change, decision-making support, and responsible AI governance rather than one of algorithmic performance. Drawing on a structured retrospective analysis of 214 AI implementation engagements documented over four years (2021–2025) with business leaders, nonprofit executives, and other organizational decision-makers, we present the CREATE Framework: a systematic, six-stage decision-making methodology designed to enable non-technical leadership to evaluate, select, and deploy AI solutions strategically. The framework comprises six stages: Customer (problem-first orientation), Research (structured landscape assessment), Expand/Narrow (divergent–convergent ideation), Assemble (strategic technology portfolio construction), Test (rapid validation protocols), and Expand (scalable deployment strategies). The study’s contribution is integrative rather than algorithmic: (1) an explicit data-readiness gate sequenced before technology selection, (2) operational accessibility criteria that keep each stage executable by leaders without data-science training, and (3) a responsible-AI overlay embedding ethics, fairness, and governance checkpoints within every stage rather than treating them as a separate workstream. We validate the framework through three pilot case studies with matched baseline conditions and operationally defined outcome metrics: adoption time, a seven-item stakeholder alignment index, and a four-criterion implementation success rubric. Across the pilots, framework-guided projects reached sustained deployment at the six-month mark, with a mean adoption time 55% shorter than matched baselines. We argue that the primary bottleneck to AI value realization is not algorithmic performance but organizational readiness, leadership capability, and the integration of responsible-AI practice into everyday technology adoption decisions. © The Author(s), under exclusive license to Springer Nature Switzerland AG 2027.

Title: Human-Centered AI in Live Streaming: A Developer’s Perspective
Abstract: With AI technology more often being introduced to the masses with the help of live-streaming platforms and tools; it is most essential to know how developers take into consideration the hu-man-centered principles when coming up with these systems. Title: Modularization Barriers and Barrier Breakers in Capital Projects
Abstract: Modularization is an execution strategy that transfers work from the project site to an offsite location for improved project performance. It is expected to have significant growth and wide acceptance, leading to enhanced productivity and competitiveness of capital projects. However, many practitioners in capital projects are still unfamiliar with modularization and resist changing from a traditional approach. The implementations have been limited to lower levels of modularization (e.g., prefabs or pipe racks) and lower extents of modularization. Although previous research has investigated barriers to modular/offsite construction in residential and commercial sectors, there is a lack of studies identifying barriers specific to capital projects (including but not limited to petrochemical plants, manufacturing plants, power generation facilities, and mining operations). Thus, this study focuses on identifying barriers to modularization implementation and proposing solutions to break these barriers in capital projects. First, 33 barriers were identified through iterative sessions with the Construction Industry Institute (CII) Research Team (RT-396), a panel of 15 subject matter experts averaging more than 15 years of modularization experience and 28 executed modular studies/projects. Subsequently, a survey based on these barriers was distributed to CII member companies, gathering data from experts affiliated with globally leading owner and contractor organizations, who possess an average of 23 years of industry experience and 11 years of specific modular expertise. The results identified nine top-rated barriers: (1) requirement of early scope/design freeze; (2) unavailability of vendor data; (3) noncompelling business cases; (4) exclusion of modularization from initial design; (5) incompatible project delivery methods; (6) owner reluctance; (7) lack of final drivers; (8) insufficient early fabricator involvement; and (9) lack of project standardization. These findings contribute to the management-in-engineering body of knowledge by showing that modularization adoption in capital projects is constrained primarily by front-end managerial and organizational conditions rather than by technical concerns alone. Title: The Readiness Level of Quality 4.0 Among German Medium-Sized Companies in the Sensor Industry
Source title: Lecture Notes on Data Engineering and Communications Technologies
Abstract: The transformation of manufacturing under Industry 4.0 has introduced the concept of Quality 4.0, which integrates advanced digital technologies—such as data analytics, artificial intelligence, and the Internet of Things (IoT)—into modern quality management systems. This study investigates the readiness level of German medium-sized enterprises operating in the sensor industry to adopt Quality 4.0 principles. The findings indicate that while most companies have adopted automation and digital monitoring systems, the broader application of data-driven decision-making and predictive quality analytics remains limited. Key barriers include insufficient digital competencies, fragmented data infrastructures, and a lack of strategic integration between quality and IT departments. Conversely, companies with a clear digital strategy and leadership commitment demonstrate higher readiness and stronger innovation capabilities. The study contributes to both academic and managerial understanding by presenting a Quality 4.0 readiness framework tailored to the sensor industry. This framework outlines maturity levels, critical success factors, and practical recommendations for advancing toward a fully digitalized and resilient quality management environment. Title: CSR focus under competitive pressure: The role of national institutions
Abstract: How does competitive pressure shape CSR strategy, and does this relationship vary across national institutional contexts? We challenge the prevailing binary framing that competitive pressure either promotes or suppresses CSR by arguing that competition reshapes how firms configure their CSR portfolios, not merely how much they engage. We introduce CSR focus strategy: a firm's selective emphasis on specific CSR dimensions while deliberately de-emphasizing others, allowing simultaneous differentiation and cost-economization through CSR under some conditions. Employing multilevel linear modeling (MLM) on a global dataset of 41 countries comprising 2294 firms from 2002 to 2020, we demonstrate that competitive intensity drives adoption of CSR focus strategy. Critically, this effect is contingent on national market-supporting institutions and firm size, where CSR focus strategies are most pronounced in institutionally weaker environments characterized by limited property rights protection and among smaller firms with limited stakeholder relational capital and opportunities. Further analyses reveal two subtypes, namely CSR excellence and CSR distinction , reflecting different portfolio configurations under competition. By establishing that institutional context shapes firms' CSR portfolio configuration under competition, our study advances international business research and reconciles opposing theoretical positions in the competition-CSR debate. Collectively, these findings extend the emerging portfolio-based view of CSR into the cross-country competitive domain. © 2026 The Author(s).

Abstract: Drawing on the micro-foundations of dynamic capabilities, this study examines the interplay among digital management capability, ethical leadership, and environmental, social, and governance (ESG) performance within E-Business Information Systems. Analyzing survey data from 357 Chinese small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), the results demonstrate that digital management capability positively influences both ESG performance and ethical leadership. Notably, digital management capability positively moderates the ethical leadership—ESG performance link, suggesting that digitally competent ethical leaders are better positioned to drive sustainability. This research extends the micro-foundations perspective by emphasizing the human-specific aspects of digital information systems management. Practically, the findings underscore the need for SMEs to integrate ethical and digital leadership to enhance sustainability in the digital era. © IFIP International Federation for Information Processing 2027.

Title: Exploring the correlation between community empowerment and social innovation in faith-based enterprise: Basis for a university extension program
Abstract: Faith-based enterprises (FBEs) play a pivotal role in community empowerment and social innovation by integrating moral, spiritual, and entrepreneurial principles to address social, economic, and environmental challenges. This study employed a descriptive correlational research design to examine the influence of FBEs on community well-being among 85 residents of Nampicuan, Nueva Ecija. Data were collected via a validated and pilot-tested structured questionnaire (Cronbach’s alpha = 0.87) and analyzed using descriptive statistics and Pearson correlation coefficients. Focus group discussions provided additional contextual insights. Results revealed significant positive correlations between community empowerment and social innovation practices (economic: r = 0.63–0.68; social: r = 0.69–0.73; spiritual: r = 0.78–0.79, p < 0.05), as well as between empowerment and sustainability and mission integrity of FBEs (economic: r = 0.64–0.70; social: r = 0.71–0.75; spiritual: r = 0.70–0.76, p < 0.05). Social innovation variables, particularly entrepreneurial innovation, spiritual leadership, and ethical governance, were strongly associated with sustainability outcomes (r = 0.71–0.82, p < 0.05). These findings indicate that FBEs enhance economic self-reliance, social cohesion, ethical leadership, and innovative capacity, while strengthening organizational sustainability and mission alignment. Based on the results, an extension program integrating faith-driven entrepreneurship, product development, marketing, and capacity-building was developed to address the community’s holistic needs. This study highlights FBEs as transformative hybrid organizations that combine economic activity with social and moral objectives, fostering sustainable social innovation and community well-being. © 2027, Malque Publishing. Title: Analyzing Generation Z Online Purchase Behavior Using Theory of Planned Behavior-Grounded Machine Learning with Explainable Artificial Intelligence
Source title: International Journal of Engineering, Transactions A: Basics
Abstract: Understanding online purchase behavior of Generation Z consumers is critical for e-commerce businesses due to this cohort's strong reliance on digital technologies. Although the Theory of Planned Behavior (TPB) has been widely used to explain consumer purchase intentions and behaviors, prior studies often rely on conventional statistical models or machine learning approaches with limited interpretability, resulting in a gap between predictive accuracy and behavioral explanation. To address this gap, this study proposes a data-driven and explainable framework for analyzing Generation Z online purchase behavior. TPB constructs attitude, subjective norm, and perceived behavioral control are operationalized as predictive features and evaluated using multiple machine learning models. Explainable artificial intelligence techniques, including SHAP and LIME, are employed to interpret model predictions and assess the influence of behavioral factors. Results show that machine learning models, particularly CatBoost, achieve superior predictive performance. Explainability analyses indicate that attitude and perceived behavioral control play a dominant role in shaping self-reported purchase behavior, while subjective norm has a supportive influence. The proposed framework provides actionable insights for targeted marketing and improved decision-making in online retail contexts. ©2027 The author(s). Title: Graduate Unemployment by Field of Study in the Košice Region, Slovakia

Title: Signaling for success in university research funding applications
Abstract: Signaling theory explains how organizations convey credible information under conditions of information asymmetry. Yet, while recent work highlights that signals often interact—reinforcing or substituting—most studies have treated signals as independent and additive, and empirical evidence of configurational interaction patterns remains limited. This study addresses this limitation by examining how multiple institutional signals jointly shape evaluators’ judgments in peer-reviewed university research funding. Using fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA), we identify distinct configurations of capability, reputation, and status signals that lead to both high and low funding success. Title: When Security Meets Ethics: Balancing Control, Privacy, and Trust in Digital Systems

This paper examines how the pursuit of digital security—through practices such as data collection, monitoring, automation, and AI-driven decision-making—often intersects with, and occasionally undermines, the ethical principles of privacy, autonomy, fairness, and transparency. Using ethical frameworks including deontology, consequentialism, and virtue ethics, the study analyzes key challenges such as algorithmic bias, digital surveillance, cybercrime, and digital burnout. It argues that achieving a sustainable balance between control and trust requires not only robust technical protections but also clear institutional policies and user-centered ethical guidelines. Additionally, current systems have trouble understanding natural language inputs or combining unstructured data, like driver complaints, which are important for finding complex problems. Title: NS-S2FM: An auditable neuro-symbolic expert decision system for scenario-aware franchise operations under uncertainty
Abstract: Sports franchise operation provides a high-uncertainty testbed for expert decision systems because competitive performance, market demand, injury exposure, star-player dependency, financial pressure, and league-level events are tightly coupled. This study proposes NS-S2FM, an auditable neuro-symbolic, scenario-aware expert decision system for uncertain franchise operations. The framework turns heterogeneous signals and institutional rules into a decision object that reports an action, a diagnosed scenario, constraint and risk evidence, and an explanation. We evaluate NS-S2FM through controlled simulation, rule-defined franchise profiles, a WNBA 2022–2024 sports-performance and attendance panel with semi-real business variables, ablation analysis, sensitivity analysis, CVaR-style and CPPO-style constrained comparators, explanation-augmented baselines, and statistical evidence checks. The evidence supports three bounded decision-support findings: strong multi-objective DSS behavior in controlled settings, pre-specified operator-preference diagnostic scores under conservative, growth-oriented, and risk-averse scalarizations, and stronger traceability and scenario adaptability in the real-world panel evaluation. Results from the real-world panel also show the intended trade-off: unconstrained and profit-focused baselines remain competitive on short-horizon numerical scores. Evaluation-index sensitivity and constraint-binding analyses make this interpretation scope explicit by showing metric sensitivity and limited feasibility-mask binding. The contribution is an auditable, constraint-aware, and preference-diagnostic DSS mechanism under transparent proxy-based evidence; stronger claims about audited business outcomes, manager-validated usefulness, or organizational intervention effects require future data. © 2026 Elsevier Ltd. Title: Avoiding Digital Disappointment: A Retrospective Study Applying DSM-NPV to a European Shipyard Innovation

Abstract: Investments in digital technologies in engineer-to-order shipyards are often justified with optimistic business cases that emphasize direct costs and early benefits, yet value delivery is frequently delayed by integration and adoption work. This paper applies the DSM–NPV evaluation framework in a retrospective case on the introduction of a pipe spool tracking system within the piping department of a shipyard. The system was introduced to replace fragmented manual status reporting. Title: Cross-Channel effects of online reputation and offline event participation in B2B Platforms: Synergy or Attenuation?
Abstract: This study examines how online reputation and offline event participation jointly relate to seller performance on B2B platforms. Title: Asymmetries in Legal Status and Market Conditions Between Southeast European and Eu Transport Operators
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: The economic and legal disparities between transport operators from Southeast Europe and those based in the European Union significantly influence competitiveness, market access, and operational efficiency within the international transport sector. This paper analyzes the consequences of differing regulatory frameworks, licensing requirements, labor standards, and financial obligations that shape the business environment for non-EU carriers. From an economic perspective, the study examines cost structures, barriers to market entry, competitive pressures, and the resulting asymmetries in service pricing and fleet modernization. Title: Smart Innovations in Biosphere Reserves
Abstract: The paper aims to define the smart innovations in biosphere reserve from the theoretical point of view and subsequently, identify the examples of good practice in their real conditions, based on it summarize the key features of smart innovation in biosphere reserves. Title: Bridging Strategy and Practice of Performance Management in Industrial Enterprise

Abstract: Employee performance management is an important part of business management. However, for effective performance management, it is important not only to have a unified performance management system in place, but also to ensure that the performance management process enables the organizational strategic goals to be met. The study focuses on analyzing the employee performance management system in an industrial enterprise operating in the railway industry. The aim was to evaluate its current settings, identify its strengths and weaknesses, and propose recommendations for its improvement in line with modern trends in human resource management. The research was based on an analysis of professional literature, internal documentation, and interviews with managers. Title: Media reach and the market reaction to negative ESG media stories: do industry affiliation and ESG performance matter?
Abstract: Using an event study of U.S.-listed firms, we examine how media reach conditions the stock market reactions to adverse environmental, social, and governance (ESG) news across firms with different ESG performance and industry affiliations. On average, we find that a one-unit increase in media reach is associated with a decrease of 0.13 percentage points in cumulative abnormal returns, indicating an economically meaningful valuation effect. Further analysis shows that this effect is mainly concentrated among low-ESG firms in controversial industries. For high-ESG firms in these industries, media reach makes stock price declines significantly less severe than for low-ESG firms, indicating a media reach insurance effect. However, unless adverse news receives the highest-reach media coverage, we do not find evidence that high ESG performance provides an overall insurance effect. By identifying media reach as a key moderator, this study refines the ESG insurance hypothesis and clarifies when markets value ESG performance. © 2026 The Author(s). Published by Elsevier Inc. Title: Artificial Intelligence - Driven Supply Chain Green Innovation: Its Impact on Sustainable Development
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: In the context of globalization and rapid technological advancement, traditional supply chains face mounting pressure to address environmental challenges like high energy use, waste, and carbon emissions. Growing sustainability awareness compels firms to innovate. Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a key enabler of green supply chain transformation, offering advanced data processing, pattern recognition, and decision optimization to enhance both efficiency and sustainability. This study examines how AI-driven green innovation affects sustainable development across economic, environmental, and social dimensions. Using a mixed-methods approach—comprising a literature review, enterprise surveys, and case studies—the research quantifies AI’s benefits, including cost savings, lower emissions, and reduced waste, while identifying barriers such as high implementation costs, poor partner coordination, and inadequate infrastructure. Findings indicate that AI significantly advances sustainability by optimizing logistics, improving demand forecasting, cutting energy use, and enabling integration with technologies like blockchain and IoT to boost transparency and resilience. The study contributes theoretically by clarifying how AI fosters green innovation and offers practical guidance for businesses and policymakers to support AI adoption in pursuit of sustainable development goals. Title: Comparative Analysis of Classical and Large-Scale Multilingual Speech Synthesis Models for Saudi Arabic Dialect
Source title: Lecture Notes in Networks and Systems
Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have been recently integrated with the speech modality for enhancing the naturalness and expressiveness of generated speech. Nevertheless, the performance of these LLM-based Text-To-Speech (TTS) models in morphologically rich, dialectally diverse languages such as Arabic has not been extensively discussed yet. In this work, we compare the conventional and LLM approaches for speech synthesis in Saudi Arabia. The fine-tuning set, a proprietary 43-hour single-speaker dataset drawn from Intellas’ internal business recordings and not made publicly available, is used to fine-tune four Text-To-Speech models: the classical Tacotron 2 and three LLM-based architectures, Sesame_CSM_1B, Orpheus_3B, and Spark_TTS_0.5B, which are trained under the same fine-tuning framework for methodological consistency. Evaluation included automatic metrics such as Word Error Rate (WER), Character Error Rate (CER), and accuracy, along with similarity scores, which are calculated based on Intella Voice Speech-To-Text (STT) model, and the agreement by native Saudi speakers through perceptual listening tests. Moreover, Statistical analysis via paired t-tests (N = 3322 utterances) revealed highly significant performance differences (p< 0.001) between LLM-based models and classical architectures across all automatic evaluation metrics. Experiments showed that LLM-based models (Spark_TTS_0.5B & Orpheus_3B) performed better in terms of intelligibility and prosody, with a WER of 23.4% ± 0.19 (t = – 39.51, p< 0.001) *** & 28.1% ± 0.21 (t = – 29.14, p< 0.001) *** and hence a CER of 11% ± 0.12 (t = – 33.15, p< 0.001) *** & 14.3% ± 0.14 (t = – 24.52, p< 0.001) ***, than the fine-tuned Tacotron 2 (baseline), which achieved a WER of 44.3% ± 0.24 and a CER of 25% ± 0.20.
